questions.question: To enter a constant-airspeed descent from level-cruising flight, and maintain cruising airspeed, the pilot should

answers.A: first adjust the pitch attitude to a descent using the attitude indicator as a reference, then adjust the power to maintain the cruising airspeed.
answers.B: first reduce power, then adjust the pitch using the attitude indicator as a reference to establish a specific rate on the VSI.
answers.C: simultaneously reduce power and adjust the pitch using the attitude indicator as a reference to maintain the cruising airspeed.

explanations.A:
because airspeed will increase if you
adjust the pitch attitude first.
explanations.B:
because airspeed will decrease if you
first reduce power. You use the airspeed, not vertical speed,
indicator to maintain a constant airspeed.
explanations.C:
To enter a constant-airspeed descent from
level cruising flight and maintain cruising airspeed, you should
simultaneously reduce the power smoothly to the desired setting
and reduce the pitch attitude slightly by using the attitude
indicator as a reference to maintain the cruising airspeed.

questions.question: To level off at an airspeed higher than the descent speed, the addition of power should be made, assuming a 500 FPM rate of descent, at approximately

answers.A: 50 to 100 feet above the desired altitude.
answers.B: 100 to 150 feet above the desired altitude.
answers.C: 150 to 200 feet above the desired altitude.

explanations.A:
because, to level off at descent airspeed,
not a higher airspeed, lead the desired altitude by approximately
50 to 100 ft.
explanations.B:
To level off from a descent at an airspeed
higher than the descent speed, it is necessary to start the level-off
before reaching the desired altitude. At 500 fpm, an effective
practice is to lead the desired altitude by approximately 100 to
150 ft. above the desired altitude. At this point, add power to the
appropriate level flight cruise setting.
explanations.C:
because 150 to 200 ft. above the desired
altitude is not a lead point when descending at 500 fpm.

questions.question: To level off from a descent maintaining the descending airspeed, the pilot should lead the desired altitude by approximately

answers.B: 50 feet.
answers.C: 60 feet.
answers.A: 20 feet.

explanations.A:
because you should lead the desired
altitude by approximately 50 ft., not 20 ft., when leveling off from a
descent at descent airspeed.
explanations.B:
To level off from a descent at descent
airspeed, lead the desired altitude by approximately 50 ft.,
simultaneously adjusting the pitch attitude to level flight and
adding power to a setting that will hold airspeed constant. Trim
ff the control pressures and continue with the normal
straight-and-level flight cross-check.
explanations.C:
because you should lead the desired

altitude by approximately 50 ft., not 60 ft, when leveling off from a
descent at descent airspeed.

questions.question: While cruising at 160 knots, you wish to establish a climb at 130 knots. When entering the climb (full panel), it is proper to make the initial pitch change by increasing back elevator pressure until the

answers.A: attitude indicator, airspeed, and vertical speed indicate a climb.
answers.B: vertical speed indication reaches the predetermined rate of climb.
answers.C: attitude indicator shows the approximate pitch attitude appropriate for the 130-knot climb.

explanations.A:
because, for the predetermined climb
speed, the adjustment should be to the climb attitude, not just a
climb indication on the instruments.
explanations.B:
because the airspeed is predetermined,
i.e., constant climb speed, not constant climb rate.
explanations.C:
To enter a constant-airspeed climb from
cruising air-speed, raise the miniature aircraft in the attitude
indicator to the approximate nose-high indication appropriate to
the predetermined climb speed. The attitude will vary according
to the type of airplane you are flying. Apply light elevator back
pressure to initiate and maintain the climb attitude. The amount of
back pressure will increase as the airplane decelerates.

questions.question: While cruising at 190 knots, you wish to establish a climb at 160 knots. When entering the climb (full panel), it would be proper to make the initial pitch change by increasing back elevator pressure until the

answers.B: attitude indicator, airspeed, and vertical speed indicate a climb.
answers.C: airspeed indication reaches 160 knots.
answers.A: attitude indicator shows the approximate pitch attitude appropriate for the 160-knot climb.

explanations.A:
To enter a constant-airspeed climb from
cruising air speed, raise the miniature aircraft in the attitude
indicator to the approximate nose-high indication appropriate to
the predetermined climb speed. The attitude will vary according
to the type of airplane you are flying. Apply light elevator back
pressure to initiate and maintain the climb attitude. The required
back pressure will increase as the airplane decelerates.
explanations.B:
because, for the predetermined climb
speed, you make the adjustment to the climb attitude, not just a
climb indication on the instruments.
explanations.C:
because you make an initial pitch
adjustment, not an increasing adjustment; i-e., airspeed will
decrease gradually.

questions.question: What is the first fundamental skill in attitude instrument flying?

answers.B: Instrument cross-check.
answers.C: Instrument interpretation.
answers.A: Aircraft control.

explanations.A:
because the third, not first, fundamental
skill in attitude instrument flying is aircraft control. Aircraft control

is composed of three components: pitch, bank, and power
control.
explanations.B:
The first fundamental skill in attitude
instrument flying is instrument cross-check. Cross-checking is the

Continuous and logical observation of instruments for attitude and
performance information.
explanations.C:
because the second, not first,
fundamental skill in attitude instrument flying is instrument
interpretation. For each maneuver, you must know the
performance to expect and the combination of instruments that

you must interpret in order to control airplane attitude during the
maneuver.

questions.question: What are the three fundamental skills involved in attitude instrument flying?

answers.A: Instrument interpretation, trim application, and aircraft control.
answers.B: Cross-check, instrument interpretation, and aircraft control.
answers.C: Cross-check, emphasis, and aircraft control.

explanations.A:
because trim application is only one
aspect of aircraft control.
explanations.B:
The three fundamental skills involved in all
instrument flight maneuvers are instrument cross-check,
instrument interpretation, and aircraft control. Cross-checking is
the continuous and logical observation of the instruments for
attitude and performance information. Instrument interpretation
requires you to understand each instrument's construction,
operating principle, and relationship to the performance of your
airplane. Aircraft control requires you to substitute instruments for
outside references.
explanations.C:
because emphasis (along with fixation
and omission) are common errors in instrument cross-checking.

questions.question: What is the third fundamental skill in attitude instrument flying?

answers.B: Power control.
answers.C: Aircraft control.
answers.A: Instrument cross-check.

explanations.A:
because instrument cross-check is the
first, not third, fundamental skill in attitude instrument flying.
Cross-checking is the continuous and logical observation of
instruments for attitude and per formance information.
explanations.B:
because power control is only one
component of aircraft control.
explanations.C:
The third fundamental skill in instrument

flying is aircraft control. It consists of pitch, bank, and power
control.

questions.question: What is the correct sequence in which to use the three skills used in instrument flying?

answers.B: Instrument interpretation, cross-check, and aircraft control.
answers.C: Cross-check, instrument interpretation, and aircraft control.
answers.A: Aircraft control, cross-check, and instrument interpretation.

explanations.A:
because aircraft control is the third, not
first, skill used in instrument flying.
explanations.B:
because instrument interpretation is the
second, not first, skill and cross-check is the first, not second,
skill used in instrument fiying.
explanations.C:
The correct sequence in which to use the
three fundamental skills of instrument flying is cross-check,
instrument interpretation, and aircraft control. Although you learn
these skills separately and in deliberate sequence, a measure of
your proficiency in precision flying will be your ability to integrate
these skills into unified, smooth, positive control responses to
maintain any desired flight path.

questions.question: As power is reduced to change airspeed from high to low cruise in level flight, which instruments are primary for pitch, bank, and power, respectively?

because the primary pitch instrument is
the altimeter, not attitude indicator.

because the primary bank instru ment is

the heading indicator, not attitude indicator, and the primary

power instrument is the manifold pressure gauge or tachometer,
not airspeed indicator.
explanations.C:
In straight-and-level flight, when reducing
airspeed from high to low cruise, the primary instrument for pitch
is the altimeter; the primary instrument for bank is the heading
indicator, and the primary instrument for power is the manifold
pressure gauge or tachometer.

because the heading indicator is the
primary, not supporting, bank instrument in a straight climb.

because the heading indicator is the

because the turn coordinator is the
supporting, not primary, bank instrument and the heading

instrument when establishing a standard-rate turn.

because the attitude indicator is a

questions.question: For maintaining level flight at constant thrust, which instrument would be the least appropriate for determining the need for a pitch change?

because, since level flight means a

To maintain level flight at constant thrust,

questions.question: The gyroscopic heading indicator is inoperative. What is the primary bank instrument in unaccelerated straight-and-level flight?

explanations.B:

coordinator is the primary bank instrument in established
standard-rate turns, not in straight flight.

questions.question: What instruments are primary for pitch, bank, and power, respectively, when transitioning into a constant airspeed climb from straight-and-level flight?

because the heading indicator, not

gauge, not airspeed indicator, is primary for power.
explanations.C:
because the attitude indicator, not vertical
speed indicator, is the primary instrument for pitch, and the
heading indicator, not attitude indicator, is primary for bank.

The initial primary bank instrument when
establishing a level standard-rate turn is the attitude indicator.

questions.question: What is the primary bank instrument while transitioning from straight-and-level flight to a standard-rate turn to the left?

answers.B: Heading indicator.
answers.C: Turn coordinator (miniature aircraft).
answers.A: Attitude indicator.

explanations.A:
The initial primary bank instrument when
establishing a level standard-rate of turn is the attitude indicator.
explanations.B:
because the heading indicator is the
primary bank instrument for straight flight.
explanations.C:
because only after the turn is established
does the turn coordinator become the primary bank instrument.

questions.question: What instrument(s) is(are) supporting bank instrument when entering a constant airspeed climb from straight-and-level flight?

answers.A: Heading indicator.
answers.B: Attitude indicator and turn coordinator.
answers.C: Turn coordinator and heading indicator.

explanations.A:
because the heading indicator is the
primary, not supporting, bank instrument for straight flight.
explanations.B:
When entering a constant-airspeed climb
from straight-and-level flight, the primary bank instrument is the

heading indicator. Supporting bank instruments are the turn
coordinator and the attitude indicator.
explanations.C:
because the heading indicator is the
primary, not supporting, bank instrument for straight flight.

questions.question: What is the primary pitch instrument during a stabilized climbing left turn at cruise climb airspeed?

answers.B: VSI.
answers.C: Airspeed indicator.
answers.A: Attitude indicator.

explanations.A:
because the attitude indicator is a
supporting, not primary, pitch instrument in a stabilized climb.
explanations.B:
because the vertical speed indicator is a
supporting, not primary, pitch instrument in a stabilized climb.
explanations.C:
In a climbing left turn at a constant

airspeed, the airspeed indicator is the primary instrument for
pitch once the climb is established.

questions.question: Which instruments are considered to be supporting instruments for pitch during change of airspeed ina level turn?

answers.A: Airspeed indicator and VSI.
answers.B: Altimeter and attitude indicator.
answers.C: Attitude indicator and VSI.

explanations.A:
because the airspeed indicator is a
supporting power, not pitch, instrument during a change of
airspeed ina level turn. It becomes the primary power instrument
as the desired airspeed is reached.
explanations.B:
because the altimeter is the primary, not
supporting, pitch instrument in level flight.
explanations.C:
The supporting instruments for pitch during
‘a change of airspeed in a level turn are the attitude indicator and
the vertical speed indicator. The primary instrument is the
altimeter.

questions.question: Which instrument is considered primary for power as the airspeed reaches the desired value during change of airspeed in a level turn?

answers.B: Attitude indicator.
answers.C: Altimeter.
answers.A: Airspeed indicator.

explanations.A:
The airspeed indicator is the primary
power instrument as the airspeed reaches the desired value
during a change of airspeed in a level turn.
explanations.B:
because the attitude indicator is a
supporting pitch and bank instrument.
explanations.C:
because the altimeter is the primary pitch
instrument.

questions.question: Which instrument indicates the quality of a turn?

answers.B: Heading indicator or magnetic compass.
answers.C: Ball of the turn coordinator.
answers.A: Attitude indicator.

explanations.A:
because the attitude indicator provides
both pitch and bank information.
explanations.B:
because the heading indicator and/or

magnetic compass show current direction and changes in
direction, not quality of a turn.
explanations.C:
The quality (coordination) of a turn relates
to whether the horizontal component of lift balances the
centrifugal force. It is indicated by the ball of the turn coordinator
or the ball in a turn-and-slip indicator. The airplane is neither

slipping nor skidding when the ball is centered, indicating the
desired quality of a turn.

questions.question: As power is increased to enter a 500 feet per minute rate of climb in straight flight, which instruments are primary for pitch, bank, and power respectively?

answers.A: Attitude indicator, heading indicator, and manifold pressure gauge or tachometer.
answers.B: VSI, attitude indicator, and airspeed indicator.
answers.C: Airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, and manifold pressure gauge or tachometer.

explanations.A:
As the power is increased to enter a
constant-rate climb in straight flight, the primary pitch instrument
is the attitude indicator until the vertical speed indicator stabilizes
at the desired rate of climb (then the vertical speed indicator
becomes primary). The primary bank instrument is the heading
indicator. The primary power instrument is the manifold pressure
gauge or tachometer.
explanations.B:
because the vertical speed indicator is
the primary pitch instrument once the constant-rate climb is
established. Also, the manifold pressure gauge, not the airspeed
indicator, is primary for power.
explanations.C:
because the heading indicator, not the
attitude indicator, is primary for bank in straight flight.

questions.question: Fiqure 145 57. (Refer to figure 145.) What is the correct sequence for recovery from the unusual attitude indicated?

answers.A: Reduce power, increase back elevator pressure, and level the wings.
answers.B: Reduce power, level the wings, bring pitch attitude to level flight.
answers.C: Level the wings, raise the nose of the aircraft to level flight attitude, and obtain desired airspeed.

explanations.A:
because the wings should be level before
you increase back pressure to decrease the load factor during

leveling off.
explanations.B:
In Fig. 145, a nose-low attitude is indicated
by a negative vertical speed indicator, high airspeed (i.e., near
Vne), and the airplane below the horizon on the attitude indicator.
For nose-low unusual attitudes, the correct sequence for recovery
is to reduce power to prevent excessive airspeed and loss of
altitude; level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder
pressure to straight flight by referring to the turn coordinator; and
raise the nose to level flight attitude by smooth back elevator
pressure.

b
explanations.C:
because the power should be reduced
first.

questions.question: While recovering from an unusual flight attitude without the aid of the attitude indicator, approximate level pitch attitude is reached when the

answers.A: airspeed and altimeter stop their movement and the VSI reverses its trend.
answers.B: airspeed arrives at cruising speed, the altimeter reverses its trend, and the vertical speed stops its movement.
answers.C: altimeter and vertical speed reverse their trend and the airspeed stops its movement.

explanations.A:
As the rate of movement of the altimeter
and airspeed indicator needles decreases, the attitude is
approaching level flight. When the needles stop and reverse
direction, the aircraft is passing through level flight.
explanations.B:
because the vertical speed indicator will
be lagging, i.e., showing a decrease in vertical movement when
vertical movement has stopped.
explanations.C:
because the rate is only slowing and has
not stabilized when the altimeter reverses its trend; i.e., it must
stop to indicate level flight.

questions.question: Figure 147 59. (Refer to figure 147.) Which is the correct sequence for recovery from the unusual attitude indicated?

answers.A: Level wings, add power, lower nose, descend to original attitude, and heading.
answers.B: Add power, lower nose, level wings, return to original attitude and heading.
answers.C: Stop turn by raising right wing and add power at the same time, lower the nose, and return to original attitude and heading.

explanations.A:
because you should both add power and
lower the nose before you level the wings.
explanations.B:
In Fig. 147, a nose-high attitude is
indicated by the increasing altitude, the rate-of-climb indication
‘on the vertical speed indicator, and the decreasing airspeed. The
correct sequence for recovery is to add power, apply forward
elevator pressure to lower the nose and prevent a stall, level the
wings with coordinated aileron and rudder pressure to straight
flight, and return to original altitude and heading.

«|

b>
explanations.C:
because you should both add power and
lower the nose before you level the wings.

questions.question: if an airplane is in an unusual flight attitude and the attitude indicator has exceeded its limits, which instruments should be relied on to determine pitch attitude before starting recovery?

answers.A: Turn indicator and VSI.
answers.B: Airspeed and altimeter.
answers.C: VSI and airspeed to detect approaching VSI or VMO.

explanations.A:
because the turn indicator indicates
nothing about pitch attitude.
explanations.B:
If the attitude indicator is inoperative, a
nose-low or nose-high attitude can be determined by the
airspeed and altimeter. In a nose-high attitude, airspeed is

decreasing and altimeter is increasing, and vice versa for
nose-low attitudes.
explanations.C:
because the altimeter, not the VSI, is the

primary pitch instrument. Note the FAA answer selection has VSI
and VMO, which should be Vs; and Vo, respectively.

questions.question: Which is the correct sequence for recovery from a spiraling, nose-low, increasing airspeed, unusual flight attitude?

answers.A: Increase pitch attitude, reduce power, and level wings.
answers.B: Reduce power, correct the bank attitude, and raise the nose toa level attitude.
answers.C: Reduce power, raise the nose to level attitude, and correct the bank attitude.

explanations.A:
because the power should be decreased
first, then the wings leveled.
explanations.B:
For nose-low unusual attitudes, one should
reduce the power, level the wings, and then increase the pitch to
raise the nose to a level attitude.
explanations.C:
because the wings should be leveled
before the nose is raised to minimize the load factor.

questions.question: During recoveries from unusual attitudes, level flight is attained the instant

answers.A: the horizon bar on the attitude indicator is exactly overlapped with the miniature airplane.
answers.B: a zero rate of climb is indicated on the VSI.
answers.C: the altimeter and airspeed needles stop prior to reversing their direction of movement.

explanations.A:
because the attitude indicator has a

tendency to precess during an unusual attitude and may not be
Teliable.
explanations.B:
because there is a lag or delay in the

vertical speed indicator. It cannot be relied on for determining the
instant level flight is attained.
explanations.C:
In unusual attitudes, you can determine the
attainment of level flight (not vertical movement) when the
altimeter and airspeed needles stop prior to reversing their
direction of movement.

questions.question: Figure 146 63. (Refer to figure 146.) Identify the system that has failed and determine a corrective action to return the airplane to straight-and-level flight.

answers.A: Static/pitot system is blocked; lower the nose and level the wings to levelfight attitude by use of attitude indicator.
answers.B: Vacuum system has failed; reduce power, roll left to level wings, and pitchup to reduce airspeed.
answers.C: Electrical system has failed; reduce power, roll left to level wings, and raise the nose to reduce airspeed.

explanations.A:
In Fig. 146, the airplane is in a right turn as
indicated by the attitude indicator, the heading indicator, and the
turn coordinator; thus the vacuum and electrical instruments are
consistent with each other. Since the attitude indicator indicates
explanations.B:
because the attitude indicator and
heading indicator are consistent with the turn coordinator.
explanations.C:
because the turn coordinator, which is
normally electric, is consistent with the attitude indicator, which is
normally a vacuum system instrument.

questions.question: Figure 148 64. (Refer to figure 148.) What is the flight attitude? One system which transmits information to the instruments has malfunctioned.

answers.A: Climbing turn to left.
answers.B: Climbing tum to right.
answers.C: Level turn to left.

explanations.A:
because the turn is to the right, not the
left.
explanations.B:
Fig. 148 illustrates a climbing turn to the
right. Note that the attitude indicator shows a climbing turn to the
right, the heading indicator shows a turn to the right, and both the
altimeter and vertical speed indicator indicate a climb. The turn
coordinator shows no turn and is malfunctioning.
explanations.C:
because the attitude indicator, altimeter,

and vertical speed indicator all indicate a climb, and the turn is to
the right, not left.

questions.question: Figure 149 65. (Refer to figure 149.) What is the flight attitude? One system which transmits information to the instruments has malfunctioned.

answers.A: Level turn to the right.
answers.B: Level tur to the left.
answers.C: Straight-and-level flight.

explanations.A:
because the vacuum system (i.e., the
attitude and heading indicators) is inoperative, and the airplane
is in straight flight, not a right turn.
explanations.B:
because the vacuum system (i.e., the

attitude and heading indicators) is inoperative, and the airplane
is in straight flight, not a left turn.
explanations.C:
In Fig. 149, the vertical speed indicator,
altimeter, and turn coordinator all indicate straight-and-level flight.
The heading indicator indicates a turn to the south from west,
which is a tu to the left. The attitude indicator indicates a turn to
the right; i.e., the attitude indicator and heading indicator are in
conflict. Thus, the vacuum system must be malfunctioning, and
the airplane must be in straight-and-level flight.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 150.) What is the flight attitude? One instrument has malfunctioned.

answers.A: Climbing turn to the right.
answers.B: Climbing turn to the left.
answers.C: Descending turn to the right.

explanations.A:
In Fig. 150, the airplane is in a climb as
evidenced by the vertical speed indicator, altimeter, and
airspeed indicator. The heading indicator indicates a turn from
west to north, which is a turn to the right. The turn coordinator also
indicates a turn to the right. Thus, the airplane is in a climbing turn
to the right. The attitude indicator is the instrument that is
malfunctioning since it indicates a level turn to the left.
explanations.B:
because the attitude indicator is
inoperative; thus, the airplane is turning to the right, not left.
explanations.C:
because the airspeed indicator,

altimeter, and vertical speed indicator all show that the airplane is
climbing, not descending.

questions.question: Cinura 464 67. (Refer to figure 151.) What is the flight attitude? One instrument has malfunctioned.

answers.A: Climbing turn to the right.
answers.B: Level turn to the right.
answers.C: Level turn to the left.

explanations.A:
because flight is level, not climbing,

according to the vertical speed indicator, altimeter, and attitude
indicator.
explanations.B:
The vertical speed indicator, altimeter, and
attitude indicator indicate level flight. The turn coordinator,
attitude indicator, and heading indicator indicate a turn to the
right. Accordingly, there is a level turn to the right, and the
airspeed should not be near the stall speed. Thus, the ram air
inlet and the drain hole of the pitot tube are clogged. The
airspeed indicator will react the same way as an altimeter, if the
static port is open, by showing a decrease in airspeed as altitude
decreases and an increase in speed as altitude increases.

Pile |
explanations.C: because the turn is to the right, not left.

questions.question: If you fly into severe turbulence, which flight condition should you attempt to maintain?

answers.A: Constant airspeed (Va).
answers.B: Level flight attitude.
answers.C: Constant altitude and constant airspeed.

explanations.A:
because you want to maintain an
airspeed at or below Va, but in severe turbulence, there will be
large variations in airspeed, and you will not be able to keep it
constant.
explanations.B:
In severe turbulence, you should attempt to
maintain a level flight attitude. You will not be able to maintain a
constant altitude and/or airspeed, but you should fly at or below
design maneuvering speed (Va) and attempt to maintain a level
flight attitude.
explanations.C:
because, in severe turbulence, you will

not be able to maintain a constant altitude and/or constant
airspeed.

questions.question: If severe turbulence is encountered during your IFR flight, the airplane should be slowed to the design maneuvering speed because the

answers.A: maneuverability of the airplane will be increased.
answers.B: amount of excess load that can be imposed on the wing will be decreased.
answers.C: airplane will stall at a lower angle of attack, giving an increased margin of safety.

explanations.A:
because you should slow the airspeed to
reduce excessive loads, not because the airplane will be more
maneuverable at a slow airspeed.
explanations.B:
Flight at or below the design maneuvering

speed (Va) means that the airplane will stall before excess loads
can be imposed on the wings.
explanations.C:
because an airplane will always stall
when the critical angle of attack is exceeded.

questions.question: When a climb or descent through an inversion or wind-shear zone is being performed, the pilot should be alert for which of the following change in airplane performance?

answers.A: A fast rate of climb and a slow rate of descent.
answers.B: A sudden change in airspeed.
answers.C: A sudden surge of thrust.

explanations.A:
because a fast rate of climb and a slow

rate of descent are usually not a safety problem, as the reverse
could be.
explanations.B:
When climbing through an inversion or
wind-shear zone, the danger is a sudden change in airspeed. If
the airplane were to move abruptly from a headwind to a tailwind,
the airspeed would slow dramatically, and a stall or rapid descent
could be induced.
explanations.C:
because the amount of thrust does not
change as a result of wind shears.

questions.question: Which distance is displayed by the DME indicator?

answers.A: Slant range distance in NM.
answers.B: Slant range distance in SM.
answers.C: Line-of-sight direct distance from aircraft to VORTAC in SM.

explanations.A:
DME (distance measuring equipment)

displays line-of-sight direct distance, i.e., slant range, from the
aircraft to the VORTAC in nautical miles.
explanations.B:
because the measurement is in nautical
miles, not statute miles.
explanations.C:
because the measurement is in nautical
miles, not statute miles.

questions.question: As a rule of thumb, to minimize DME slant range error, how far from the facility should you be to consider the reading as accurate?

answers.A: Two miles or more for each 1,000 feet of altitude above the facility.
answers.B: One or more miles for each 1,000 feet of altitude above the facility.
answers.C: No specific distance is specified since the reception is line-of-sight.

explanations.A:
because the accuracy is 1 NM, not 2 NM,
for each 1,000 ft. AGL.
explanations.B:
You should consider the DME slant range
error negligible if the airplane is 1 NM or more from the ground
facility for each 1,000 ft. of altitude above the elevation of the
facility.
explanations.C:
because a specific distance is required
because the reception is line-of-sight.

questions.question: As a rule of thumb, to minimize DME slant range error, how far from the facility should you be to consider the reading as accurate?

answers.A: Two miles or more for each 1,000 feet of altitude above the facility.
answers.B: One or more miles for each 1,000 feet of altitude above the facility.
answers.C: No specific distance is specified since the reception is line-of-sight.

explanations.A:
because the accuracy is 1 NM, not 2 NM,
for each 1,000 ft. AGL.
explanations.B:
You should consider the DME slant range
error negligible if the airplane is 1 NM or more from the ground
facility for each 1,000 ft. of altitude above the elevation of the
facility.
explanations.C:
because a specific distance is required
because the reception is line-of-sight.

questions.question: Where does the DME indicator have the greatest error between ground distance to the VORTAC and displayed distance?

answers.A: High altitudes far from the VORTAC.
answers.B: High altitudes close to the VORTAC.
answers.C: Low altitudes far from the VORTAC.

explanations.A:
because, as you get farther away from the
‘station, the slant range error of the DME becomes minimal.
explanations.B:
Because the DME reads slant range
distance, its greatest error occurs at high altitudes very close to
the VORTAC. For example, if one were at 12,000 ft. directly over

the VOR, the DME would show a distance from the VOR of
approximately 2 NM.
explanations.C:
because the DME has the greatest error
at high, not low, altitudes close to, not far from, the VORTAC.

questions.question: Which DME indication should you receive when you are directly over a VORTAC site at approximately 6,000 feet AGL?

explanations.A:
because the DME would only indicate
Zero if you were at ground level next to the VORTAC.
explanations.B:
Because the DME indicates slant range
distance, it will indicate your altitude if you are directly above the

VORTAC. One nautical mile equals approximately 6,000 ft., so
the DME would read 1 NM.
explanations.C:
because it would mean that your altitude
was about 8,000 ft. AGL (6,000 x 1.3).

questions.question: By which means may a pilot determine if a Loran C equipped aircraft is approved for IFR operations?

answers.A: Not necessary; Loran C is not approved for IFR.
answers.B: Check aircraft logbook.
answers.C: Check the Airplane Flight Manual Supplement.

explanations.A:
because some LORAN C receivers are
approved for IFR operations by the FAA.
explanations.B:
because the operational approval level

may be found in the aircraft maintenance records, not necessarily
the aircraft logbook.
explanations.C:
Pilots must be aware of the authorized
operational approval level (e.g., VFR or IFR) of a LORAN
receiver installed in their aircraft. Approval information is
contained in the Aircraft Flight Manual Supplement, on FAA Form
337, in aircraft maintenance records, or possibly on a placard
installed near or on the control panel.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 107.) Where should the bearing pointer be located relative to the wing-tip reference to maintain the 16 DME range in a right-hand arc with a right crosswind component?

Since you are flying a right-hand arc, you should be using VOR 2,

questions.question: (Refer to figure 108.) Where should the bearing pointer be located relative to the wing-tip reference to maintain the 16 DME range in a left-hand arc with a left crosswind component?

because En Route Low Altitude Charts

do not indicate VOR receiver ground checkpoints, only VOT
frequencies.
explanations.C:
The Airport/Facility Directory provides a
listing of available VOR receiver ground checkpoints.

questions.question: Which is the maximum tolerance for the VOR indication when the CDI is centered and the aircraft is directly over the airborne checkpoint?

answers.A: Plus or minus 6° of the designated radial.
answers.B: Plus 6° or minus 4° of the designated radial.
answers.C: Plus or minus 4° of the designated radial.

explanations.A:
Airborne checkpoints consist of certified
radials that should be received over specific landmarks while
airborne in the immediate vicinity of an airport. The maximum
tolerance when the CDI is centered is +6°.
explanations.B:
because the tolerance for an airborne
checkpoint is +6°, not +6° or -4°.
explanations.C:
because the tolerance for an airborne

checkpoint is +6°, not +4°, which is the tolerance for a ground
checkpoint or a VOT.

questions.question: When the CDI needle is centered during an airborne VOR check, the omni-bearing selector and the TO/FROM indicator should read

answers.B: within 6° of the selected radial.
answers.C: 0° TO, only if you are due south of the VOR.
answers.A: within 4° of the selected radial.

explanations.A:
because the maximum error for a ground,
not airborne, VOR check is +4°.
explanations.B:
Airborne VOR checkpoints consist of
certified radials that should be received over specific landmarks.
Ifno checkpoint is available, a prominent ground point should be
selected more than 20 NM from a VOR station that is along an
established VOR airway. Once over this point with the CDI
centered, the OBS should indicate within 6° of the published
radial.
explanations.C:
because you should use a certified

airborne checkpoint or select a ground reference that is under an
established VOR airway, not a randomly selected radial.

questions.question: When making an airborne VOR check, what is the maximum allowable tolerance between the two indicators of a dual VOR system (units independent of each other except the antenna)?

answers.A: 4° between the two indicated radials of a VOR.
answers.B: Plus or minus 4° when set to identical radials of a VOR.
answers.C: 6° between the two indicated radials of a VOR.

explanations.A:
If a dual system VOR (units independent of
each other except for the antenna) is installed in the airplane, one
system may be checked against the other in place of other VOR
check procedures. The test consists of tuning both systems to the
same VOR and centering the CDI needles, then noting the
bearing variation between the two VOR units. It should be less
than 4°.
explanations.B:
because the CDIs are to be centered, not
set to the same radials.
explanations.C:
because it is a maximum tolerance of 4°,
not 6°.

questions.question: While airborne, what is the maximum permissible variation between the two indicated bearings when checking one VOR system against the other?

answers.B: 4° between the two indicated bearings to a VOR.
answers.C: Plus or minus 6° when set to identical radials of a VOR.
answers.A: Plus or minus 4° when set to identical radials of a VOR

explanations.A:
because the CDIs must be centered, not
set to identical radials.
explanations.B:
If a dual system VOR (units independent of
each other except for the antenna) is installed in the airplane, one
system may be checked against the other in place of other check
procedures. The test consists of tuning both systems to the same
VOR with the CDI centered and noting the bearing variation
between the two VOR units. It should be less than 4°.
explanations.C:
because it is a maximum permissible
variation of 4°, not 6°, between the indicated bearings.

questions.question: How should the pilot make a VOR receiver check when the aircraft is located on the designated checkpoint on the airport surface?

answers.A: With the aircraft headed directly toward the VOR and the OBS set to 000°, the CDI should center within plus or minus 4° of that radial with a TO indication.
answers.B: Set the OBS on the designated radial. The CDI must center within plus or minus 4° of that radial with a FROM indication.
answers.C: Set the OBS on 180° plus or minus 4°; the CDI should center with a FROM indication.

explanations.A:
because VOR indications are given the
same no matter which heading the aircraft is on. The VOR
indication is based upon position, not heading.
explanations.B:
A VOR receiver check is a checkpoint on
the airport surface near a VOR. When the aircraft is on the
checkpoint, the designated radial should be set on the OBS. The

CDI must then center within 4° of the radial. Also, there will be a
FROM indication.
explanations.C:
because the specified radial, not 180°,
should be set on the OBS.

questions.question: How should the pilot make a VOR receiver check when the aircraft is located on the designated checkpoint on the airport surface?

answers.A: Set the OBS on 180° plus or minus 4°; the CDI should center with a FROM indication.
answers.B: Set the OBS on the designated radial. The CD! must center within plus or minus 4° of that radial with a FROM indication.
answers.C: With the aircraft headed directly toward the VOR and the OBS set to 000°, the CDI should center within plus or minus 4° of that radial with a TO indication.

explanations.A:
because the specified radial, not 180°,
should be set on the OBS.
explanations.B:
A VOR receiver check is a checkpoint on
the airport surface near a VOR. When the airplane is on the
checkpoint, the designated radial should be set on the OBS. The
CDI must then center within 4° of the radial. Also, there will be a
FROM indication.
explanations.C:
because VOR indications are given the
same no matter which heading the aircraft is on. The VOR
indication is based upon position, not heading.

questions.question: When using VOT to make a VOR receiver check, the CDI should be centered and the OBS should indicate that the aircraft is on the

explanations.B:

A VOT transmits only the 360° radial.
Thus, with the CDI centered, the OBS should indicate 0° with a

questions.question: Which indications are acceptable tolerances when checking both VOR receivers by use of the VOT?

answers.A: 360° TO and 003° TO, respectively.
answers.B: 001° FROM and 005° FROM, respectively.
answers.C: 176° TO and 003° FROM, respectively.

explanations.A:

because it exceeds the 4° maximum error

A VOT transmits a 360° radial in all

error of 4°.

explanations.A:
because, in illustration 1, the needles

explanations.B:
because, in illustration 2, there is a 10°

When performing an operational check of

questions.question: What indication should a pilot receive when a VOR station is undergoing maintenance and may be considered unreliable?

answers.A: No coded identification, but possible navigation indications.
answers.B: Coded identification, but no navigation indications.
answers.C: Avoice recording on the VOR frequency announcing that the VOR is out of service for maintenance.

explanations.A:
The only positive method of identifying a
VOR is by Morse Code identification and/or by the recorded
voice identification, which is always indicated by use of the word
"VOR" following the VOR name. During periods of maintenance,
the facility identification is removed, although navigational signals
may still be transmitted.
explanations.B:
because the coded identi fication is
removed when the station is undergoing maintenance.
explanations.C:
because an out-of-service VOR is not
announced by a voice recording.

questions.question: A particular VOR station is undergoing routine maintenance. This is evidenced by

answers.A: removal of the navigational feature.
answers.B: broadcasting a maintenance alert signal on the voice channel.
answers.C: removal of the identification feature.

explanations.A:
because the navigational signals may
Continue even though they are not accurate.
explanations.B:
because an out-of-service VOR is not
announced by a voice recording.
explanations.C:
The only positive method of identifying a
VOR is by Morse Code identification or by the recorded voice
identification, which is always indicated by use of the word
"VOR" following the VOR name. During periods of maintenance,

the coded and/or voice facility identification is removed, although
navigational signals may still be transmitted.

questions.question: When a VOR/DME is collocated under frequency pairings and the VOR portion is inoperative, the DME identifier will repeat at an interval of

answers.B: 30 second intervals at 1350 Hz.
answers.C: 60 second intervals at 1350 Hz.
answers.A: 20 second intervals at 1020 Hz.

explanations.A:
because the DME identifier repeats at
30-sec., not 20-sec., intervals at 1350 Hz, not 1020 Hz.
explanations.B:
The DME/TACAN coded identification is
transmitted at 1350 Hz once for each three or four times the VOR
or localizer coded identification is transmitted. When either the
VOR or the DME is operative, but not both, it is important to
recognize which identifier is retained for the operative facility. A
single-coded identification repeated at intervals of approximately
30 sec. indicates that the DME is operative and the VOR is not.
explanations.C:
because the DME identifier repeats at
30-sec., not 60-sec., intervals.

questions.question: What is the meaning of a single coded identification received only once approximately every 30 seconds from a VORTAC?

answers.A: The VOR and DME components are operative.
answers.B: VOR and DME components are both operative, but voice identification is out of service.
answers.C: The DME component is operative and the VOR component is inoperative.

explanations.A:
because a constant series of identity
codes indicates that both the VOR and DME are operative.
explanations.B:
because voice identification operates
independently of the identity codes.
explanations.C:
The DME/TACAN coded identification is
transmitted at 1350 Hz once for each three or four times the VOR
or localizer coded identification is transmitted. When either the
VOR or the DME is operative, but not both, it is important to
recognize which identifier is retained for the operative facility. A
single-coded identification repeated at intervals of approximately
30 sec. indicates that the DME is operative and the VOR is not.

questions.question: What angular deviation from a VOR course centerline is represented by a full-scale deflection of the CDI? A4. B.5°.

explanations.A:
because 4° is indicated by a 2-dot
deflection on a 5-dot VOR scale.
explanations.B:
because 5° is indicated by a 2-dot
deflection on a 4-dot VOR scale.
explanations.C:
On VORs, full needle deflection from the
center position to either side of the dial indicates that the aircraft
is 10° or more off course, assuming normal needle sensiti

questions.question: Full scale deflection of a CDI occurs when the course deviation bar or needle

answers.A: deflects from left side of the scale to right side of the scale.
answers.B: deflects from the center of the scale to either far side of the scale.
answers.C: deflects from half scale left to half scale right.

explanations.A:
because it indicates moving from a left full
deflection to a right full deflection, i.e., 10° left of course to 10°
right of course.
explanations.B:
Full-scale deflection of a CDI occurs when
the needle deflects from the center of the scale to either far side
of the scale. This indicates that the aircraft is 10° or more off
course, assuming normal needle sensitivity.
explanations.C:
because it indicates moving from a left
half deflection to a right half deflection, i.e., 5° left of course to 5°
right of course.

questions.question: For operations off established airways at 17,000 feet MSL in the contiguous U.S., (H) Class VORTAC facilities used to define a direct route of flight should be no farther apart than

answers.A: 75 NM.

explanations.A:
because 75 NM is the range of an (HH)
Class NDB facility, not an (H) Class VORTAC.
explanations.B:
because 100 NM is the range of an (H)
Class VORTAC at 17,000 ft. MSL; thus the distance between two
(H) Class VORTAC facilities can be 200 NM.
explanations.C:
(H) Class VORTAC facilities have a range
of 100 NM from 14,500 ft. AGL up to 18,000 ft. Thus, (H) Class
VORTAC facilities should be no farther apart than 200 NM.

questions.question: For IFR operations off of established airways below 18,000 feet, VOR navigational aids used to describe the "route of flight" should be no more than

answers.A: 80 NM apart.
answers.B: 40 NM apart.
answers.C: 70 NM apart.

explanations.A:
(H) Class VOR facilities have a range of
40 NM from 1,000 ft. AGL up to 14,500 ft. AGL, and a range of
100 NM from 14,500 ft. AGL up to 18,000 ft. Thus, in general,
VOR navigational aids used to describe a route of flight off of
established airways below 18,000 ft. (more-specifically, below
14,500 ft. AGL) should be no more than 80 NM apart.
explanations.B:
because 40 NM is the range of an (H)
Class VOR from 1,000 ft. AGL to 14,500 ft. AGL. VORs used to
describe a route of flight off of established airways below 14,500
ft. AGL should be no more than 80 NM apart.
explanations.C:
because VORs should be no more than
80 NM, not 70 NM, apart to define a route of flight off of
established airways below 14,500 ft. AGL.

questions.question: When using VOR for navigation, which of the following should be considered as station passage?

answers.A: The first movement of the CDI as the airplane enters the zone of confusion.
answers.B: The moment the TO-FROM indicator becomes blank.
answers.C: The first positive, complete reversal of the TO-FROM indicator.

explanations.A:
because it indicates flight into the zone of
confusion over the VOR, not station passage.
explanations.B:
because it is an indication that you are in
the zone of confusion over the VOR, not an indication of station
passage.
explanations.C:
When approaching a VOR, the TO-FROM
indicator and the CDI flicker as the airplane flies into the zone of

confusion (no signal area). Station passage is shown by
complete reversal of the TO-FROM indicator.

questions.question: Which of the following should be considered as station passage when using VOR?

answers.A: The first flickering of the TO-FROM indicator and CDI as the station is approached.
answers.B: The first full-scale deflection of the CDI.
answers.C: The first complete reversal of the TO-FROM indicator.

explanations.A:
because it indicates flight into the zone of
confusion over the VOR, not station passage.
explanations.B:
because it is an indication that you are in

the zone of confusion over the VOR, not an indication of station
passage.
explanations.C:
When approaching a VOR, the TO-FROM
indicator and the CDI flicker as the airplane flies into the zone of
confusion (no signal area). Station passage is shown by
complete reversal of the TO-FROM indicator.

questions.question: When checking the sensitivity of a VOR receiver, the number of degrees in course change as the OBS is rotated to move the CDI from center to the last dot on either side should be between

explanations.A:
because 5° to 6° of course change should
result in a %-scale, not full-scale, needle deflection.
explanations.B:
because 8° to 10° of course change
should result in a %-scale, not full-scale, needle deflection.
explanations.C:
In addition to VOR receiver checks, course
sensitivity may be checked by noting the number of degrees of

questions.question: A VOR receiver with normal five-dot course sensitivity shows a three-dot deflection at 30 NM from the station. The aircraft would be displaced approximately how far from the course centerline?

answers.B: 3NM.
answers.C: 5NM.

centerline.

because five dots, not three dots,
indicate 5 NM off course.

questions.question: How cana pilot determine if a Global Positioning System (GPS) installed in an aircraft is approved for IFR en route and IFR approaches?

answers.A: Flight manual supplement.
answers.B: GPS operator's manual.
answers.C: Aircraft owner's handbook.

explanations.A:
A supplement to the aircraft's POH (flight
manual) is required for newly installed equipment. A supplement
should state that the GPS is approved for IFR operations (en
route and approaches).
explanations.B:
because the GPS operator's manual will
describe how to operate the GPS unit but will not provide
approval for its use in a particular aircraft.
explanations.C:
because the aircraft owner's handbook
(i-e., information manual or POH) may not have any information
ona GPS unit unless the unit was installed as a standard feature.

questions.question: Hand-held GPS systems, and GPS systems certified for VFR operation, may be used during IFR operations as

answers.A: the principal reference to determine en route waypoints.
answers.B: an aid to situational awareness.
answers.C: the primary source of navigation.

explanations.A:
because hand-held and VFR-only GPS
systems are not approved for IFR operations, and may only be
used as an aid to situational awareness. Passage of en route
reporting points and fixes (i.e., waypoints) must be verified by
some other means (e.g., VOR, ADF, radar, etc.).
explanations.B:
In order to use a GPS as the primary
means of navigation under IFR or to perform instrument
approaches, both the GPS receiver and the aircraft installation
must FAA-approved. Additionally, the receiver must have a
current database of waypoints and instrument approach
procedures. Hand-held GPS systems and VFR- only GPS
systems are not FAA-approved for IFR operations, and may only
be used during IFR operations as an aid to situational awareness.
explanations.C:
because hand-held and VFR-only GPS
systems are not approved as the primary source of navigation

under IFR; they may only be used as an aid to situational
awareness.

questions.question: During IFR en route and terminal operations using an approved GPS system for navigation, ground based navigational facilities

answers.A: are only required during the approach portion of the flight.
answers.B: must be operational along the entire route.
answers.C: must be operational only if RAIM predicts an outage.

explanations.A:
because ground-based navigational
facilities appropriate to the route must be available and
operational along the entire route of flight, not just the approach
portion.
explanations.B:
In order to conduct IFR en route and
terminal operations using an approved GPS system, the avionics
necessary to receive all of the ground-based facilities that are
appropriate for the route to the destination airport and to any
alternate airport must be installed and operational, and the
ground-based facilities necessary for these routes must be
operational.
explanations.C:
because ground-based navigational
facilities appropriate to the route must be available and
operational regardless of Receiver Autonomous Integrity
Monitoring (RAIM) status. However, unless RAIM predicts an
outage, active monitoring of these facilities is not necessary.

questions.question: During IFR operation using an approved GPS system for navigation,

answers.A: no other navigation system is required.
answers.B: active monitoring of an alternate navigation system is always required.
answers.C: the aircraft must have an approved and operational alternate navigation system appropriate for the route.

explanations.A:
because aircraft using an approved GPS
system for IFR operations must be equipped with an approved
and operational alternate means of navigation appropriate to the
flight.
explanations.B:
because active monitoring of an alternate
navigation system is only required when GPS RAIM capability is
lost or when an outage is predicted, not at all times.
explanations.C:
Aircraft using GPS under IFR must be
equipped with an approved and operational alternate means of
navigation appropriate for the route. Active monitoring of
alternative navigation equipment is not required if the GPS
receiver uses Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring (RAIM).
However, active monitoring of an alternate means of navigation is
required when the RAIM capability of the GPS equipment is lost,
or if RAIM predicts an outage.

questions.question: Which flight time may be logged as instrument time when on an instrument flight plan?

answers.A: All of the time the aircraft was not controlled by ground references.
answers.B: Only the time you controlled the aircraft solely by reference to flight instruments.
answers.C: Only the time you were flying in IFR weather conditions. Answer (C) is incorrect because time under the hood (i.e., simulated IFR) as well as actual IFR conditions counts as instrument time.

explanations.A:
because VFR flight can be conducted
above a cloud layer without visual ground references, i.e.,
VFR-on-top.
explanations.B:
A pilot may log as instrument flight time
‘only that time during which (s)he operates the aircraft solely by
reference to instruments, under actual or simulated instrument
flight conditions.
explanations.C:
because time under the hood (i.e.,

simulated IFR) as well as actual IFR conditions counts as
instrument time.

questions.question: What portion of dual instruction time may a certificated instrument flight instructor log as instrument flight time?

answers.A: All time during which the instructor acts as instrument instructor, regardless of weather conditions.
answers.B: All time during which the instructor acts as instrument instructor in actual instrument weather conditions.
answers.C: Only the time during which the instructor flies the aircraft by reference to instruments. Answer (C) is incorrect because instructing in (as well as flying in) actual IFR weather conditions can be logged as instrument time by the instructor.

explanations.A:
because the flight conditions must be IMC.
for the instructor to log flight instruction as instrument time.
explanations.B:
An instrument flight instructor may log as
instrument time that time during which (s)he acts as instrument
flight instructor in actual instrument weather conditions.
explanations.C:
because instructing in (as well as flying in)

actual IFR weather conditions can be logged as instrument time
by the instructor.

No pilot may act as pilot in command of a

procedures, and intercepting and tracking courses through the

ina flight simulator or flight training device that is representative

questions.question: To carry passengers for hire in an airplane on cross-country flights of more than 50 NM from the departure airport, the pilot in command is required to hold at least

Certificate.

because no passengers may be carried

certificate must hold an instrument rating (airplane), or the

prohibiting the carriage of passengers for hire in airplanes on

questions.question: During an IFR flight in IMC, a distress condition is encountered, (fire, mechanical, or structural failure). The pilot should

because a distress condition is perilous
and you should not hesitate to declare an emergency.
explanations.C:
because you should contact ATC and
declare that an emergency, not urgency, condition exists and
obtain an amended clearance, not a request for consideration.

questions.question: When must an operational check on the aircraft VOR equipment be accomplished when used to operate under IFR?

answers.A: Within the preceding 10 days or 10 hours of flight time.
answers.B: Within the preceding 30 days or 30 hours of flight time.
answers.C: Within the preceding 30 days. Answer (C) is correct. explanations.A:
because it must be checked every 30
days, not 10 days or 10 hr.
explanations.B:
because there is no time requirement

explanations.C:
No person may operate a civil aircraft

VOR equipment of that aircraft is maintained, checked, and
inspected under an approved procedure, or has been
operationally checked within the preceding 30 days and was
found to be within the limits of the permissible indicated bearing
error.

questions.question: When making an airborne VOR check, what is the maximum allowable tolerance between the two indicators of a dual VOR system (units independent of each other except the antenna)?

answers.A: 4° between the two indicated bearings of a VOR.
answers.B: Plus or minus 4° when set to identical radials of a VOR. C_ 6° between the two indicated radials of a VOR. Answer (C) is incorrect because the maximum allowable difference between the two VORs is 4°, not 6°, of the indicated radial.

explanations.A:
If a dual VOR system (units independent of
each other except the antenna) is installed in the aircraft, you may
check one system against the other. You tune both systems to the
same VOR station and note the indicated bearings to that
station. The maximum permissible variation between the two
indicated bearings is 4°.
explanations.B:
because you center the CDI and note the
bearing, not set both VORs to the same radial.
explanations.C:
because the maximum allowable

difference between the two VORs is 4°, not 6°, of the indicated
radial.

questions.question: Which checks and inspections of flight instruments or instrument systems must be accomplished before an aircraft can be flown under IFR?

answers.A: VOR within 30 days, altimeter systems within 24 calendar months, and transponder within 24 calendar months.
answers.B: ELT test within 30 days, altimeter systems within 12 calendar months, and transponder within 24 calendar months.
answers.C: VOR within 24 calendar months, transponder within 24 calendar months, and altimeter system within 12 calendar months. Answer (C) is incorrect because VORs must be checked within 30 days, not 24 months, and altimeter systems must be inspected within 24 months, not 12 months.

explanations.A:
No person may operate a civil aircraft
under IFR using the VOR system of radio navigation unless the
VOR equipment of that aircraft is maintained, checked, and
inspected under an approved procedure, or has been
operationally checked within the preceding 30 days and was
found to be within the limits of the permissible indicated bearing
error. Also, within the preceding 24 calendar months, each
altimeter system and transponder must be tested, inspected, and
found to comply with the regulations.
explanations.B:
because check and inspection of the
altimeter system is required every 24 months, not 12 months, and

ELTs must be inspected every 12 months, not tested within 30
days.
explanations.C:
because VORs must be checked within

30 days, not 24 months, and altimeter systems must be
inspected within 24 months, not 12 months.

questions.question: Except when necessary for takeoff or landing or unless otherwise authorized by the Administrator, the minimum altitude for IFR flight is

answers.B: 3,000 feet over designated mountainous terrain; 2,000 feet over terrain elsewhere.
answers.C: 2,000 feet above the highest obstacle over designated mountainous terrain; 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle over terrain elsewhere. Answer (C) is correct. Except when necessary for takeoff or landing, no person may operate an aircraft under IFR below 2,000 ft. above the highest obstacle within a horizontal distance of 4 NM from the course to be flown over designated mountainous terrain, or 1,000 ft. above the highest obstacle within a horizontal distance of 4 NM from the course to be flown over terrain elsewhere.

because the minimum IFR altitude is
2,000 ft. above the highest obstacle over mountainous terrain or
1,000 ft. over the highest obstacle over terrain elsewhere, not
3,000 ft. over all terrain.
explanations.B:
because the minimum IFR altitude is
2,000 ft., not 3,000 ft., above the highest obstacle over
mountainous terrain, or 1,000 ft., not 2,000 ft., above the highest
obstacle over terrain elsewhere.
explanations.C:
Except when necessary for takeoff or
landing, no person may operate an aircraft under IFR below
2,000 ft. above the highest obstacle within a horizontal distance
of 4 NM from the course to be flown over designated
mountainous terrain, or 1,000 ft. above the highest obstacle

questions.question: What minimum navigation equipment is required for IFR flight?

answers.A: VORILOC receiver, transponder, and DME.
answers.B: VOR receiver and, if in ARTS Ill environment, a coded transponder equipped for altitude reporting.
answers.C: Navigation equipment appropriate to the ground facilities to be used. Answer (C) is correct. The minimum navigation equipment requirement for IFR flight is navigation equipment that is appropriate to the ground facilities to be used.

explanations.A:
because a VOR/LOC receiver and DME
are required only if VORTAC stations will be used for navigation
and DME fixes need to be identified. If you are using alternative
means of navigation (e.g., LORAN), this equipment is not
needed. A transponder is not a navigation system.
explanations.B:
because a VOR is required only if using
VOR stations for navigation. If using NDB stations, a VOR is not
required. A transponder is not a navigation system.
explanations.C:
The minimum navigation equipment

requirement for IFR flight is navigation equipment that is
appropriate to the ground facilities to be used.

questions.question: Where is DME required under IFR?

answers.A: At or above 24,000 feet MSL if VOR navigational equipment is required.
answers.B: In positive control airspace.
answers.C: Above 18,000 feet MSL. Answer (C) is incorrect because Class A airspace begins at 18,000 ft. MSL and DME is required at or above FL 240, if VOR navigational equipment is required.

explanations.A:
If VOR navigational equipment is required,
no person may operate a U.S.-registered civil aircraft within the
50 states and the District of Columbia, at or above 24,000 ft.
MSL (FL 240), unless that aircraft is equipped with approved
distance measuring equipment (DME).
explanations.B:
because, if VOR navigational equipment
is required, DME is required at or above FL 240, not only in
positive control airspace. Positive control airspace is that

airspace in which ATC separates all aircraft, e.g., Class A, Class
B, Class C.
explanations.C:
because Class A airspace begins at

18,000 ft. MSL and DME is required at or above FL 240, if VOR
navigational equipment is required.

‘only one, not two, VOR is required under FAR Part 91.

(directional gyro or equivalent).

questions.question: What is the oxygen requirement for an unpressurized aircraft at 15,000 feet?

answers.A: All occupants must use oxygen for the entire time at this altitude.
answers.B: Crew must start using oxygen at 12,000 feet and passengers at 15,000 feet.
answers.C: Crew must use oxygen for the entire time above 14,000 feet and ngers must be provided supplemental oxygen only above 15,000 feet. Answer (C) is correct. No one may operate a U.S. civil aircraft at cabin pressure altitudes above 14,000 ft. MSL unless the required minimum flight crew is provided with and uses supplemental oxygen during the entire flight time at those altitudes. At cabin pressure altitudes above 15,000 ft. MSL, each passenger must be provided with supplemental oxygen.

explanations.A:
because the required minimum flight crew
must use oxygen above 14,000 ft. MSL and others must be
provided with oxygen above 15,000 ft. MSL.
explanations.B:
because the crew must start using oxygen
at 14,000 ft. MSL or after 30 min. above 12,500 ft. MSL.
explanations.C:
No one may operate a U.S. civil aircraft at
cabin pressure altitudes above 14,000 ft. MSL unless the
required minimum flight crew is provided with and uses
supplemental oxygen during the entire flight time at those
altitudes. At cabin pressure altitudes above 15,000 ft. MSL, each
passenger must be provided with supplemental oxygen.

questions.question: What is the maximum IFR altitude you may fly in an unpressurized aircraft without providing passengers with supplemental oxygen?

answers.C: 15,000 feet. Answer (C) is correct. At cabin pressure altitudes above 15,000 ft. MSL, each occupant must be provided with supplemental oxygen.

explanations.A:
because, at cabin pressure altitudes
above 12,500 ft. MSL up to and including 14,000 ft. MSL, only the
minimum flight crew must use supplemental oxygen for that part
of the flight at those altitudes that is more than 30 min. duration.
explanations.B:
because, at cabin pressure altitudes

above 14,000 ft. MSL, only the required minimum flight crew must
use supplemental oxygen.
explanations.C:
At cabin pressure altitudes above 15,000

ft. MSL, each occupant must be provided with supplemental
oxygen.

questions.question: What is the maximum cabin pressure altitude at which a pilot can fly for longer than 30 minutes without using supplemental oxygen?

answers.C: 12,500 feet. Answer (C) is correct. No one may operate a U.S. civil aircraft at cabin pressure altitudes above 12,500 ft. MSL up to and including 14,000 ft. MSL unless the required minimum flight crew uses supplemental oxygen for that part of the flight at those altitudes that is of more than 30 min. duration.

explanations.A:
because supplemental oxygen is not
required at any time at 10,500 ft.
explanations.B:
because supplemental oxygen is not
required at any time at 12,000 ft.
explanations.C:
No one may operate a U.S. civil aircraft at
cabin pressure altitudes above 12,500 ft. MSL up to and
including 14,000 ft. MSL unless the required minimum flight crew
uses supplemental oxygen for that part of the flight at those
altitudes that is of more than 30 min. duration.

questions.question: if an unpressurized aircraft is operated above 12,500 feet MSL, but not more than 14,000 feet MSL, for a period of 2 hours 20 minutes, how long during that time is the minimum flightcrew required to use supplemental oxygen?

answers.A: 2 hours 20 minutes.
answers.B: 1 hour 20 minutes.
answers.C: 1 hour 50 minutes. Answer (C) is correct. No one may operate a U.S. civil aircraft at cabin pressure altitudes above 12,500 ft. MSL up to and including 14,000 ft. MSL unless the required imum flight crew uses supplemental oxygen for that part of the flight at those altitudes that is of more than 30 min. duration. If the flight lasts 2 hr. and 20 min., the crew must use supplemental oxygen for all but 30 min., or 1 hr. and 50 min.

explanations.A:
because one may fly for 30 min. without

supplemental oxygen between 12,500 ft. MSL and 14,000 ft.
MSL.
explanations.B:
because 30 min. of flight, not 1 hr., is

permitted without supplemental oxygen between 12,500 ft. MSL
up to and including 14,000 ft. MSL.
explanations.C:
No one may operate a U.S. civil aircraft at
cabin pressure altitudes above 12,500 ft. MSL up to and
including 14,000 ft. MSL unless the required imum flight crew
uses supplemental oxygen for that part of the flight at those
altitudes that is of more than 30 min. duration. If the flight lasts 2
hr. and 20 min., the crew must use supplemental oxygen for all
but 30 min., or 1 hr. and 50 min.

Within the preceding 24 calendar months,
each static pressure system, each altimeter instrument, and each
automatic pressure altitude reporting system must be tested,
inspected, and found to comply with the regulations. The
24-calendar-month period following January of this year begins
February 1, this year, and ends on January 31, 2 years hence.

questions.question: An aircraft altimeter system test and inspection must be accomplished within

answers.A: 12 calendar months.
answers.B: 18 calendar months.
answers.C: 24 calendar months. Answer (C) is correct. Within the preceding 24 calendar months, each static pressure system, each altimeter instrument, and each automatic pressure altitude reporting system must be tested, inspected, and found to comply with the regulations.

explanations.A:
because an annual inspection, not the

altimeter system, must be accomplished within the preceding 12
calendar months.
explanations.B:
because the aircraft's altimeter system
must be tested and inspected within 24, not 18, calendar months.
explanations.C:
Within the preceding 24 calendar months,
each static pressure system, each altimeter instrument, and each
automatic pressure altitude reporting system must be tested,
inspected, and found to comply with the regulations.

questions.question: Which publication covers the procedures required for aircraft accident and incident reporting responsibilities for pilots?

answers.B: FAR Part 91.
answers.C: NTSB Part 830.
answers.A: FAR Part 61

explanations.A:
because FAR Part 61 concerns
certification of pilots, flight instructors, and ground instructors.
explanations.B:
because FAR Part 91 concerns general
operating and flight rules.
explanations.C:
NTSB Part 830 contains rules pertaining
to the following:

1. Notification and reporting aircraft accidents and incidents and
certain other occurrences in the operation of aircraft when they
involve civil aircraft of the U.S. wherever they occur, or foreign
civil aircraft when such events occur in the U.S., its territories, or

3. Preservation of aircraft wreckage, mail, cargo, and records

questions.question: PRECISION INSTRUMENT RUNWAY Figure 137 1. (Refer to figure 137.) What is the distance (A) from the beginning of the runway to the fixed distance marker? A_ 500 feet.

answers.B: 1,000 feet.
answers.C: 1,500 feet.

explanations.A:
because the six parallel lines (somewhat
lighter and narrower than the fixed distance marker) 500 ft. from
the threshold of the runway are the touchdown zone marker.
explanations.B:
The fixed distance marker on precision
instrument runways consists of two heavy lines parallel to the
direction of the runway, 1,000 ft. from the runway threshold.
explanations.C:
because the marker at roughly 1,500 ft.
from the threshold is the next marker beyond the fixed distance
marker, not the fixed distance marker.

questions.question: PRECISION INSTRUMENT RUNWAY Figure 137 2. (Refer to figure 137.) What is the distance (B) from the beginning of the runway to the touchdown zone marker?

answers.A: 250 feet.
answers.B: 500 feet.
answers.C: 750 feet.

explanations.A:
because there is no standardized
marking 250 ft. from the beginning of the runway.
explanations.B:
The distance from the runway threshold to
the touchdown zone marker is 500 ft. The touchdown zone
marker consists of six lines parallel to the runway.
explanations.C:
because there is no standardized
marking 750 ft. from the beginning of the runway.

questions.question: PRECISION INSTRUMENT RUNWAY Figure 137 3. (Refer to figure 137.) What is the distance (C) from the beginning of the touchdown zone marker to the beginning of the fixed distance marker?

answers.A: 1,000 feet.
answers.B: 500 feet.
answers.C: 250 feet.

explanations.A:
because 1,000 ft. is the distance from the
beginning of the runway to the fixed distance marker.
explanations.B:
Since the touchdown zone marker is 500 ft.
from the runway threshold and the fixed distance marker is 1,000
ft. from the runway threshold, the distance from the beginning of

the touchdown zone marker to the beginning of the fixed distance
marker is 500 ft. (1,000 - 500).
explanations.C:
because 250 ft. is not a standard
distance between runway markings.

questions.question: The primary purpose of runway end identifier lights, installed at many airfields, is to provide

answers.A: rapid identification of the approach end of the runway during reduced visibility.
answers.B: a warning of the final 3,000 feet of runway remaining as viewed from the takeoff or approach position.
answers.C: rapid identification of the primary runway during reduced visibility.

explanations.A:
Runway end identifier lights (REIL) are
effective for rapid and positive identification of the approach end
of a runway which is surrounded by a preponderance of other
lighting, which lacks contrast with surrounding terrain, and/or

which has reduced visibility. They are white strobe lights, one on
each side of the runway threshold.
explanations.B:
because it describes runway remaining
lights in the center of the runway, not REIL.
explanations.C:
because REIL of other than the primary

runway may be used to help identify the airport. In other words,

REIL may be flashing at the end of a runway which is not the
primary runway.

questions.question: Which type of runway lighting consists of a pair of synchronized flashing lights, one on each side of the runway threshold?

answers.B: HIRL.
answers.C: REIL.
answers.A: RAIL.

explanations.A:
because RAIL refers to runway alignment

indicator lights, which are sequenced flashing lights that are used
in combination with other approach lighting systems.
explanations.B:
because HIRL refers to high-intensity
runway lights, which are a runway edge light system.
explanations.C:
Runway end identifier lights (REIL) consist

of a pair of synchronized flashing lights, one on each side of the
runway threshold.

questions.question: Which runway marking indicates a displaced threshold on an instrument runway?

answers.A: Arrows leading to the threshold mark.
answers.B: Centerline dashes starting at the threshold.
answers.C: Red chevron marks in the nonlanding portion of the runway.

explanations.A:
On any runway, a displaced threshold is
marked with a series of arrows in the middle of the runway
pointing to the threshold mark, which is a solid line across the
runway. A displaced threshold is available for taxiing, landing
rollout, and takeoff, but not landing.
explanations.B:
because it describes the centerline
marking of a runway.
explanations.C:
because chevron marks are usually
yellow. They indicate a nonusable portion of the runway that is
only available for emergency use (overrun and stopway areas).

questions.question: L_< Figure 138 (Refer to figure 138.) What night operations, if any, are authorized between the approach end of the runway and the threshold lights?

answers.A: No aircraft operations are permitted short of the threshold lights.
answers.B: Only taxi operations are permitted in the area short of the threshold lights.
answers.C: Taxi and takeoff operations are permitted, providing the takeoff operations are toward the visible green threshold lights.

explanations.A:
because overrun areas are areas where

‘only emergency operations are permitted. Overrun areas do not
have any runway edge lights.
explanations.B:
because landing rollout and takeoff
operations are also permitted behind displaced thresholds.
explanations.C:
On displaced thresholds, runway edge
lights appear red when taxiing toward the green threshold lights
and white when taxiing away from the threshold to the departure
end of the runway. The area behind the displaced runway

threshold is available for taxiing, landing rollout, and takeoff of
aircraft.

questions.question: Under which conditions is hydroplaning most likely to occur?

answers.A: When rudder is used for directional control instead of allowing the nosewheel to contact the surface early in the landing roll on a wet runway.
answers.B: During conditions of standing water, slush, high speed, and smooth runway texture.
answers.C: During a landing on any wet runway when brake application is delayed until a wedge of water begins to build ahead of the tires.

explanations.A:
because the nosewheel cannot
hydroplane if it is not put down to the runway surface.
explanations.B:
In hydroplaning, the aircraft tire is
separated from the runway by water. It is more apt to happen at

higher speeds, with standing water or slush on the runway, and on
explanations.C:
because hydroplaning occurs regardless
of brake timing.

answers.B: white lettering with a red background.
answers.C: black lettering with a yellow background.

because yellow lettering on a black
background denotes taxiway or runway location signs (where the
aircraft is located).
explanations.B:
Mandatory airport instruction signs have a
red background with white lettering and are used to denote an

entrance to a runway or critical area, and areas where an aircraft
is prohibited from entering.
explanations.C:
because black lettering on a yellow
background denotes direction, destination, and information
signs.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 94.) What sign is designated by illustration 7?

because location signs use yellow

Mandatory instruction signs have a red
background with white lettering. The sign designated by
illustration 7 (15-APCH) protects the approach to RWY 15 and/or
the departure for RWY 33.
explanations.C:
because direction signs use black
lettering on a yellow background.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 94.) What colors are runway holding position signs?

answers.A: White with a red background.
