questions.question: What conditions are necessary before ATC can authorize a visual approach?

answers.A: You must have the preceding aircraft in sight, and be able to remain in VFR weather conditions.
answers.B: You must have the airport in sight or the preceding aircraft in sight, and be able to proceed to, and land in IFR conditions.
answers.C: You must have the airport in sight or a preceding aircraft to be followed, and be able to proceed to the airport in VFR conditions.

explanations.A:
because you can have the airport in sight
instead of having the preceding aircraft in sight.
explanations.B:
because you must be able to land in VFR,
not IFR, conditions.
explanations.C:
ATC may authorize airplanes to conduct
visual approaches to an airport or to follow another airplane when
flight to and landing at the airport can be accomplished in VFR

weather. You must have the airport or preceding aircraft in sight
before the clearance is issued.

questions.question: What are the main differences between a visual approach and a contact approach?

answers.A: The pilot must request a contact approach; the pilot may be assigned a visual approach and higher weather minimums must exist
answers.B: The pilot must request a visual approach and report having the field in sight, ATC may assign a contact approach if VFR conditions exist.
answers.C: Anytime the pilot reports the field in sight, ATC may clear the pilot for a contact approach; for a visual approach, the pilot must advise that the approach can be made under VFR conditions.

explanations.A:
Contact approaches can be issued only
upon pilot request, but visual approaches may be assigned by
ATC. Visual approaches require VFR conditions. Contact

approaches require 1 SM flight visibility and the ability to remain
clear of clouds.
explanations.B:
because ATC may assign visual

approaches without pilot request, and ATC cannot issue a
contact approach clearance without the pilot's request.
explanations.C:
because ATC cannot issue a contact
approach clearance without the pilot's request.

questions.question: Acontact approach is an approach procedure that may be used

answers.A: inlieu of conducting a SIAP.
answers.B: if assigned by ATC and will facilitate the approach.
answers.C: in lieu of a visual approach.

explanations.A:
A contact approach may be requested by
the pilot if there is 1 SM flight visibility and the pilot can operate

clear of clouds. It is an alternative to a standard instrument
approach procedure (SIAP).
explanations.B:
because ATC cannot assign a contact
approach; pilots must request them.
explanations.C:
because using a contact approach is not
necessary if a visual approach is possible.

questions.question: You arrive at your destination airport on an IFR flight plan. Whichis a prerequisite condition for the performance of a contact approach?

answers.A: Aground visibility of at least 2 SM.
answers.B: A flight visibility of at least 1/2 NM.
answers.C: Clear of clouds and at least 1 SM flight visibility.

explanations.A:
because the flight, not ground, visibility
must be at least 1 SM, not 2 SM.
explanations.B:
because the flight visibility must be at
least 1 SM, not 1/2 NM.
explanations.C:
A contact approach may be requested by

the pilot if there is 1 SM flight visibility and the pilot can operate
clear of clouds.

questions.question: What are the requirements for a contact approach to an airport that has an approved IAP, if the pilot is on an instrument flight plan and clear of clouds?

answers.A: The controller must determine that the pilot can see the airport at the altitude flown and can remain clear of clouds.
answers.B: The pilot must agree to the approach when given by ATC and the controller must have determined that the visibility was at least 1 mile and be reasonably sure the pilot can remain clear of clouds.
answers.C: The pilot must request the approach, have at least 1-mile visibility, and be reasonably sure of remaining clear of clouds.

explanations.A:
because the pilot must deter mine
whether (s)he can reasonably expect to continue to the airport in
at least 1 SM flight visibility and clear of clouds, not the controller.
explanations.B:
because the pilot must request a contact
approach; ATC does not solicit or assign contact approaches.
explanations.C:
Pilots operating in accordance with anIFR
flight plan, provided they are clear of clouds, have at least 1 SM
flight visi and can reasonably expect to continue to the
destination airport in those conditions, may request ATC
authorization for a contact approach.

questions.question: Whenis radar service terminated during a visual approach?

answers.A: Automatically when ATC instructs the pilot to contact the tower.
answers.B: Immediately upon acceptance of the approach by the pilot.
answers.C: When ATC advises, "Radar service terminated; resume own. navigation."

explanations.A:
During a visual approach, radar service is
automatically terminated without advising the pilot once the pilot
has been instructed to contact the tower or change to advisory
frequency.
explanations.B:
because approach clearance is given
well before radar service is terminated.
explanations.C:
because "resume own navigation" is

generally an en route instruction and is not applicable to
approaches.

questions.question: When may you obtain a contact approach?

answers.A: ATC may assign a contact approach if VFR conditions exist or you report the runway in sight and are clear of clouds.
answers.B: ATC may assign a contact approach if you are below the clouds and the visibility is at least 1 mile.
answers.C: ATC will assign a contact approach only upon request if the reported visibility is at least 1 mile.

explanations.A:
because ATC may assign a visual, not a

contact, approach if VFR weather conditions exist. ATC may not
assign a contact approach.
explanations.B:
because ATC may not assign a contact
approach. The pilot must request one.
explanations.C:
ATC will assign a contact approach only
upon pilot request if the pilot is operating clear of clouds, has at

least 1 SM flight visibility, and expects to reach the airport and
land in those conditions.

questions.question: What are the main differences between the SDF and the localizer of an ILS?

answers.A: The useable off-course indications are limited to 35° for the localizer and up to 90° for the SDF.
answers.B: The SDF course may not be aligned with the runway and the course may be wider.
answers.C: The course width for the localizer will always be 5° while the SDF course will be between 6° and 12°.

explanations.A:
because the off-course indications are
limited to 35° for both types of approach.
explanations.B:
The approach techniques and procedures.
used in performance of an SDF instrument approach are
essentially identical to those employed to execute a standard
localizer approach, except that the SDF course may not be

aligned with the runway and the course may be wider, resulting in
less precision.
explanations.C:
because the course width for the localizer

is usually between 3° and 6°, and SDF is either 6° or 12° (not
between).

questions.question: Whatis the difference between a Localizer-Type Directional Aid (LDA) and the ILS localizer?

answers.A: The LDA is not aligned with the runway.
answers.B: The LDA uses a course width of 6° or 12°, while an ILS uses only bie
answers.C: The LDA signal is generated from a VOR-type facility and has no glide slope.

explanations.A:
The localizer-type directional aid (LDA) is
similar to a localizer but is not part of a complete ILS, and it is not
aligned with the runway.
explanations.B:
because the LDA uses the same course
width as the ILS, i.e., 3° to 6°. The SDF uses 6° or 12°.
explanations.C:
because the LDA is a localizer-type, not
VOR-type, signal.

questions.question: How wide is an SDF course?

answers.B: Either 6° or 12°.
answers.C: Varies from 5° to 10°.
answers.A: Either 3° or 6°.

explanations.A:
because either 3° or 6° is half the course
width of an SDF.
explanations.B:
The simplified directional facility (SDF)
signal is fixed at either 6° or 12° as necessary to provide
maximum flyability and optimum course quality.
explanations.C:
because a course 5° to 10° wide does
not relate to ILS, LDA, or SDF.

questions.question: What is a difference between an SDF and an LDA facility?

answers.B: The SDF course has no glide slope guidance while the LDA does.
answers.C: The SDF has no marker beacons while the LDA has at least an OM.
answers.A: The SDF course width is either 6° or 12° while the LDA course width is approximately 5°.

explanations.A:
The localizer-type directional aid (LDA) is
of comparable utility and accuracy as a localizer but is not part of
explanations.B:
because only some LDA approaches

provide glide slope guidance, but this is not a requirement of the
system.
explanations.C:
because both SDF and LDA may have
marker beacons.

questions.question: What does the Runway Visual Range (RVR) value, depicted on certain straight-in IAP Charts, represent?

answers.A: The slant range distance the pilot can see down the runway while crossing the threshold on glide slope.
answers.B: The horizontal distance a pilot should see when looking down the runway from a moving aircraft.
answers.C: The slant visual range a pilot should see down the final approach and during landing.

explanations.A:
because RVR is the horizontal, not slant
Tange, distance the pilot will see down the runway.
explanations.B:
RVR is an instrumentally derived value that
represents the horizontal distance the pilot will see down the
runway from the approach end. It is based on the measurement
of a transmissometer near the touchdown point of the instrument
runway and is reported in hundreds of feet.
explanations.C:
because RVR is the horizontal, not slant
range, distance the pilot will see down the runway, not the final
approach.

questions.question: The RVR minimums for takeoff or landing are published in an IAP, but RVR is inoperative and cannot be reported for the runway at the time. Which of the following would apply?

answers.A: RVR minimums which are specified in the procedure should be converted and applied as ground visibility.
answers.B: RVR minimums may be disregarded, providing the runway has an operative HIRL system.
answers.C: RVR minimums may be disregarded, providing all other components of the ILS system are operative.

explanations.A:
If RVR minimums for takeoff or landing are
prescribed in an instrument approach procedure, but RVR is
inoperative and cannot be reported for the runway of intended
operation, the RVR minimum shall be converted to ground

visibility and shall be the visibility minimum for takeoff or landing
on that runway.
explanations.B:
because RVR minimums must be
converted to ground visibility, not disregarded.
explanations.C:
because RVR minimums must be
converted to ground visibility, not disregarded.

questions.question: RVR minimums for landing are prescribed in an IAP, but RVR is inoperative and cannot be reported for the intended runway at the time. Which of the following would be an operational consideration?

answers.A: RVR minimums which are specified in the procedures should be converted and applied as ground visibility.
answers.B: RVR minimums may be disregarded, providing the runway has an operative HIRL system.
answers.C: RVR minimums may be disregarded, providing all other components of the ILS system are operative.

explanations.A:
If RVR minimums for takeoff or landing are
prescribed in an instrument approach procedure, but RVR is
inoperative and cannot be reported for the runway of intended
operation, the RVR minimum shall be converted to ground

visibility and shall be the visibility minimum for takeoff or landing
on that runway.
explanations.B:
because RVR minimums must be
converted to ground visibility, not disregarded.
explanations.C:
because RVR minimums must be
converted to ground visibility, not disregarded.

questions.question: Ifthe RVR equipment is inoperative for an IAP that requires a visibility of 2400 RVR, how should the pilot expect the visibility requirement to be reported in lieu of the published RVR?

answers.A: Asa slant range visibility of 2,400 feet.
answers.B: As an RVR of 2,400 feet.
answers.C: As a ground visibility of % SM.

explanations.B:
because RVR cannot be reported if the
RVR equipment is inoperative. It must be converted to ground
visibility.
explanations.C:
Refer to Legend 11 for a chart of

RVR\ visibility comparable values. An RVR of 2,400 ft. may be
converted to % SM visibility when the RVR is not reported.

questions.question: Ifthe RVR is not reported, what meteorological value should you substitute for 2400 RVR?

answers.A: Aground visibility of % NM.
answers.B: Asslant range visibility of 2,400 feet for the final approach segment of the published approach procedure.
answers.C: A ground visibility of ¥% SM.

explanations.A:
because RVR is converted into statute,
not nautical, miles.
explanations.B:
because when RVR is not reported,
ground visibility, not slant range visibility on approach, is
substituted.
explanations.C:
Refer to Legend 11 for a chart of

RVR\ visibility comparable values. An RVR of 2,400 ft. may be
converted to % SM visibility when the RVR is not reported.

questions.question: If an early missed approach is initiated before reaching the MAP, the following procedure should be used unless otherwise cleared by ATC.

answers.A: Proceed to the missed approach point at or above the MDA or DH before executing a turning maneuver.
answers.B: Begin a climbing turn immediately and follow missed approach procedures.
answers.C: Maintain altitude and continue past MAP for 1 minute or 1 mile whichever occurs first.

explanations.A:
When an early missed approach is
executed, the pilot should, unless otherwise directed by ATC, fly
the IAP as specified on the approach plate to the missed
approach point at or above the MDA or DH before executing a

turning maneuver.
explanations.B:
because one should continue to the MAP
before executing any turns.
explanations.C:
because one need only continue to, not
past, the MAP.

questions.question: If the pilot loses visual reference while circling to land from an instrument approach and ATC radar service is not available, the missed approach action should be to

answers.A: execute a climbing turn to parallel the published final approach course and climb to the initial approach altitude.
answers.B: climb to the published circling minimums then proceed direct to the final approach fix.
answers.C: make a climbing turn toward the landing runway and continue the turn until established on the missed approach course.

explanations.A:
because the climbing turn should be

toward the landing runway; then the pilot should execute the
published missed approach procedures.
explanations.B:
because there should be a climbing turn
toward the landing runway.
explanations.C:
If visual reference is lost while circling to
land, the missed approach specified for that particular procedure
must be followed. To become established on the prescribed
missed approach course, the pilot should make an initial
climbing turn toward the landing runway and continue the turn until
established on the missed approach course.

questions.question: If all ILS components are operating and the re established, the missed approach should be it ed visual references are not jated upon

answers.A: arrival at the DH on the glide slope.
answers.B: arrival at the middle marker.
answers.C: expiration of the time listed on the approach chart for missed approach.

explanations.A:
The missed approach procedure should
be executed upon arrival at the decision height (DH) on the glide
slope if the visual reference requirements are not met. Thus, DH
onan ILS is the MAP.
explanations.B:
because the DH rather than the middle
marker is the MAP.
explanations.C:
because the time listed on the approach
chart for missed approaches is used in conjunction with the
localizer for a timed approach if the glide slope fails during the
ILS approach; i.e., itis not the primary indicator.

questions.question: if during an ILS approach in IFR conditions, the approach lights are not visible upon arrival at the DH, the pilot is

answers.A: required to immediately execute the missed approach procedure.
answers.B: permitted to continue the approach and descend to the localizer MDA.
answers.C: permitted to continue the approach to the approach threshold of the ILS runway.

explanations.A:
The missed approach procedure should
be executed upon arrival at the decision height (DH) on the glide

slope if the visual reference requirements are not met. Thus, the
DH onan ILS is the MAP.
explanations.B:
because the DH is the MAP on anILS,
which is lower than the localizer MDA.
explanations.C:
because the pilot may continue the

approach below the DH only if the required visual references
(e.g., approach lights) are established.

questions.question: How does a pilot determine if DME is available on an ILS/LOC?

answers.B: LOC\DME are indicated on en route low altitude frequency box.
answers.C: LOC\DME frequencies available in the Airman's Information Manual.
answers.A: IAP indicate DME\TACAN channel in LOC frequency box.

explanations.A:
If DME is available on an ILS or localizer
approach, the DME/TACAN channel will be indicated in the
localizer frequency box on the approach plate.
explanations.B:
because LOC/DME frequencies are
available on approach plates, not en route charts.
explanations.C:
because the A/M gives general
information on navigation systems, not specific frequencies.

questions.question: Approximately what height is the glide slope centerline at the MM of a typical ILS?

answers.A: 100 feet.
answers.B: 200 feet.
answers.C: 300 feet.

explanations.A:
because the glide slope centerline at the

inner, not middle, marker on a Category II ILS is at 100 ft. above
the TDZE.
explanations.B:
The ILS glide path projection angle is
normally 3° above horizontal so it intersects the middle marker

(MM) at 200 ft. and the outer marker (OM) at about 1,400 ft.
above the touchdown zone elevation (TDZE).
explanations.C:
because the glide slope centerline at the
MM is usually 200 ft. AGL, not 300 ft.

questions.question: (Refer to figures 139 and 140.) Which displacement from the localizer and Glide slope at the 1.9 NM point is indicated?

answers.B: 710 feet to the right of the localizer centerline and 140 feet above the glide slope.
answers.C: 430 feet to the right of the localizer centerline and 28 feet above the glide slope.
answers.A: 710 feet to the left of the localizer centerline and 140 feet below the glide slope.

explanations.A:
because the airplane is to the right, not
left, of the localizer and above, not below, the glide slope.
explanations.B:
The airplane is to the right of the localizer
and above the glide slope each by 2 dots at 1.9 NM out. Per Fig.
139, 2 dots at 1.9 NM are 140 ft. above the glide slope and 710
ft. to the right of the localizer.
explanations.C:
because the 430-ft. and 28-ft. deviations
are at 1,300 ft, not 1.9 NM.

questions.question: ieersaweh' LOCALIZER \ (s.6 Nae) 24. (Refer to figures 139 and 141.) Which displacement from the localizer centerline and glide slope at the 1,300-foot point from the runway is indicated?

answers.B: 28 feet above the glide slope and approximately 250 feet to the left of the runway centerline.
answers.C: 21 feet above the glide slope and approximately 320 feet to the left of the runway centerline.
answers.A: 21 feet below the glide slope and approximately 320 feet to the fight of the runway centerline.

explanations.A:
because the airplane is above, not below,
the glide slope, and to the left, not right, of the localizer.
explanations.B:
because 28 ft. is 2 dots, and 250 ft. is
less than 1% dots.
explanations.C:
The airplane is above the glide slope and
to the left of the localizer by 1% dots each at 1,300 ft. out. Per
extrapolation and Fig. 139, this displacement is 21 ft. above the
glide slope and about 320 ft. to the left of the localizer.

questions.question: om PE 2pore. 281 teorsie GLIDE SLOPE LOCALIZER 25. (Refer to figures 139 and 142.) Which displacement from the localizer and glide slope at the outer marker is indicated?

answers.A: 1,550 feet to the left of the localizer centerline and 210 feet below the glide slope.
answers.B: 1,550 feet to the right of the localizer centerline and 210 feet above the glide slope. C.775 feet to the left of the localizer centerline and 420 feet below the glide slope.

explanations.A:
The airplane is below the glide slope by 1
dot and to the left of the localizer by 2 dots at the outer marker.
Per Fig. 139, 1 dot on the glide slope is 210 ft. at the outer
marker (OM), and 2 dots on the localizer is 1,550 ft.
explanations.B:
because the airplane is to the left, not
right, of the localizer, and below, not above, the glide slope.
explanations.C:
because at the OM 775 ft. is 1 dot on the

localizer, not the glide slope, and 420 ft. is 2 dots on the glide
slope, not the localizer.

questions.question: Which range facility associated with the ILS is identified by the last two letters of the localizer identification group?

answers.A: Inner marker.
answers.B: Outer marker.
answers.C: Middle compass locator.

explanations.A:
because marker beacons are not
identified by letters when they are not compass locators.
explanations.B:
because marker beacons are not
identified by letters when they are not compass locators.
explanations.C:
Compass locators transmit two-letter
identification groups. The outer locator transmits the first two
letters of the localizer identification group, and the middle locator
transmits the last two letters of the localizer identification group.

questions.question: Which indications will a pilot receive where an IM is installed on a front course ILS approach?

answers.A: One dot per second and a steady amber light.
answers.B: Six dots per second and a flashing white light.
answers.C: Alternate dashes and a blue light.

explanations.A:
because the middle marker, not the inner

marker, has an amber light with 95 dot-dash combinations per
minute.
explanations.B:
The inner marker (IM) indicates a point at
which an airplane is at a designated decision height (DH) on the
glide slope between the middle marker and the landing threshold.
It is identified with continuous dots keyed at the rate of 6 dots per
second and a white marker beacon.
explanations.C:
because the outer marker, not the inner
marker, has continuous, not alternate, dashes and a blue light.

questions.question: Which range facility associated with the ILS can be identified by a two-letter coded signal?

answers.A: Middle marker.
answers.B: Outer marker.
answers.C: Compass locator.

explanations.A:
because marker beacons are not
identified by letters when they are not a compass locator.
explanations.B:
because marker beacons are not
identified by letters when they are not a compass locator.
explanations.C:
Each compass locator (middle and outer)
is identified by a two-letter coded signal.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding Parallel ILS approaches?

answers.A: Parallel ILS approach runway centerlines are separated by at least 4,300 feet and standard IFR separation is provided on the adjacent runway.
answers.B: Parallel ILS approaches provide aircraft a minimum of 1% miles radar separation between successive aircraft on the adjacent localizer course.
answers.C: Landing minimums to the adjacent runway will be higher than the minimums to the primary runway, but will normally be lower than the published circling minimums.

explanations.A:
because parallel approach runway
centerlines are separated by at least 4,300 ft., a minimum of 2
mi. diagonal radar separation is between successive aircraft, not

standard IFR separation.
explanations.B:
Aircraft are afforded a minimum of 1% mi.
radar separation diagonally between successive aircraft on the
adjacent localizer course and a minimum 2% mi. radar
separation from aircraft on the same final approach during
parallel ILS operations.
explanations.C:
because a side-step maneuver, not a
parallel ILS approach, will have landing minimums to the adjacent
runway which are higher than the minimums to the primary
runway, but these minimums will normally be lower than the
published circling minimums.

questions.question: Which pilot action is appropriate if more than one component of an ILS is unusable?

answers.A: Use the highest minimum required by any single component that is unusable.
answers.B: Request another approach appropriate to the equipment that is useable.
answers.C: Raise the minimums a total of that required by each component that is unusable.

explanations.A:
Landing minimums published on
instrument approach procedure charts are based upon full
operation of all components and the use of visual aids
associated with the particular instrument approach chart. Higher
visibility minimums are required with inoperative components or
visual aids as specified in FAA tables. If more than one
component is inoperative, each minimum is raised to the highest
minimum required by any single component that is inoperative.
explanations.B:
because an ILS can be used with some
components inoperative. Those inoperative components would
increase the approach minimums, but you would not need to
request another approach appropriate to the equipment that is
usable.
explanations.C:
because it is not cumulative; you need
only use the highest minimum required as a result of any one
component's being unusable.

questions.question: Which substitution is permitted when an ILS component is inoperative?

answers.A: Acompass locator or precision radar may be substituted for the ILS outer or middle marker.
answers.B: ADF or VOR bearings which cross either the outer or middle marker sites may be substituted for these markers.
answers.C: DME, when located at the localizer antenna site, should be ‘substituted for the outer or middle marker.

explanations.A:
A compass locator or precision radar may
be substituted for an inoperative outer or middle marker.
Compass locators, precision radar, DME, VOR, or
nondirectional fixes authorized in the standard instrument
approach or surveillance radar may be substituted for an
inoperative outer marker.
explanations.B:
because ADF and VOR bearings can be
substituted for the outer marker but not the middle marker.
explanations.C:
because DME can be substituted for the
outer marker but not the middle marker.

questions.question: What facilities, if any, may be substituted for an inoperative middle marker during an ILS approach without affecting the straight-in minimums?

answers.B: Substitution not necessary, minimums do not change.
answers.C: Compass locator, PAR, and ASR.
answers.A: ASR.

explanations.A:
because no substitution is necessary for
an inoperative MM since the landing minimums do not change.
explanations.B:
Refer to Legend 22, Inoperative
Components or Visual Aids Table. Note that an inoperative
middle marker (MM) is not listed as an inoperative ILS
component that would require an increase in the visibility
minimum. While a compass locator or PAR may be substituted
for an inoperative MM, no substitution is necessary since the
landing minimums are not changed.
explanations.C:
because no substitution is necessary for
an inoperative MM since the landing minimums do not change.

questions.question: Which of these facilities may be substituted for an MM during a complete ILS. IAP?

answers.A: Surveillance and precision radar.
answers.B: Compass locator and precision radar.
answers.C: AVORIDME fix.

explanations.A:
because airport surveillance radar may
be substituted for the outer marker but not the middle marker.
explanations.B:
Compass locators or precision radar may
be substituted for the outer or middle marker.
explanations.C:
because a VOR/DME fix authorized in

the standard instrument approach may only be substituted for the
outer marker.

questions.question: When installed with the ILS and specified in the approach procedures, DME may be used

answers.B: in lieu of visibility requirements.
answers.C: to determine distance from TDZ.
answers.A: inlieu of the OM.

explanations.A:
When installed with the ILS and specified

in the approach procedure, DME may be used in lieu of the outer
marker (OM).
explanations.B:
because DME has no effect on visibility
requirements.
explanations.C:
because touchdown zone (TDZ) is the
first 3,000 ft. of the runway, not a specific point.

questions.question: Which substitution is appropriate during an ILS approach?

answers.A: AVOR radial crossing the outer marker site may be substituted for the outer marker.
answers.B: LOC minimums should be substituted for ILS minimums whenever the glide slope becomes inoperative.
answers.C: DME, when located at the localizer antenna site, should be substituted for either the outer or middle marker.

explanations.A:
because a VOR radial must be
authorized in the standard approach procedure to be used as a

‘substitute.
explanations.B:
When the glide slope becomes inoperative
during an ILS approach, the approach can be conducted as a
localizer approach and the LOC minimums apply.
explanations.C:
because DME can be substituted for the
outer marker, but not the middle marker.

questions.question: Immediately after passing the final approach fix in bound during an ILS approach in IFR conditions, the glide slope warning flag appears. The pilot is

answers.A: permitted to continue the approach and descend to the DH.
answers.B: permitted to continue the approach and descend to the localizer MDA.
answers.C: required to immediately begin the prescribed missed approach procedure.

explanations.A:
because, once the glide slope is
inoperative, the localizer may be used only for a nonprecision
approach, which uses MDA, not DH.
explanations.B:
When the glide slope fails, the approach
can continue as a nonprecision localizer approach. Accordingly,
if the glide slope fails on an ILS approach, the pilot may switch to
the localizer approach and descend to the localizer MDA.
(minimum descent altitude).
explanations.C:
because one should execute the missed

approach procedure only after reaching the missed approach
point.

questions.question: Apilot is making an ILS approach and is past the OM to a runway which has a VASI. What action should the pilot take if an electronic glide slope malfunction occurs and the pilot has the VASI in sight?

answers.A: The pilot should inform ATC of the malfunction and then descend immediately to the localizer DH and make a localizer approach.
answers.B: The pilot may continue the approach and use the VASI glide slope in place of the electronic glide slope.
answers.C: The pilot must request an LOC approach, and may descend below the VASI at the pilot's discretion.

explanations.A:
because, once the pilot has the

necessary visual references, the approach may be continued
visually.
explanations.B:
Once the necessary specified visual
requirements, e.g., the VASI, are attained for the intended
tunway, the pilot may continue the approach and use the VAS in
place of the electronic glide slope.
explanations.C:
because, once the pilot has the
necessary visual references, the approach may be continued

visually. Descent below the VASI glide path shall occur only when
necessary for a safe landing.

questions.question: The rate of descent on the glide slope is dependent upon

answers.A: true airspeed.
answers.B: calibrated airspeed.
answers.C: ground speed.

explanations.A:
because the rate of descent is based on
ground speed, not true airspeed.
explanations.B:
because the rate of descent is based on
ground speed, not calibrated airspeed.
explanations.C:
The rate of descent required to stay on the
ILS glide slope depends on the ground speed because the
descent must be constant relative to the distance traveled over
the ground. Thus, the descent must be decreased if ground
speed is decreased.

questions.question: The rate of descent required to stay on the ILS glide slope

answers.A: must be increased if the ground speed is decreased.
answers.B: will remain constant if the indicated airspeed remains constant.
answers.C: must be decreased if the ground speed is decreased.

explanations.A:
because, if ground speed decreases and
descent increases, the airplane will go below the glide slope.
explanations.B:
because ground speed rather than
airspeed determines the rate of descent.
explanations.C:
The rate of descent required to stay on the
ILS glide slope is dependent on the ground speed because the
descent must be constant relative to the distance traveled over

the ground. Thus, the descent must be decreased if ground
speed is decreased.

questions.question: To remain on the ILS glidepath, the rate of descent must be

answers.A: decreased if the airspeed is increased.
answers.B: decreased if the ground speed is increased.
answers.C: increased if the ground speed is increased.

explanations.A:
because the rate of descent must be

based upon ground speed, not airspeed, while on the glide
slope.
explanations.B:
because, if one decreases the rate of

descent with ground speed increasing, the airplane will rise
above the glide slope.
explanations.C:
The rate of descent required to stay on the
ILS glide slope depends on the ground speed because the
descent must be constant relative to the distance traveled over

the ground. Thus, the descent must be increased if ground speed
is increased.

questions.question: When passing through an abrupt wind shear which involves a shift from a tailwind to a headwind, what power management would normally be required to maintain a constant indicated airspeed and ILS glide slope?

answers.A: Higher than normal power initially, followed by a further increase as the wind shear is encountered, then a decrease.
answers.B: Lower than normal power initially, followed by a further decrease as the wind shear is encountered, then an increase.
answers.C: Higher than normal power initially, followed by a decrease as the shear is encountered, then an increase.

explanations.A:
because initially there is
lower-than-normal, not higher-than-normal, power with a tailwind,
and when the headwind is encountered, a decrease, not an
increase, in power is required.
explanations.B:
When an airplane is on the ILS glide slope
and there is a change from a tailwind to a headwind, the
groundspeed will decrease. During the tailwind,
lower-than-normal power will be required. When the wind shear is
encountered, even lower power will be required to decrease the
spurt in airspeed. Once the wind shifts to a headwind, the
airplane will require an increase in power to maintain the
necessary groundspeed to stay on the ILS glide slope.
explanations.C:
because initially there is
lower-than-normal, not higher-than-normal, power with a tailwind.

questions.question: What effect will a change in wind direction have upon maintaining a 3° glide slope at a constant true airspeed?

answers.A: When ground speed decreases, rate of descent must increase.
answers.B: When ground speed increases, rate of descent must increase.
answers.C: Rate of descent must be constant to remain on the glide slope.

explanations.A:
because, if you increase the rate of
descent when the ground speed decreases, you will fly below the
glide slope.
explanations.B:
The rate of descent required to stay on the
ILS glide slope is dependent on the ground speed because the
descent must be constant relative to the distance traveled over

the ground. Thus, the descent must be increased if ground speed
is increased.
explanations.C:
because the rate of descent must change
with changes in ground speed.

questions.question: The glide slope and localizer are centered, but the airspeed is too fast. Which should be adjusted initially?

answers.A: Pitch and power.
answers.B: Power only.
answers.C: Pitch only.

explanations.A:
because, although the pitch and power

adjustments must be closely coordinated, the power is actually
adjusted first.
explanations.B:
If the glide slope and localizer are centered
but the airspeed is too fast, you should reduce power initially.
Aimost immediately, you will then have to make pitch adjustments

to compensate for the power adjustment to maintain the
glidepath.
explanations.C:
because adjusting pitch initially would
cause you to fly above the glide path.

questions.question: While being vectored, if crossing the ILS final approach course becomes imminent and an approach clearance has not been issued, what action should be taken by the pilot?

answers.A: Turn outbound on the final approach course, execute a procedure turn, and inform ATC.
answers.B: Turn inbound and execute the missed approach procedure at the outer marker if approach clearance has not been received.
answers.C: Maintain the last assigned heading and query ATC.

explanations.A:
because you should maintain the last

assigned heading until you receive an amended clearance.
When in doubt, query ATC.
explanations.B:
because you should maintain the last
assigned heading until you receive an amended clearance.
When in doubt, query ATC.
explanations.C:
While being vectored, if you determine that
crossing the final approach course is imminent and you have not
been informed that you will be vectored across it, you should
question the controller. You should not turn inbound on the final

approach course unless you have received an approach
clearance.

questions.question: Thrust is managed to maintain IAS, and glide slope is being flown. What characteristics should be observed when a headwind shears to be a constant tailwind?

answers.A: PITCH ATTITUDE: Increases; REQUIRED THRUST: Increased, then reduced; VERTICAL SPEED: Increases; IAS: Increases, then decreases to approach speed.
answers.B: PITCH ATTITUDE: Decreases; REQUIRED THRUST: Increased, then reduced; VERTICAL SPEED: Increases; IAS: Decreases, then increases to approach speed.
answers.C: PITCH ATTITUDE: Increases; REQUIRED THRUST: Reduced, then increased; VERTICAL SPEED: Decreases; IAS: Decreases, then increases to approach speed.

explanations.A:
because the airspeed decreases, not
increases, initially as the headwind shears to a tailwind, causing
the pitch to decrease, not increase.
explanations.B:
When a headwind shears to a tailwind, the
airplane's airspeed drops, its nose pitches down, and its vertical
speed increases. The power must be increased initially to
resume normal approach speed, then reduced as airspeed
stabilizes to maintain the glide slope due to the increased
groundspeed.
explanations.C:
because the pitch attitude decreases, not
increases, due to the decreased airspeed, causing the vertical
speed to increase, not decrease. Initially, the thrust must be
increased, not decreased, to maintain approach airspeed.

questions.question: While flying a 3° glide slope, a constant tailwind shears to a calm wind. Which conditions should the pilot expect?

answers.A: Airspeed and pitch attitude decrease and there is a tendency to go below glide slope.
answers.B: Airspeed and pitch attitude increase and there is a tendency to go below glide slope.
answers.C: Airspeed and pitch attitude increase and there is a tendency to go above glide slope.

explanations.A:
because the airspeed and pitch increase,
not decrease, and there is a tendency to go above, not below, the
glide slope.
explanations.B:
because the tendency is to go above, not
below, the glide slope.
explanations.C:
When a constant tailwind shears to a calm
wind, the airplane's airspeed increases, its nose pitches up, and
it has a tendency to go above the glide slope. The nose pitches
up due to the increased lift from the increased airspeed.

questions.question: While flying a 3° glide slope, a headwind shears to a tailwind. Which conditions should the pilot expect on the glide slope?

answers.A: Airspeed and pitch attitude decrease and there is a tendency to go below glide slope.
answers.B: Airspeed and pitch attitude increase and there is a tendency to go above glide slope.
answers.C: Airspeed and pitch attitude decrease and there is a tendency to remain on the glide slope.

explanations.A:
When a headwind shears to a tailwind, the
airplane's airspeed drops, its nose pitches down, and it begins to
drop below the glide slope. The airplane will be both slow and
power deficient.
explanations.B:
because airspeed and pitch decrease,
not increase, and there is a tendency to go below, not above, the
glide slope.
explanations.C:
because there is a tendency to go below,
not remain on, the glide slope.

questions.question: During a precision radar or ILS approach, the rate of descent required to remain on the glide slope will

answers.A: remain the same regardless of groundspeed.
answers.B: increase as the groundspeed increases.
answers.C: decrease as the groundspeed increases.

explanations.A:
because the descent rate varies with the
groundspeed.
explanations.B:
The rate of descent required to stay on the
ILS glide slope is dependent on the groundspeed because the
descent must be constant relative to the distance traveled over
the ground. Thus, the descent must be increased if groundspeed
is increased.
explanations.C:
because the descent rate must increase,
not decrease, as groundspeed increases.

questions.question: When tracking in bound on the localizer, which of the following is the proper procedure regarding drift corrections?

answers.A: Drift corrections should be accurately established before reaching the outer marker and completion of the approach should be accomplished with heading corrections no greater than 2°.
answers.B: Drift corrections should be made in 5° increments after passing the outer marker.
answers.C: Drift corrections should be made in 10° increments after passing the outer marker.

explanations.A:
When you are tracking in bound on the
localizer, your drift correction should be small and reduced
proportionately as the course narrows. By the time you reach the
outer marker, your drift correction should be established
accurately enough to permit completion of the approach with
heading corrections no greater than 2°.
explanations.B:
because, after you pass the outer marker,
your drift corrections should be no greater than 2°, not 5°.
explanations.C:
because, after you pass the outer marker,
your drift corrections should be no greater than 2°, not 10°.

questions.question: Which information, in addition to headings, does the radar controller provide without request during an ASR approach?

answers.A: The recommended altitude for each mile from the runway.
answers.B: When reaching the MDA.
answers.C: When to commence descent to MDA, the aircraft's position each mile on final from the runway, and arrival at the MAP.

explanations.A:
because the recommended altitude for
each mile from the runway is provided only upon request.
explanations.B:
because the controller does not have
precise altitude capability.
explanations.C:
A surveillance approach (ASR) provides
navigation guidance in azimuths (direction) only. The pilot is
furnished headings to align the airplane with the extended
centerline of the landing runway and will be advised when to
commence descent to the MDA and the MAP. In addi tion, the
pilot will be advised of the airplane's position each mile on the
final approach from the runway or MAP as appropriate.

questions.question: Where may you use a surveillance approach?

answers.B: At any airport which has radar service.
answers.C: At airports for which civil radar instrument approach minimums have been published.
answers.A: Atany airport that has an approach control.

explanations.A:
because specific procedures, minimums,
missed approach points, etc., must be established before a
surveillance approach can be conducted by ATC.
explanations.B:
because specific procedures, minimums,
missed approach points, etc., must be established before a
surveillance approach can be conducted by ATC.
explanations.C:
ASR (surveillance) approaches are
available at airports for which radar instrument approach
minimums have been published and a separate approach chart
is available. That is, a surveillance approach must have
previously been authorized and established by the FAA for a
particular runway at a particular airport prior to its availability.

questions.question: How is ATC radar used for instrument approaches when the facility is approved for approach control service?

answers.A: Precision approaches, weather surveillance, and as a substitute for any inoperative component of a navigation aid used for approaches.
answers.B: ASR approaches, weather surveillance, and course guidance by approach control.
answers.C: Course guidance to the final approach course, ASR and PAR approaches, and the monitoring of nonradar approaches.

explanations.A:
because approach control radar is not
designed for weather surveillance.
explanations.B:
because approach control radar is not
designed for weather surveillance.
explanations.C:
Where radar is approved for approach
control service, it is used not only to provide course guidance for
radar approaches but also to provide vectors in conjunction with
published nonradar approaches based on radio NAVAIDs.

questions.question: During a "no-gyro” approach and prior to being handed off to the final approach controller, the pilot should make all turns A_ one-half standard rate unless otherwise advised.

answers.B: any rate not exceeding a 30° bank.
answers.C: standard rate unless otherwise advised.

explanations.A:
because one-half the standard-rate turn
should be used in conjunction with the final approach controller.
explanations.B:
because the turn should be at the
standard rate unless otherwise advised.
explanations.C:
During "no-gyro" approaches prior to the

final approach, all turns should be made at the standard rate
unless otherwise advised by ATC.

questions.question: After being handed off to the final approach controller during a "no-gyro" surveillance or precision approach, the pilot should make all turns

answers.A: one-half standard rate.
answers.B: based upon the groundspeed of the aircraft.
answers.C: standard rate.

explanations.A:
After being handed off to the final

approach controller on a "no-gyro" surveillance or precision
approach, all turns should be at one-half the standard rate.
explanations.B:
because the established procedure is to
turn at one-half the standard rate regardless of groundspeed.
explanations.C:
because a standard-rate turn should be

used on "no-gyro” approaches prior to working with the final
approach controller.

questions.question: When cleared to execute a published sidestep maneuver for a specific approach and landing on the parallel runway, at what point is the pilot expected to commence this maneuver?

answers.B: As soon as possible after the runway or runway environment is in sight.
answers.C: At the localizer MDA minimum and when the runway is in sight.
answers.A: At the published minimum altitude for a circling approach.

explanations.A:
because the side-step maneuver should
be performed only when the runway environment is in sight.
explanations.B:
Pilots are expected to commence the
side-step maneuver as soon as possible after the runway or
runway environment is in sight.
explanations.C:
because the side-step maneuver should

be performed as soon as the runway environment is in sight,
which may be before reaching the MDA.

questions.question: Assume this clearance is received: "CLEARED FOR ILS RUNWAY 07 LEFT APPROACH, SIDE-STEP TO RUNWAY 07 RIGHT." When would the pilot be expected to commence the side-step maneuver?

answers.A: As soon as possible after the runway environment is in sight.
answers.B: Any time after becoming aligned with the final approach course of Runway 07 left, and after passing the final approach fix.
answers.C: After reaching the circling minimums for Runway 07 right.

explanations.A:
Pilots are expected to commence the
side-step maneuver as soon as possible after the runway or
runway environment is in sight.
explanations.B:
because the side-step maneuver should

be performed as soon as possible but only after the runway or
funway environment is in sight.
explanations.C:
because the side-step maneuver should

be performed as soon as possible but only after the runway or
runway environment is in sight.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is required before "timed approaches from a holding fix" may be conducted?

answers.A: If more than one missed approach procedure is available, only one may require a course reversal.
answers.B: If more than one missed approach procedure is available, none may require a course reversal.
answers.C: Direct communication between the pilot and the tower must be established prior to beginning the approach.

explanations.A:
because no course reversals are
permitted on a missed approach procedure if more than one
missed approach procedure is available.
explanations.B:
Timed approaches from a holding fix may
be conducted when a control tower is in operation at the airport
of intended landing and direct communications are maintained
between the pilot and center approach until switching to the
tower. Course reversals are not permitted when more than one
missed approach procedure exists.
explanations.C:
because, prior to beginning the

approach, the pilot must be in contact with approach, not the
tower.

questions.question: If only one missed approach procedure is available, which of the following conditions is required when conducting "timed approaches from a holding fix"?

answers.A: The pilot must contact the airport control tower prior to departing the holding fix in bound.
answers.B: The reported ceiling and visibility minimums must be equal to or greater than the highest prescribed circling minimums for the IAP.
answers.C: The reported ceiling and visibility minimums must be equal to or greater than the highest prescribed straight in MDA minimums for the IAP.

explanations.A:
because the pilot contacts the tower when
so directed by approach or center.
explanations.B:
If only one mi: approach procedure is
available, the reported ceiling and visibility must be equal to or
greater than the highest prescribed circling minimums for the IAP.
explanations.C:
because the ceiling and visibility

minimums must exceed the highest circling, not straight in,
minimums.

questions.question: Prior to conducting "timed approaches from a holding fix," which one of the following is required?

ins when the inbound turn is completed, not when it is
initiated.
explanations.C:
because the timing of the pattern is
adjusted by varying the length of the outbound leg. Once inbound,
you must fly to the holding fix and cannot adjust the length of the
leg.

questions.question: When holding at an NDB, at what point should the timing begin for the second leg outbound?

answers.A: When the wings are level and the wind drift correction angle is established after completing the turn to the outbound heading.

because only when you cannot determine
position abeam the fix should you start the timing when the turn is
complete.
explanations.B:
because timing of the outbound leg
begins when abeam the fix, not when the wings are level.
explanations.C:
Outbound timing begins over or abeam the
fix, whichever occurs later. If the abeam position cannot be
determined, start timing when the turn to outbound is completed.

questions.question: To ensure proper airspace protection while holding at 5,000 feet in a civil aircraft, what is the maximum indicated airspeed a pilot should use?

answers.B: 200 knots.

explanations.A:
because 230 kt. is the maximum holding
speed from 6,001 ft. through 14,000 ft.
explanations.B:
The maximum airspeed in holding patterns
for a civil aircraft is 200 kt. from the minimum holding altitude
(MHA) through 6,000 ft.
explanations.C:
because 210 kt. is the maximum holding
airspeed from 6,001 ft. through 14,000 ft. where published.

executed within the time or leg length published in the profile view
of the IAP.
explanations.B:
because a radius of 5 mi. for a procedure
turn can be specified only for category A or helicopter aircraft.
explanations.C:
because ATC does not specify a holding

speed. You need only remain below the maximum allowable
holding speed.

The fixes depicted on Instrument Approach

because IAFs are specifically identified
with "IAF."

questions.question: Aircraft approach categories are based on

answers.A: certificated approach speed at maximum gross weight.
answers.B: 1.3 times the stall speed in landing configuration at maximum gross landing weight.
answers.C: 1.3 times the stall speed at maximum gross weight.

explanations.A:
because aircraft do not have certificated
approach speeds.
explanations.B:
IFR approach minimums are specified for
various aircraft speed/weight combinations. Speeds are based
upon the value of 1.3 times the stall speed of the aircraft in the
landing configuration at maximum certified gross landing weight.
explanations.C:
because speeds are based on 1.3 times

the stall speed in landing configuration at maximum gross landing
weight, not just maximum gross weight.

questions.question: What does the symbol T within a black triangle in the minimums section of the IAP for a particular airport indicate?

answers.A: Takeoff minimums are 1 mile for aircraft having two engines or less and % mile for those with more than two engines.
answers.B: Instrument takeoffs are not authorized.
answers.C: Takeoff minimums are not standard and/or departure procedures are published.

explanations.A:
because it gives the standard minimums
for takeoff when there is a published instrument approach.
explanations.B:
because the alternate takeoff procedures
will indicate if instrument takeoffs are not authorized.
explanations.C:
The symbol in the question indicates that
takeoff minimums are not standard and/or departure procedures
are published, and one should consult the alternate takeoff
procedures. Takeoff minimums apply to operations under Parts
121, 125, 127, 129, and 135, i.e., operations other than Part 91.

questions.question: What does the absence of the procedure turn barb on the plan view on an approach chart indicate?

answers.A: Aprocedure turn is not authorized.
answers.B: Teardrop-type procedure turn is authorized.
answers.C: Racetrack-type procedure turn is authorized.

explanations.A:
The absence of the procedure turn barb in

the plan view indicates that a procedure turn is not authorized for
that approach.
explanations.B:
because the absence of a procedure turn
barb indicates that all, not just teardrop-type, procedure turns are
not authorized.
explanations.C:
because the absence of a procedure turn

barb indicates that all, not just racetrack-type, procedure turns
are not authorized.

questions.question: During an instrument approach, under what conditions, if any, is the holding pattern course reversal not required?

answers.A: When radar vectors are provided.
answers.B: When cleared for the approach.
answers.C: None, since it is always mandatory.

explanations.A:
A course reversal (procedure turn) is not
required when radar vectors are being provided.
explanations.B:
because a course reversal may be
required when cleared for a full approach.
explanations.C:
because a course reversal is not
mandatory when radar vectors are provided.

questions.question: When making an instrument approach at the selected alternate airport, what landing minimums apply?

answers.A: Standard alternate minimums (600-2 or 800-2).
answers.B: The IFR alternate minimums listed for that airport.
answers.C: The landing minimums published for the type of procedure selected.

explanations.A:
because alternate minimums refer to the
minimum forecast weather allowable to list an airport as an
alternate on the flight plan.
explanations.B:
because alternate minimums refer to the

minimum forecast weather allowable to list an airport as an
alternate on the flight plan.
explanations.C:
Published landing minimums always apply
when making an instrument approach to an airport.

questions.question: When the approach procedure involves a procedure turn, the maximum speed should not be greater than

answers.A: 180 knots IAS.
answers.B: 200 knots IAS.
answers.C: 250 knots IAS.

explanations.A:
because the maximum speed that should
be used is 200 kt, not 180 kt.
explanations.B:
When the approach procedure involves a
procedure turn, a maximum speed of not greater than 200 kt. IAS

should be observed, and the turn should be executed within the
distance specified in the profile view.
explanations.C:
because the maximum speed that should
be used is 200 kt., not 250 kt.

questions.question: What obstacle clearance and navigation signal coverage is a pilot assured with the Minimum Sector Altitudes depicted on the IAP charts?

answers.A: 1,000 feet and acceptable navigation signal coverage within a 25 NM radius of the navigation facility.
answers.B: 1,000 feet within a 25 NM radius of the navigation facility but not acceptable navigation signal coverage.
answers.C: 500 feet and acceptable navigation signal coverage within a 10 NM radius of the navigation facility.

explanations.A:
because minimum sector altitudes do not
guarantee acceptable signal coverage.
explanations.B:
Minimum sector altitudes are depicted on
approach charts and provide at least 1,000 ft. of obstacle
clearance within a 25-NM radius of the navigation facility upon
which the procedure is predicated. These altitudes are for

emergency use only and do not necessarily assure acceptable
navigational signal coverage.
explanations.C:
because minimum sector altitudes do not
guarantee acceptable signal coverage, and they provide 1,000
ft, not 500 ft., of obstacle clearance.

questions.question: During an instrument precision approach, terrain and obstacle clearance depends on adherence to

answers.A: minimum altitude shown on the IAP.
answers.B: terrain contour information.
answers.C: natural and man-made reference point information.

explanations.A:
A pilot adhering to the altitudes, flight
paths, and weather minimums depicted on the IAP chart is
assured of terrain and obstruction clearance.
explanations.B:
because the design of IAPs takes terrain
and obstacle clearance into account.
explanations.C:
because, during instrument approaches,

instrument, not visual, reference points are used to assure terrain
and obstacle clearance.

questions.question: When being radar vectored for an ILS approach, at what point may you start a descent from your last assigned altitude to a lower minimum altitude if cleared for the approach?

answers.A: When established on a segment of a published route or IAP.
answers.B: You may descend immediately to published glide slope interception altitude.
answers.C: Only after you are established on the final approach unless informed otherwise by ATC.

explanations.A:
When you are cleared for the approach
while being radar vectored, you must maintain your last assigned
altitude until the airplane is established on a segment of a
published route or IAP. Then use the published altitude to
descend within each succeeding route or approach segment.
explanations.B:
because you must wait to descend until
you are on part of the published procedure.
explanations.C:
because you should follow prescribed

altitudes whenever you are on a segment of a published route or
IAP.

questions.question: While being radar vectored, an approach clearance is received. The last assigned altitude should be maintained until

answers.A: reaching the FAF.
answers.B: advised to begin descent.
answers.C: established on a segment of a published route or IAP.

explanations.A:
because published altitudes may be used

as soon as the aircraft is on a published route, which should be
before the FAF.
explanations.B:
because, when ATC issues an approach

clearance, descent to published altitudes is left to the discretion
of the pilot.
explanations.C:
When an approach clearance is received,
the last assigned altitude should be maintained until the aircraft is

established on a segment of a published route or IAP. Then
published altitudes apply.

questions.question: When simultaneous approaches are in progress, how does each pilot receive radar advisories?

answers.A: On tower frequency.
answers.B: On approach control frequency.
answers.C: One pilot on tower frequency and the other on approach control frequency.

explanations.A:
When simultaneous approaches are in
progress, each pilot will be advised to monitor the tower
frequency to receive advisories and instructions.
explanations.B:
because pilots will receive radar
advisories on tower, not approach control, frequency.
explanations.C:
because both pilots will receive radar
advisories on tower frequency.

questions.question: When may a pilot make a straight-in landing, if using an IAP having only circling minimums?

answers.A: Astraight-in landing may not be made, but the pilot may continue to the runway at MDA and then circle to land on the runway.
answers.B: The pilot may land straight-in if the runway is the active runway and (s)he has been cleared to land.
answers.C: A straight-in landing may be made if the pilot has the runway in sight in sufficient time to make a normal approach for landing, and has been cleared to land.

explanations.A:
because a straight-in landing may be
made if it is the appropriate runway.
explanations.B:
because the pilot must also have
sufficient time to make a normal approach for a landing.
explanations.C:
When the normal rate of descent or the
runway alignment factor of 30° is exceeded, a straight-in
minimum is not published, and a circling minimum applies. Even
without published straig] minimums, the pilot may land
straight-in if (s)he has the active runway in sight in sufficient time
to make a normal landing and has been cleared to land.

questions.question: Which procedure should be followed by a pilot who is circling to landina Category B airplane, but is maintaining a speed 5 knots faster than the maximum specified for that category?

excess of the upper limit of the speed range for any category, the
minimums for the next higher category should be used.
explanations.B:
because a pilot should use minimums for

the category appropriate to the approach speed being used.
explanations.C:
because Category D minimums do not
necessarily apply to all circling approaches.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 128.) What is the purpose of the 10,300 MSA on the Price/Carbon County Airport Approach Chart?

answers.A: It provides safe clearance above the highest obstacle in the defined sector out to 25 NM.
answers.B: It provides an altitude above which navigational course guidance is assured.

The MSA in PUC sector R-110 to R-200
at 10,300 ft. provides safe clearance above the highest
obstacle plus 1,000 ft. in the defined sector out to 25 NM.
explanations.B:
because navigational course guidance
is not assured by the MSA.
explanations.C:
because MSA gives a safe clearance
altitude, not a minimum vector altitude.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 123.) The symbol on the plan view of the VOR/DME-A procedure at 7D3 represents a minimum safe sector altitude within 25 NM of

explanations.C:
because an MSA is always based ona

navigation facility or a waypoint (GPS or RNAV approach), not

questions.question: (Refer to figure 123.) What minimum navigation equipment is required to complete the VOR/DME-A procedure?

VORTAC, only one VOR receiver is required. DME is also

explanations.C:
because only one VOR receiver, not two
receivers, is required.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 129.) What indication should you get when it is time to turn in bound while in the procedure turn at LABER?

because no 12-NM distance is shown
from LIT.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 129.) What type of entry is recommended to the missed approach holding pattern if the inbound heading is 050°?

questions.question: (Refer to figure 129.) How should the missed approach point be identified when executing the RNAV RWY 36 approach at Adams Field?

answers.A: When the TO-FROM indicator changes.
answers.B: Upon arrival at 760 feet on the glidepath.

The MAP is a waypoint and is identified
when the TO-FROM indicator changes, which indicates station
passage at the waypoint; i.e., you have arrived at the MAP and
the visual references are not there, so you must execute a
missed approach.
explanations.B:
because you will be at 760 ft. ona RWY
36 approach for approximately 17 NM before reaching the
MAP.
explanations.C:
because, on the RNAV RWY 36

approach, the MAP is identified by a waypoint, not by the time
from the FAF.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 129.) What minimum airborne equipment is required to be operative for RNAV RWY 36 approach at Adams Field?

answers.A: An approved RNAV receiver that provides both horizontal and vertical guidance.
answers.B: A transponder and an approved RNAV receiver that provides both horizontal and vertical guidance.
answers.C: Any approved RNAV receiver.

explanations.A:
because RNAV receivers with vertical
guidance are not required for RNAV approaches.
explanations.B:
because RNAV receivers with vertical
guidance are not required for RNAV approaches.
explanations.C:
An approved RNAV receiver is required
for RNAV approaches. Area navigation, when approved by the
FAA, is sufficient to conduct RNAV approaches. Area
navigation simply moves the location of VORs based upon
internal circuitry.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 130.) How does an LDA facility, such as the one at Roanoke Regional, differ from a standard ILS approach facility?

answers.A: The LOC is wider.
answers.B: The LOC is offset from the runway.
answers.C: The GS is unusable beyond the MM.

explanations.A:
because the LOC in an LDA is similar in
width to the localizer in an ILS.
explanations.B:
LDA (localizer-type directional aid) has
utility and accuracy comparable to a localizer but is not part of a
complete ILS. The LDA is not aligned with the runway.
explanations.C:
because the note in the profile view of

Fig. 130 states that the glide slope is unusable inside, not
beyond, the MM.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 130.) What are the procedure turn restrictions on the LDA RWY 6 approach at Roanoke Regional?

answers.A: Remain within 10 NM of CLAMM INT and on the north side of the approach course.
answers.B: Remain within 10 NM of the airport on the north side of the approach course.

In the IAP chart, the profile view indicates
in its upper left corner: "Remain within 10 NM." That means 10
NM from the final approach fix, which is the CLAMM INT on the
Callahan NDB. The procedure turn also indicates right turn
outbound, which means that one must remain on the north side
of the approach course.
explanations.B:
because the 10-NM ring is around the
FAF, not the airport.
explanations.C:
because the 10-NM ring is around the
FAF, not the outer marker.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 130.) What are the restrictions regarding circle to land procedures for LDA RWY/GS 6 approach at Roanoke Regional?

answers.A: Circling to runway 24 not authorized.
answers.B: Circling not authorized NW of RWY 6-24.

because circling to runway 15, not 24, is

explanations.B:
In the remarks section of the IAP chart, it
is noted that circling is not authorized (NA) northwest of RWY
6-24 and to RWY 15.

because the minimum circling visibility
goes up 1/4 to 3/4 SM, depending on aircraft category.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 130.) At what minimum altitude should you cross CLAMM intersection during the S-LDA 6 approach at Roanoke Regional?

explanations.A:
On the final approach using the S-LDA 6
approach, you presumably do not have glide slope capability
(otherwise you will use S-LDA/GS 6). Thus, the minimum
altitude at CLAMM is 4,200 ft. MSL (see the note at 4,500 glide
slope interception altitude).
explanations.B:
because 4,182 ft. is the GS altitude at
CLAMM.
explanations.C:
because 2,800 ft. is the minimum
altitude after CLAMM and prior to SKIRT OM.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 130.) How should the pilot identify the missed approach point for the S-LDA GS 6 approach to Roanoke Regional?

answers.A: Arrival at 1,540 feet on the glide slope.
answers.B: Arrival at 1.0 DME on the LDA course.
answers.C: Time expired for distance from OM to MAP.

explanations.A:
Since the S-LDA/GS 6 is a precision
approach (due to the electronic glide slope), the MAP is arrival
at decision height (1,540 ft. for Categories A, B, and C aircraft)
on the glide slope.
explanations.B:
because 1.3 DME, not 1.0 DME, is the
MAP on the LDA, not LDA GS, approach.
explanations.C:
because precision approaches do not
provide for time expiration to the MAP, other than as a backup.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 131.) What determines the MAP for the straight-in VOR/DME RNAV RWY 4R approach at BOS?

answers.B: 5 NMto RULSY way point.
answers.C: 2.5 NM to RULSY at 840 feet MSL.

because the missed approach point is

RULSY WP" above the missed approach point means that the
missed approach point is located 0.5 NM from RULSY way
point. Therefore, the missed approach procedure should begin
when .05 NM remains before reaching RULSY way point.
explanations.C:
because 2.5 NM to RULSY way point at

840 ft. MSL is the visual descent point, indicated by the heavy
"V" in the profile view, not the missed approach point.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 131.) The control tower at BOS reports “tall vessels" in the approach area. What are the VOR/DME RNAV RWY 4R straight-in approach minimums for Category A aircraft?

explanations.A:
There is a note in the second line of
information at the top of the VOR/DME RNAV RWY 4R,
approach chart which states that category A aircraft making the
straight-in approach must increase the visibility minimums to
RVR 4,000 when the control tower reports tall vessels in the
approach area. No adjustments to the MDA are required, so the
minimums are 840 ft. MSL and RVR 4,000.
explanations.B:
because the visibility minimums must be

increased to RVR 4,000, and there is no 890 ft. MSL MDA for
the VOR/DME RNAV RWY 4R approach at BOS.
explanations.C:
because there is no 890 ft. MSL MDA
for the VOR/DME RNAV RWY 4R approach at BOS.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 131.) Other than VOR/DME RNAV, what additional navigation equipment is required to conduct the VOR/DME RNAV RWY 4R approach at BOS?

answers.A: None
answers.B: VNAV.
answers.C: Transponder with altitude encoding and Marker Beacon.

explanations.A:
No additional equipment is required to
conduct the VOR/DME RNAV RWY 4R approach at Boston. All
approach waypoints, including the missed approach waypoint,
the missed approach holding waypoint, and the minimum safe

altitude (MSA) circle center waypoint, require the use of just the
VOR/DME RNAV equipment.
explanations.B:
because vertical navigation (VNAV)
equipment may be used if available, but it is not required. If it is
available and is used, the profile view of the approach chart
shows a 3.00° descent angle. The visual descent point shown 2
miles from the missed approach waypoint on the profile view of
the chart is not a mandatory descent point and is based on
distance from the runway at the MDA of 840 ft. MSL, not on
vertical navigation.
explanations.C:
because, even though a transponder
with altitude encoding (Mode C) would normally be required to
operate in the Boston Class B airspace, it is not required
equipment to conduct any instrument approach procedure. In
addition, no marker beacon is shown on the instrument
approach chart, therefore, none is required.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 131.) What is the landing distance available for the VOR/DME RNAV RWY 4R approach at BOS?

explanations.A:
because 7,000 ft. is the length of runway
9-27, not the available landing distance on runway 4R.

notation signifies that the runway length available for landing is
8,850 ft.; the remainder of the 10,005 ft. runway length is a

explanations.C:
because 10,005 ft. is the total length of
runway 4R, not the runway length available for landing.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 131.) During a missed approach from the VOR/DME RNAV RWY 4R approach at BOS, what course should be flown to the missed approach holding way point?

answers.B: Runway heading.

because the missed approach

because the missed approach

procedure is fly to WAXEN via the 033° track (course), not via
runway heading.
explanations.C:
In the upper right corner of Fig. 131, just
under "Boston, Massachusetts," there is a missed approach
procedure information box. It reads, "MISSED APPROACH:
Climb to 3000 via 033° track to WAXEN WP and hold." Also, on

climb to 3,000 feet on a track of 033° to WAXEN.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 124.) What options are available concerning the teardrop course reversal for LOC RWY 35 approach to Duncan/Halliburton Field?

answers.A: Ifa course reversal is required, only the teardrop can be executed.
answers.B: The point where the turn is begun and the type and rate of turn are optional.

When a procedure turn track is specified
for the LOC RWY 35 approach, the turn must be flown exactly as
depicted. Thus, only the teardrop can be executed.
explanations.B:
because the turn must be begun at a
point such that the aircraft remains within 10 NM of the VOR,
and the procedure turn must be a teardrop.
explanations.C:
because the procedure turn must be a
teardrop.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 124.) The point on the teardrop procedure where the turn in bound (LOC RWY 35) Duncan/Halliburton, is initiated is determined by

answers.A: DME and timing to remain within the 10-NM limit.
answers.B: Timing for a 2 minute maximum.
answers.C: Estimating ground speed and radius of turn.

explanations.A:
The pilot may use DME and/or timing to

discretion as long as (s)he remains within 10 NM of Duncan
VOR.

because the only maximum limit on the

because estimating ground speed and

tadius of turn is only part of what is required. The pilot must also
remain within 10 NM.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 133.) How should a pilot reverse course to get established on the in bound course of the ILS RWY 9, if radar vectoring or the three IAF's are not utilized?

answers.A: Execute a standard 45° procedure turn toward Seal Beach VORTAC or Pomona VORTAC.

because to execute a standard 45°

explanations.B:

Lake outer marker/intersection.

because the depicted holding pattem is

the only type of course reversal authorized for the ILS RWY 9

questions.question: (Refer to figure 133.) What type of entry is recommended for the missed approach holding pattern at Riverside Municipal?

answers.A: Direct.
answers.B: Parallel.

3.000 ft. to Jaser INT. then descend to 2.500 ft. on the localizer

questions.question: A particular instrument departure procedure requires a minimum climb rate of 210 feet per NM to 8,000 feet. If you climb with a ground speed of 140 knots, what is the rate of climb required in feet per minute?

explanations.B:
because the required climb rate is 490
fpm, not 450 fpm.
explanations.C:
Use the Rate of Climb Table in Legend
16. Required climb rate (ft. per NM) is found on the left margin
and ground speed (kt.) is found on the top. Since 210 ft. per NM

per NM at 140 kt. At 200 ft. per NM the climb rate is 467 fpm,
and at 250 ft. per NM it is 583 fpm. Interpolate for 210 ft. per NM
to determine a rate of climb of 490 fpm.

questions.question: If Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring (RAIM) is not available when setting up a GPS approach, the pilot should

answers.A: select another type of navigation and approach system.
answers.B: continue to the MAP and hold until the satellites are recaptured.
answers.C: continue the approach, expecting to recapture the satellites before reaching the FAF.

explanations.A:
RAIM outages may occur due to an
insufficient number of satellites or due to unsuitable satellite
geometry, which causes the error in the position solution to
become too large. If RAIM is not available when setting up a
GPS approach, you must select another type of navigation and
approach system.
explanations.B:
because, if RAIM is not available when
setting up a GPS approach, you should select another type of

navigation and approach system. You should not fly to the MAP
and hold. Additionally, there is no holding pattern at the MAP.
explanations.C:
because, if RAIM is not available when
setting up a GPS approach, you should select another type of
navigation and approach system. If RAIM failure occurs while
you are setting up the GPS approach or conducting a GPS

approach, you must not continue the approach hoping that RAIM
will become available before the FAF.

questions.question: When using GPS for navigation and instrument approaches, any required alternate airport must have

because authorization to fly approaches
under IFR using GPS avionics systems requires that the GPS

unit and installation meet FAA standards and receive FAA
approval.
explanations.C:
because any required alternate airport
must have an approved instrument approach procedure other
than GPS, not a GPS approach, that is anticipated to be
operational and available at the ETA.

questions.question: Why is hypoxia particularly dangerous during flights with one pilot?

answers.A: Night vision may be so impaired that the pilot cannot see other aircraft.
answers.B: Symptoms of hypoxia may be difficult to recognize before the pilot's reactions are affected.
answers.C: The pilot may not be able to control the aircraft even if using oxygen.

explanations.A:
because hypoxia, which is a lack of
‘sufficient oxygen, affects all mental and physical activity, not just
night vision.
explanations.B:
Hypoxia symptoms are gradual, and a pilot
may not recognize the symptoms before his/her reactions are
affected. Because the symptoms of hypoxia vary with the

individual, having two pilots increases the chance of detection
before pilot reactions are affected.
explanations.C:
because hypoxia will not occur if
supplemental oxygen is used properly.

questions.question: What action should be taken if hyperventilation is suspected?

answers.A: Breathe at a slower rate by taking very deep breaths.
answers.B: Consciously breathe at a slower rate than normal.
answers.C: Consciously force yourself to take deep breaths and breathe at a faster rate than normal.

explanations.A:
because taking deep breaths will only
aggravate hyperventilation.
explanations.B:
Hyperventilation occurs when abnormally
large amounts of air are breathed in and out of the lungs. Early
‘symptoms of hyperventilation and hypoxia are similar and include
dizziness, drowsiness, tingling of the fingers and toes, and
sensation of body heat. If hyperventilation is suspected, you
should consciously breathe at a slower rate than normal.
explanations.C:
because taking deep breaths and

breathing at a faster rate than normal is the cause, not cure, of
hyperventilation.

questions.question: Apilot is more subject to spatial disorientation if

answers.A: kinesthetic senses are ignored.
answers.B: eyes are moved often in the process of cross-checking the flight instruments.
answers.C: body signals are used to interpret flight attitude.

because spatial disorientation is

explanations.B:
because spatial disorientation is
prevented/overcome by using and trusting the flight instruments.
explanations.C:
Spatial disorientation is a state of
temporary confusion resulting from misleading information being
sent to the brain by various sensory organs. Thus, the pilot should

ignore sensations of muscles and inner ear and kinesthetic
senses (those which sense motion).

questions.question: Which procedure is recommended to prevent or overcome spatial disorientation?

answers.A: Reduce head and eye movements to the extent possible.
