because, although rapid head
movements should be avoided, eye movement is necessary for
proper scanning of the flight instruments.
explanations.B:
because the kinesthetic sense is creating
the problem; it should be ignored.
explanations.C:
To overcome the effect of spatial

disorientation, pilots should rely entirely on the indications of the
flight instruments.

because spatial disorientation can occur

at any time outside visual references are lost. This can happen on
explanations.C:

answers.B: Use a very rapid cross-check.

questions.question: How canan instrument pilot best overcome spatial disorientation?

answers.A: Use a very rapid cross-check.
answers.B: Properly interpret the flight instruments and act accordingly.
answers.C: Avoid banking in excess of 30°.

because the flight instruments should be

Panic.

pilot should read and interpret the flight instruments and ignore all

questions.question: Without visual aid, a pilot often interprets centrifugal force as a sensation of

answers.A: rising or falling.
answers.B: turning.
answers.C: motion reversal.

explanations.A:
Nerves in tendons and muscles, including
shifting of abdominal muscles, often incorrectly interpret
centrifugal force as vertical movement, i.e., rising or falling.
explanations.B:
because centrifugal force is caused by
turning but is often misinterpreted as rising or falling.
explanations.C:
because centrifugal force is caused by
turning, not motion reversal.

questions.question: Abrupt head movement during a prolonged constant rate turn in IMC or simulated instrument conditions can cause

answers.A: pilot disorientation.
answers.B: false horizon.
answers.C: elevator illusion.

explanations.A:
An abrupt head movement in a prolonged

constant-rate turn that has ceased stimulating the motion sensing
system can create the ill

ion of rotation or movement in an

entirely different axis. This illusion is called the Coriolis illusion
and can lead to spatial disorientation.
explanations.B:
because a false horizon is an illusion
caused by sloping cloud formations, an obscured horizon, a dark
scene spread with ground lights and stars, or certain geometric
patterns of ground light. This illusion creates the impression of not
being aligned correctly with the actual horizon and can also lead
to spatial disorientation.
explanations.C:
because an elevator illusion is caused by

an abrupt upward vertical acceleration, usually by an updraft. This
illusion can also lead to spatial disorientation.

questions.question: An abrupt change from climb to straight-and-level flight can create the illusion of

answers.A: tumbling backwards.
answers.B: a noseup attitude.
answers.C: a descent with the wings level.

explanations.A:
An abrupt change from climb to
straight-and-level flight can create the illusion of tumbling
backwards. The disoriented pilot will push the airplane abruptly
into a nose-low attitude, possibly intensifying this illusion, which is
called an inversion illusion.
explanations.B:
because a rapid acceleration during

takeoff can create an illusion of being in a nose-up attitude. This
is called a somatogravic illusion.
explanations.C:
because an observed loss of altitude
during a coordinated constant-rate turn that has ceased
‘stimulating the motion sensing system (i.e., inner ear) can create

the illusion of being in a descent with the wings level. This illusion
is called a graveyard spiral

questions.question: Arapid acceleration during takeoff can create the illusion of

answers.A: spinning in the opposite direction.
answers.B: being in a noseup attitude.
answers.C: diving into the ground.

explanations.A:
because a proper recovery from a spin
that has ceased stimulating the motion sensing system (i.e., inner
ear) can create the illusion of spinning in the opposite direction.
This is known as a graveyard spin.
explanations.B:
A rapid acceleration during takeoff can
create the illusion of being in a nose-up attitude. The disoriented
pilot will push the airplane into a nose-low, or dive, attitude. This
is called a somatogravic illusion.
explanations.C:
because a rapid deceleration or an
abrupt downward vertical acceleration (usually caused by a
downdraft) can cause the illusion of a nose-down, or dive,
attitude.

questions.question: Asloping cloud formation, an obscured horizon, and a dark scene spread with ground lights and stars can create an illusion known as

answers.B: autokinesis. C_ false horizons.
answers.A: elevator illusions.

explanations.A:
because elevator illusions are caused by
abrupt upward or downward vertical accelerations, usually by

updrafts and downdrafts. These lead to illusions of being ina
climb or descent.
explanations.B:
because, at night, a static light will appear
to move about when stared at for many seconds, creating an
illusion known as autokinesis.

C_ false horizons.
explanations.C:
A sloping cloud formation, an obscured
horizon, a dark scene spread with ground lights and stars, and
certain geometric patterns of ground light can create an illusion
known as false horizons. The disoriented pilot will place the
airplane in a dangerous attitude.

questions.question: Which use of cockpit lighting is correct for night flight?

answers.A: Reducing the interior lighting intensity to a minimum level.
answers.B: The use of regular white light, such as a flashlight, will not impair night adaptation.
answers.C: Coloration shown on maps is least affected by the use of direct red lighting.

explanations.A:
In darkness, vision becomes more
sensitive to light, making it possible for the pilot to see distant
objects. A pilot can achieve a moderate degree of this dark
adaptation within 20 min. under dim red cockpit lighting. White
cockpit lighting is required for map and instrument reading,
especially when operating under IFR. To maintain some night
vision, the interior lighting intensity is to be kept at a minimum
level.
explanations.B:
because, after a pilot's eyes have
become adapted to darkness, the pilot must avoid exposing

them to any bright white light, which would cause temporary night
blindness and impair night adaptation.
explanations.C:
because the colors on maps can be
‘severely distorted when using a red light.

questions.question: Which statement is correct regarding the use of cockpit lighting for night flight?

answers.A: Reducing the lighting intensity to a minimum level will eliminate blind spots.
answers.B: The use of regular white light, such as a flashlight, will impair night adaptation.
answers.C: Coloration shown on maps is least affected by the use of direct red lighting.

explanations.A:
because the minimum level of cockpit
lighting may be insufficient to read maps, gauges, etc.
explanations.B:
After a pilot's eyes have become adapted
to darkness, the pilot must avoid exposing them to any bright
white light, which would cause temporary night blindness and
impair night adaptation.
explanations.C:
because the colors on maps can be
severely distorted when using a red light.

questions.question: Which technique should a pilot use to scan for traffic to the right and left during ‘straight-and-level flight?

answers.A: Systematically focus on different segments of the sky for short intervals.
answers.B: Concentrate on relative movement detected in the peripheral vision area.
answers.C: Continuous sweeping of the windshield from right to left.

explanations.A:
The most effective way to scan for other
aircraft during daylight is to use a series of short, regularly
spaced eye movements that bring successive areas of the sky
into your central vision field. Only a very small center area of the
eye has the ability to send clear, sharply focused messages to
the brain. All other areas provide less detail.
explanations.B:
because the peripheral areas do not

send sharply focused messages to the brain. Peripheral vision is
more effective at night.
explanations.C:
because concentration for at least 1
second is needed for each 10° sector.

questions.question: What effect does haze have on the ability to see traffic or terrain features during flight?

answers.A: Haze causes the eyes to focus at infinity, making terrain features harder to see.
answers.B: The eyes tend to overwork in haze and do not detect relative movement easily.
answers.C: Haze creates the illusion of being a greater distance than actual from the runway, and causes pilots to fly a lower approach.

explanations.A:
because haze may cause the condition
known as empty-field myopia. This condition results when the
pilot has nothing specific to focus on outside the airplane and the
eyes relax and focus at a range of about 10 to 30 ft, not infinity.
explanations.B:
because in haze the eyes tend to relax,

not overwork, thus causing empty-field myopia, or looking without
seeing.
explanations.C:
Haze can create the illusion of being at a

greater distance from the runway and often causes pilots to fly a
lower approach.

questions.question: Due to visual illusion, when landing on a narrower-than-usual runway, the aircraft will appear to be

answers.A: higher than actual, leading to a lower-than-normal approach.
answers.B: lower than actual, leading to a higher-than-normal approach.
answers.C: higher than actual, leading to a higher-than-normal approach.

explanations.A:
A narrower-than-usual runway may create
the illusion that the aircraft is higher than actual, resulting ina
lower-than-normal approach.
explanations.B:
because wider, not narrower, runways
give a lower-than-actual altitude illusion.
explanations.C:
because a higher-than-actual altitude

illusion results in a lower-than-usual, not higher-than-usual,
approach.

questions.question: What visual illusion creates the same effect as a narrower-than-usual runway?

answers.A: An upsloping runway.
answers.B: A wider-than-usual runway.
answers.C: A downsloping runway.

explanations.A:
Both narrower-than-usual runway and an
upsloping runway may create the illusion that the airplane is at a
higher altitude than it actually is. The pilot will fly a lower approach
and risk striking obstructions or landing short.
explanations.B:
because a wider-than-usual runway may
create the illusion that the aircraft is at a lower altitude than it

actually is, and the unknowing pilot may land hard or overshoot
the runway.
explanations.C:
because a downsloping runway may
create the illusion that the aircraft is at a lower altitude than it

actually is, and the unknowing pilot may land hard or overshoot
the runway.

questions.question: The primary cause of all changes in the Earth's weather is

answers.A: variation of solar energy received by the Earth's regions.
answers.B: changes in air pressure over the Earth's surface.
answers.C: movement of the air masses.

explanations.A:
Every physical process of weather is
accompanied by, or is the result of, a heat exchange. Unequal
solar heating of the Earth's surface causes differences in air
pressure, which result in all changes in the Earth's weather.
explanations.B:
because changes in air pressure are a
result of varying temperatures.
explanations.C:
because movement of air masses (wind)
is a result of varying temperatures and pressures.

questions.question: Which force, in the Northern Hemisphere, acts at a right angle to the wind and deflects it to the right until parallel to the isobars?

answers.A: Centrifugal.
answers.B: Pressure gradient.
answers.C: Coriolis.

explanations.A:
because centrifugal force is a force that
acts outwardly on any object moving in a curved path.
explanations.B:
because pressure gradient causes the

wind to move perpendicular to the isobars. The wind is then
deflected by Coriolis force.
explanations.C:
Coriolis force is a result of the Earth's
rotation. As the wind moves perpendicular to the isobars (from
high to low pressure), it is apparently deflected to the right in the
Northern Hemisphere, until it is moving parallel to the isobars.
This effect is most pronounced above 2,000 ft. AGL.

questions.question: What relationship exists between the winds at 2,000 feet above the surface and the surface winds?

answers.A: The winds at 2,000 feet and the surface winds flow in the same direction, but the surface winds are weaker due to friction.
answers.B: The winds at 2,000 feet tend to parallel the isobars while the surface winds cross the isobars at an angle toward lower pressure and are weaker.
answers.C: The surface winds tend to veer to the right of the winds at 2,000 feet and are usually weaker.

explanations.A:
because the Coriolis force is less at the
‘surface, so surface winds flow in a direction different from those
aloft.
explanations.B:
Generally, winds near the surface are
weaker than those aloft due to the friction between the Earth's
surface and the wind. Also, because they are slower, winds near
the surface are less affected by the Coriolis force. The pressure
gradient forces are thus stronger near the surface, and the winds
cross the isobars at an angle instead of flowing parallel to them.
explanations.C:
because the winds aloft veer to the right
of surface winds, not the opposite.

questions.question: Winds at 5,000 feet AGL on a particular flight are southwesterly while most of the surface winds are southerly. This difference in direction is primarily due to

answers.A: a stronger pressure gradient at higher altitudes.
answers.B: friction between the wind and the surface.
answers.C: stronger Coriolis force at the surface.

explanations.A:
because the pressure differentials are
approximately uniform through the altitudes.
explanations.B:
Southerly winds at the surface will become
southwesterly winds at 5,000 ft. because the Coriolis force
deflects winds aloft to the right. This force has less effect on

‘surface winds which have been slowed by friction with the Earth's
‘surface.
explanations.C:
because the Coriolis force at the surface
is weaker with slower wind speed.

questions.question: What causes surface winds to flow across the isobars at an angle rather than parallel to the isobars?

answers.B: Surface friction.
answers.C: The greater density of the air at the surface.
answers.A: Coriolis force.

explanations.A:
because the Coriolis force is directly
Proportional to wind speed. At higher altitudes (above 2,000 to

3,000 ft. AGL), winds not slowed by surface friction are so

deflected by the Coriolis force that they flow parallel to the
isobars, not across them.
explanations.B:
Generally, winds near the surface are
weaker than those aloft due to the friction between the Earth's
surface and the wind. Also, because they are slower, winds near
the surface are less affected by the Coriolis force. The pressure
gradient forces are thus stronger near the surface, and the winds
cross the isobars at an angle instead of flowing parallel to them.
explanations.C:
because the greater air density at the
‘surface has little effect on the relationship of winds to the isobars.

questions.question: Anair mass is a body of air that

answers.B: creates a wind shift as it moves across the Earth's surface.
answers.C: covers an extensive area and has fairly uniform properties of temperature and moisture.
answers.A: has similar cloud formations associated with it.

explanations.A:
because an air mass may have cloud
formations or it may be clear and dry.
explanations.B:
because changes in wind, temperature,
etc., indicate a frontal zone between two air masses.
explanations.C:
An air mass is an extensive body of air
within which the conditions of temperature and moisture in a
horizontal plane are essentially uniformly distributed. Generally,
an air mass takes on the properties of the large area it overlies.

questions.question: Acharacteristic of the stratosphere is

answers.A: an overall decrease of temperature with an increase in altitude.
answers.B: a relatively even base altitude of approximately 35,000 feet.
answers.C: relatively small changes in temperature with an increase in altitude.

explanations.A:
because there is a slight increase, not
decrease, in temperature with increase in altitude.
explanations.B:
because the base of the stratosphere is
considerably higher at the equator than at the poles.
explanations.C:
The stratosphere is the atmospheric layer
above the tropopause. It is the band of altitude from about 7 to 22
mi. It is characterized by a slight average increase in temperature
from base to top and thus is very stable. It also has a low
moisture content and an absence of clouds.

questions.question: Ajetstream is defined as wind of

answers.A: 30 knots or greater.
answers.B: 40 knots or greater.
answers.C: 50 knots or greater.

explanations.A:
because a jet stream, by definition, is a
wind of 50 kt, not 30 kt, or greater.
explanations.B:
because a jet stream, by definition, is a
wind of 50 kt., not 40 kt., or greater.
explanations.C:
The jet stream is a roughly horizontal
‘stream of wind of 50 kt. or more (by definition) concentrated
within a narrow band embedded in the westerly winds in the high
troposphere. It occurs in an area of intensified pressure

gradients. A second or even third jet stream may form at one
time, and these may not be continuous.

questions.question: The average height of the troposphere in the middle latitudes is

explanations.A:
because the average height of the
troposphere is 25,000 to 30,000 ft. at the poles, not the
mid-latitudes.

B, 25,000 feet.
explanations.B:
because the average height of the

troposphere is 25,000 to 30,000 ft. at the poles, not the
mid-latitudes.
explanations.C:
In the mid-latitudes, the average height of
the troposphere is about 37,000 ft. It is 25,000 to 30,000 ft. at the

poles and 55,000 to 65,000 ft. at the equator. It is generally
higher in summer than in winter.

questions.question: The strength and location of the jet stream is normally

answers.A: stronger and farther north in the winter.
answers.B: weaker and farther north in the summer.
answers.C: stronger and farther north in the summer.

explanations.A:
because the jet stream is usually farther
south, not north, in winter.
explanations.B:
In the mid-latitudes, the wind speed in the
jet stream averages considerably less in the summer than in the

winter. Also, the jet stream shifts farther north in summer than in
winter.
explanations.C:
because the jet stream is usually weaker,
not stronger, in summer.

questions.question: Which feature is associated with the tropopause?

answers.B: Absolute upper limit of cloud formation.
answers.C: Abrupt change in temperature lapse rate.
answers.A: Absence of wind and turbulent conditions.

explanations.A:
because there are usually very strong
winds in the tropopause. These create narrow zones of wind
shear, which may generate hazardous turbulence.
explanations.B:
because clouds may form above the

tropopause even though there is little moisture in the
stratosphere.
explanations.C:
The tropopause is the transition layer of
atmosphere between the troposphere (surface to about 7 to 22
mi.) and the stratosphere. A characteristic of the tropopause is
that there is an abrupt change in the temperature lapse rate, i.e.,
the rate at which temperature decreases with height.

questions.question: Which weather phenomenon is always associated with the passage of a frontal system?

answers.A: Awind change.
answers.B: An abrupt decrease in pressure.
answers.C: Clouds, either ahead or behind the front.

explanations.A:
Whenever a front passes, a wind shift will

always occur. This discontinuity may be in direction, speed, or
both.
explanations.B:
because the pressure and/or temperature
may not change significantly as a weak front passes.
explanations.C:
because some fronts do not contain

enough moisture to produce clouds. Therefore, clouds are not
always associated with a frontal system.

questions.question: Whichis a characteristic of low-level wind shear as it relates to frontal activity?

answers.A: With a warm front, the most critical period is before the front passes the airport.
answers.B: With a cold front, the most critical period is just before the front passes the airport.
answers.C: Turbulence will always exist in wind-shear conditions.

explanations.A:
Wind shear associated with a warm front
occurs above an airport before the front passes the airport. A
warm front is warmer air overtaking colder air.
explanations.B:
because cold front wind shear occurs just
as or just after the front passes rather than before it passes.
explanations.C:
because wind shear can sometimes
‘occur with no forewarning from turbulence.

questions.question: Frontal waves normally form on

answers.A: slow moving cold fronts or stationary fronts.
answers.B: slow moving warm fronts and strong occluded fronts.
answers.C: rapidly moving cold fronts or warm fronts.

explanations.A:
Frontal waves and cyclones (areas of low

pressure) usually form in slow-moving cold fronts or in stationary
fronts.
explanations.B:
because frontal waves are usually not
associated with warm fronts or occluded fronts.
explanations.C:
because frontal waves usually form on

slow-moving, not rapidly moving, cold fronts and not on warm
fronts.

questions.question: Where do squall lines most often develop?

answers.B: Ina cold air mass.
answers.C: Ahead of a cold front.
answers.A: Inan occluded front.

explanations.A:
because squall lines are usually
associated with a fast-moving cold front.
explanations.B:
because they occur ahead of the cold
front, not behind the front in the cold air.
explanations.C:
A squall line is a nonfrontal band of active
thunderstorms that sometimes develops ahead of a cold front.

questions.question: Which are characteristics of an unstable cold air mass moving over a warm surface?

answers.A: Cumuliform clouds, turbulence, and poor visibility.
answers.B: Cumuliform clouds, turbulence, and good visibility.
answers.C: Stratiform clouds, smooth air, and poor visibility.

explanations.A:
because unstable air lifts and blows haze
away, resulting in good, not poor, visibility.
explanations.B:
When a cold air mass moves over a warm
surface, the warm air near the surface rises and creates an

unstable situation. These convective currents give rise to
cumuliform clouds, turbulence, and good visibility.
explanations.C:
because unstable conditions produce

cumuliform rather than stratiform clouds. Also, the air is turbulent,
and visibility is good.

questions.question: What are the characteristics of stable air?

answers.A: Good visibility, steady precipitation, and stratus-type clouds.
answers.B: Poor visibility, intermittent precipitation, and cumulus-type clouds.
answers.C: Poor visibility, steady precipitation, and stratus-type clouds.

explanations.A:
because the visibility is poor rather than
good in stable air.
explanations.B:
because the precipitation is steady and
the clouds are stratiform.
explanations.C:
Stable air is air which is still or moving
horizontally but not vertically. As a result, the pollutants hang in the
air and visibility is poor. Also, stable air forms stratus-type clouds

since the air is moving in layers. Relatedly, precipitation spreads
out over a wide area and is relatively steady.

questions.question: What type clouds can be expected when an unstable air mass is forced to ascend a mountain slope?

answers.A: Layered clouds with little vertical development.
answers.B: Stratified clouds with considerable associated turbulence.
answers.C: Clouds with extensive vertical development.

explanations.A:
because layered clouds are associated
with stable air.
explanations.B:
because stratified clouds are associated
with stable air and no turbulence.
explanations.C:
Unstable air has a greater lapse rate.
Because the air above is much colder than the air below, the
lower (warmer) air tends to rise very easily. When an unstable air
mass is forced to ascend up a mountain slope, it will probably
continue to ascend beyond the mountain slope. Once the air
expands and cools to the dew point, cumulus clouds will form with
considerable vertical development. Any unstable air mass
movement will usually result in turbulence as well.

questions.question: Whichis a characteristic of stable air?

answers.B: Stratiform clouds.
answers.C: Unlimited visibility.
answers.A: Fair weather cumulus clouds.

explanations.A:
because cumulus clouds indicate
unstable conditions.
explanations.B:
Stratiform clouds, i.e., layer-type clouds,
characteristically form in stable air. A stable atmosphere resists
any upward or downward displacement, so clouds tend to lie
horizontally instead of developing vertically.
explanations.C:
because restricted, not unlimited, visibility
near the ground is an indication of stable air.

questions.question: The general characteristics of unstable air are

answers.A: good visibility, showery precipitation, and cumuliform-type clouds.
answers.B: good visil , Steady precipitation, and stratiform-type clouds.
answers.C: poor visibility, intermittent precipitation, and cumuliform-type clouds.

explanations.A:
Unstable air is moving vertically and
usually produces cumulus clouds. The precipitation from cumulus
clouds is showery. The lifting associated with unstable air
generally clears smoke and other pollution away; thus vi:
relatively good.
explanations.B:
because unstable air generally has

showery, not steady, precipitation and cumulus, not stratiform,
clouds.
explanations.C:
because unstable air generally has good,
not poor, visibility.

questions.question: What type of clouds will be formed if very stable moist air is forced up slope?

answers.B: Vertical clouds with increasing height.
answers.C: Stratified clouds with little vertical development.
answers.A: First stratified clouds and then vertical clouds.

explanations.A:
because there would be vertical clouds if
the air were unstable rather than stable.
explanations.B:
because there would be vertical clouds if
the air were unstable rather than stable.
explanations.C:
Even when being forced up slope, stable

air forms stratus-type clouds. This is because the air resists any
further upward movement.

questions.question: Steady precipitation, in contrast to showers, preceding a front is an indication of

answers.A: stratiform clouds with moderate turbulence.
answers.B: cumuliform clouds with little or no turbulence.
answers.C: stratiform clouds with little or no turbulence.

explanations.A:
because stable air has little or no
turbulence.
explanations.B:
because stratiform rather than cumuliform
clouds form in stable air.
explanations.C:
Steady precipitation is a characteristic of
stable air because of its lack of lifting action. Also characteristic
are stratiform clouds with relatively little turbulence.

questions.question: What enhances the growth rate of precipitation?

answers.B: Upward currents.
answers.C: Cyclonic movement.
answers.A: Advective action.

explanations.A:
because advective action usually refers to
the horizontal transport of atmospheric properties by wind, such
as warm advection (warm land air moving out over colder water).
explanations.B:
The growth rate of precipitation is
enhanced by upward currents, which carry moisture particles to
cooler levels. The particles grow in size and weight (due to
condensation) until the atmosphere can no longer hold them
(saturation point) and they fall as precipitation.
explanations.C:
because cyclonic movement refers to the
counterclockwise movement around a low-pressure area.

questions.question: Which of the following combinations of weather producing variables would likely result in cumuliform-type clouds, good visibility, rain showers, and possible clear-type icing in clouds?

answers.A: Unstable, moist air, and no lifting mechanism.
answers.B: Stable, dry air, and orographic lifting.
answers.C: Unstable, moist air, and orographic lifting.

explanations.A:
because, without a lifting mechanism,
there would be no vertical development of clouds to result in
showery rain and icing in clouds.
explanations.B:
because stable conditions result in

stratiform rather than cumuliform clouds, and dry air does not
result in showery rain or icing even when lifted.
explanations.C:
Cumuliform clouds, good visibility, and
showery rain are produced as unstable, moist air is lifted into
higher, cooler regions. When the lifting is the result of movement
over terrain (e.g., up a mountain slope), it is called orographic

lifting. Clear icing is formed from large drops such as those found
in cumuliform clouds.

questions.question: What determines the structure or type of clouds which form as a result of air being forced to ascend?

answers.A: The method by which the air is lifted.
answers.B: The stability of the air before lifting occurs.
answers.C: The amount of condensation nuclei present after lifting occurs.

explanations.A:
because the stability of the air, not the
lifting mechanism, determines the type of cloud formations.
explanations.B:
The structure of clouds is determined by

the stability of the air before it is lifted. If unstable, the clouds will

have vertical development. If stable, the clouds will be horizontal,
ie., stratiform.
explanations.C:
because condensation nuclei encourage

the formation of rain droplets or ice but have no effect on the type
of cloud formations.

questions.question: Stability can be determined from which measurement of the atmosphere?

answers.A: Low-level winds.
answers.B: Ambient lapse rate.
answers.C: Atmospheric pressure.

explanations.A:
because stability refers to vertical air
movement, not horizontal air movement.
explanations.B:
The ambient lapse rate is the actual rate of
decrease in temperature with height. A great decrease in
temperature as altitude increases encourages warm air from
below to rise and creates an unstable air mass. Lifting is

inhibited by lesser or very small temperature decreases with
altitude (i.e., a low lapse rate).
explanations.C:
because atmospheric pressure is a

measure of the weight or downward force of air and does not
affect air stability.

questions.question: What are some characteristics of unstable air?

answers.A: Nimbostratus clouds and good surface visibility.
answers.B: Turbulence and poor surface visibility.
answers.C: Turbulence and good surface visibility.

explanations.A:
because stratus clouds are characteristic
of stable, not unstable, air.
explanations.B:
because poor surface visibility is a
characteristic of stable, not unstable, air.
explanations.C:
The lifting tendency of unstable air creates

turbulence and clears the surface air of clouds, dust, and other
pollution.

questions.question: Unsaturated air flowing up slope will cool at the rate of approximately (dry adiabatic lapse rate)

answers.A: 3°C per 1,000 feet.
answers.B: 2°C per 1,000 feet. C.2.5°C per 1,000 feet.

explanations.A:
The dry adiabatic lapse rate signifies a
prescribed rate of expansional cooling or compressional heating.
The dry adiabatic rate is 3°C for each 1,000 ft. Note that this rate
differs from the average normal lapse rate of 2°C for each 1,000
ft. of altitude. The average lapse rate does NOT occur in dry air,
but rather in air with "average" humidity.
explanations.B:
because 2°C per 1,000 ft. is the standard
lapse rate in stable air.
explanations.C:
because 2.5°C per 1,000 ft. is the rate at

which the temperature and dew point converge in a convective
current of unsaturated air.

questions.question: What feature is associated with a temperature inversion?

answers.A: Astable layer of air.
answers.B: An unstable layer of air.
answers.C: Air mass thunderstorms.

explanations.A:
A temperature inversion is defined as an
increase in temperature with height; i.e., the lapse rate is less
than standard. The cooler air stays near the surface, and there is
little or no vertical movement.
explanations.B:
because instability occurs when the
temperature decreases, not increases as in a temperature

inversion, with an increase in height, and the warmer air
continues to rise.
explanations.C:
because air mass thunderstorms result

from instability. They do not occur when there is a temperature
inversion.

questions.question: Which weather conditions should be expected beneath a low-level temperature inversion layer when the relative humidity is high?

answers.A: Smooth air and poor visibility due to fog, haze, or low clouds.
answers.B: Light wind shear and poor visibility due to haze and light rain.
answers.C: Turbulent air and poor visibility due to fog, low stratus-type clouds, and showery precipitation.

explanations.A:
A temperature inversion is an increase in
temperature as altitude increases; normally temperature
decreases with increases in altitude. In an inversion, warm air
rises to its own temperature and forms a stable layer of air. A
low-level inversion results in poor visibility by trapping fog,
smoke, dust, etc., in low levels of the atmosphere.
explanations.B:
because wind shear may be expected
within, not beneath, a low-level temperature inversion.
explanations.C:
because an inversion forms a stable layer

of air, thus making it smooth, not turbulent, and causing steady,
not showery, precipitation.

questions.question: A temperature inversion will normally form only

answers.B: in unstable air.
answers.C: when a stratiform layer merges with a cumuliform mass.
answers.A: instable air.

explanations.A:
In a temperature inversion, warm air
overlies colder air, i.e., the lapse rate is inverted. By definition,
this is a stable condition since there is no lifting action.
explanations.B:
because unstable air has colder air
above warm air.
explanations.C:
because a merger of stratus and cumulus

Clouds is associated with an occluded front, not necessarily a
temperature inversion.

questions.question: A common type of ground or surface based temperature inversion is that which is produced by

answers.A: warm air being lifted rapidly aloft in the vicinity of mountainous terrain.
answers.B: the movement of colder air over warm air, or the movement of warm air under cold air.
answers.C: ground radiation on clear, cool nights when the wind is light.

explanations.A:
because, when warm air is lifted,
unstable, not stable, air is the result.
explanations.B:
because a temperature inversion
consists of warm air over colder air, not colder over warm.
explanations.C:
A temperature inversion means the
temperature becomes warmer rather than cooler with increases
in altitude. A ground- or surface-based temperature inversion is
produced when the air near the surface is cooled faster than the
overlying air as a result of radiation of heat on a clear, still night.
The air very close to the surface is thus cooler than the air a few
hundred feet above.

questions.question: Which conditions are favorable for the formation of radiation fog?

answers.A: Moist air moving over colder ground or water.
answers.B: Cloudy sky and a light wind moving saturated warm air over a cool surface.
answers.C: Clear sky, little or no wind, small temperature/dew point spread, and over a land surface.

explanations.A:
because advection fog, not radiation fog,
forms when moist air moves over colder ground or water. The sky
may be cloudy over advection fog.
explanations.B:
because advection fog, not radiation fog,

forms when moist air moves over colder ground or water. The sky
may be cloudy over advection fog.
explanations.C: Conditions favorable for radiation fog are

questions.question: What situation is most conducive to the formation of radiation fog?

answers.A: Warm, moist air over low, flatiand areas on clear, calm nights.
answers.B: Moist, tropical air moving over cold, offshore water.
answers.C: The movement of cold air over much warmer water.

explanations.A: Conditions favorable for radiation fog are
explanations.B:
because advection fog forms as a result
of warm air moving over a colder surface.
explanations.C:
because steam fog forms when cold air
moves over a warmer surface.

questions.question: The most frequent type of ground- or surface-based temperature inversion is that produced by

answers.A: radiation on a clear, relatively still night.
answers.B: warm air being lifted rapidly aloft in the vicinity of mountainous terrain.
answers.C: the movement of colder air under warm air, or the movement of warm air over cold air.

explanations.A:
An inversion often develops near the
ground on clear, cool nights when the wind is light. The ground
radiates heat and cools much faster than the overlying air. Air in
contact with the ground becomes cold, while the temperature a
few hundred feet above changes very little. Thus temperature
increases with height.
explanations.B: because it describes orographic lifting.
explanations.C:
because it describes a cold front anda
warm front, respectively.

questions.question: What types of fog depend upon a wind in order to exist?

answers.A: Steam fog and down slope fog.
answers.B: Precipitation-induced fog and ground fog.
answers.C: Advection fog and up slope fog.

explanations.A:
because down slope fog is a nonsense
term.
explanations.B:
because precipitation fog forms when

warm rain or drizzle falls through cool air, and ground fog requires
little or no wind.
explanations.C:
Up slope fog forms as a result of moist,
stable air being cooled as it moves up a sloping terrain.
Advection fog forms when moist air is blown over a cold surface,
decreasing the moist air's temperature to its dew point. Thus,
both up slope fog and advection fog depend on air moving from
one area to another; i.e., they depend on wind.

questions.question: In what localities is advection fog most likely to occur?

answers.A: Coastal areas.
answers.B: Mountain slopes.
answers.C: Level inland areas.

explanations.A:
Advection fog forms when moist air moves
over colder ground or water. This type of fog is thus most
common along coastal areas. During the winter, advection fog
over the central and eastern United States results when moist air
from the Gulf of Mexico spreads northward over cold ground.
explanations.B:
because mountain slopes are required
for upslope, not advection, fog.
explanations.C:
because level inland areas will most likely
produce radiation, not advection, fog.

questions.question: In which situation is advection fog most likely to form?

answers.A: Anair mass moving inland from the coast in winter.
answers.B: A light breeze blowing colder air out to sea.
answers.C: Warm, moist air settling over a warmer surface under no-wind conditions.

explanations.A:
Advection fog forms when moist air moves
over colder ground or water. This type of fog is most likely to form
when an air mass moves from the warmer water inland from the
coast in winter. As the air moves over the cooler land, it cools to
the dew point and forms advection fog.
explanations.B:
because colder air blowing out to sea
results in steam, not advection, fog.
explanations.C:
because warm, moist air settling over a
warmer surface would not cool, so fog would not form.

questions.question: Fog is usually prevalent in industrial areas because of

answers.A: atmospheric stabilization around cities.
answers.B: an abundance of condensation nuclei from combustion products.
answers.C: increased temperatures due to industrial heating.

explanations.A:
because cities, per se, have no effect on
air stability.
explanations.B:
Fog often forms in industrial areas
because the combustion products leave dust in the air on which

water can condense. These particles are called condensation
nuclei.
explanations.C:
because the amount of heat that factories
release into the air is not significant in the formation of fog.

questions.question: Which weather condition can be expected when moist air flows from a relatively warm surface to a colder surface?

answers.A: Increased visibility.
answers.B: Convective turbulence due to surface heating.
answers.C: Fog.

explanations.A:
because fog forms, which decreases, not
increases, visibility.
explanations.B:
because the surface cools the air,
resulting in stable air with little or no convective turbulence.
explanations.C:
When moist air flows from a relatively

warm surface to a colder surface, the warm, moist air is cooled to
its dew point, and advection fog is produced.

questions.question: Under which condition does advection fog usually form?

answers.A: Moist air moving over colder ground or water.
answers.B: Warm, moist air settling over a cool surface under no-wind conditions.
answers.C: Aland breeze blowing a cold air mass over a warm water current.

explanations.A:
Advection fog forms when moist air moves
over colder ground or water. The moist air is cooled to the dew
point, and fog forms.
explanations.B:
because radiation fog, not advection fog,
forms when warm, moist air settles over a cool surface under
no-wind conditions.
explanations.C:
because steam fog, not advection fog,

forms when a land breeze blows a cold air mass over a warm
water current.

questions.question: The amount of water vapor which air can hold largely depends on

answers.A: relative humidity.
answers.B: air temperature.
answers.C: stability of air.

explanations.A:
because relative humidity is the ratio of
the existing amount of water vapor in the air at a given

temperature to the maximum amount that could be held at that
temperature.
explanations.B:
Air temperature largely determines how
much water vapor can be held by the air. Warm air, which is less
dense, can hold more water vapor than cold air.
explanations.C:
because air stability is related to the
temperature lapse rate, not moisture.

questions.question: Clouds, fog, or dew will always form when

answers.A: water vapor condenses.
answers.B: water vapor is present.
answers.C: the temperature and dew point are equal.

explanations.A:
As water vapor condenses, it becomes
visible as clouds, fog, or dew.
explanations.B:
because some water vapor is usually
present, but it does not necessarily form clouds, fog, or dew.
explanations.C:
because, even at 100% humidity (when

the dew point equals actual temperature), water vapor may not
condense if sufficient condensation nuclei are not present.

questions.question: To which meteorological condition does the term "dew point" refer?

answers.A: The temperature to which air must be cooled to become saturated.
answers.B: The temperature at which condensation and evaporation are equal.
answers.C: The temperature at which dew will always form.

explanations.A:
Dew point refers to the temperature to
which air must be cooled to become saturated by the water vapor
in the air. Dew point, when related to air temperature in aviation
weather reports, reveals how close the air is to saturation and
possible cloud, fog, or precipitation formation.
explanations.B:
because condensation (vapor to water)
occurs at low temperatures, and evaporation (water to vapor)
occurs at high temperatures.
explanations.C:
because the formation of dew depends
on relative humidity and the temperature of the collecting surface.

questions.question: Which conditions result in the formation of frost?

answers.A: The temperature of the collecting surface is at or below freezing and small droplets of moisture are falling.
answers.B: When dew forms and the temperature is below freezing.
answers.C: Temperature of the collecting surface is below the dewpoint of surrounding air and the dewpoint is colder than freezing.

explanations.A:
because the dew point must also be
below freezing and droplets of moisture are not necessary.
explanations.B:
because the formation of dew is not

required. The dew point of surrounding air must be below

freezing, and the temperature of the collecting surface must be
less than the dew point.
explanations.C:
If the air temperature drops below the dew
point, the air becomes more dense and can no longer hold the
water vapor. The water vapor will condense to form visible
moisture. Frost will form only if the temperature of the collecting

surfaces is below the dew point of the surrounding air AND the
dew point is below freezing.

questions.question: What are the four families of clouds?

answers.A: Stratus, cumulus, nimbus, and cirrus.
answers.B: Clouds formed by updrafts, fronts, cooling layers of air, and precipitation into warm air.
answers.C: High, middle, low, and those with extensive vertical development.

explanations.A:
because it describes cloud formation and
characteristic.
explanations.B:
because it describes the way various
clouds are formed.
explanations.C:
For identification purposes, clouds are
divided into four "families" based on their height range. The

families are high clouds, middle clouds, low clouds, and clouds
with extensive vertical development.

questions.question: Which family of clouds is least likely to contribute to structural icing on an aircraft?

answers.A: Low clouds.
answers.B: High clouds.
answers.C: Clouds with extensive vertical development.

explanations.A:
because low clouds can contain
supercooled water, which freezes on contact with the airplane.
explanations.B:
High clouds are least likely to contribute to
structural icing since they usually consist entirely of ice crystals.

Since ice is already frozen, it will not freeze onto the structural
surface of the airplane.
explanations.C:
because clouds with extensive vertical

development can contain supercooled water, which freezes on
contact with the airplane.

questions.question: The presence of standing lenticular altocumulus clouds is a good indication of

answers.A: ajetstream.
answers.B: very strong turbulence.
answers.C: heavy icing conditions.

explanations.A:
because the jet stream flows around the
world at high altitudes and at varying latitudes.
explanations.B:
When stable air crosses a mountain
barrier, it tends to flow in layers. The barrier may set up waves in
these layers, which remain stationary while the wind blows rapidly
through them. Wave crests extend well above the highest
mountain tops. Under each wave crestis a rotary circulation,
which can create very violent turbulence. Crests of the standing
waves may be marked by stationary lens-shaped clouds known
as standing lenticular clouds.
explanations.C:
because standing lenticular clouds occur
at varying temperatures, not only below freezing.

questions.question: The suffix "nimbus", used in naming clouds, means a

answers.A: cloud with extensive vertical development.
answers.B: rain cloud.
answers.C: dark massive, towering cloud.

explanations.A: because "cumulo," not "nimbus," denotes
explanations.B:
The prefix "nimbo" or the suffix "nimbus"

means raincloud. For example, stratified clouds from which rain
is falling are called nimbostratus clouds. A heavy, swelling,

cumulus-type cloud which produces precipitation is called a
cumulonimbus cloud.
explanations.C:
because it specifies a cumulonimbus
cloud, not any nimbus cloud.

questions.question: Standing lenticular clouds, in mountainous areas, indicate

answers.B: unstable air.
answers.C: turbulence.
answers.A: an inversion.

explanations.A:
because stratus, not standing lenticular,
Clouds indicate stable air which may be the result of a
temperature inversion.
explanations.B:
because cumulus, not standing lenticular,
Clouds indicate unstable air.
explanations.C:
The "waves" generated as wind flows
across a mountain barrier may form standing lenticular clouds at
the crest of each wave. Their presence indicates very strong
turbulence, and they should be avoided.

questions.question: Which clouds have the greatest turbulence?

answers.A: Towering cumulus.
answers.B: Cumulonimbus.
answers.C: Altocumulus castellanus.

explanations.A:
because towering cumulus clouds are
only a preliminary stage of the cumulonimbus cloud.
explanations.B:
Cumulonimbus clouds are thunderstorms
and the ultimate manifestation of instability. They are huge
vertically developed clouds with dense, billowy tops often
crowned with thick veils of dense cirrus, called the "anvil." Nearly

the entire spectrum of flying hazards is contained in these clouds,
including violent turbulence.
explanations.C:
because altocumulus castellanus is a
middle-level convective cloud which indicates rough turbulence
with some icing, but thunderstorms are far more turbulent.

questions.question: Ahigh cloud is composed mostly of

answers.B: condensation nuclei.
answers.C: ice crystals.
answers.A: ozone.

explanations.A:
because ozone is an unstable form of

oxygen. The heaviest concentrations are in the stratosphere, not
in clouds.
explanations.B:
because condensation nuclei are the

small particles in the air onto which water vapor condenses or
sublimates.
explanations.C:
The high cloud family is cirriform. It
includes cirrus, cirrocumulus, and cirrostratus clouds. They are

composed almost entirely of ice crystals. Their bases range from
16,500 ft. to 45,000 ft.

questions.question: Fair weather cumulus clouds often indicate

answers.B: poor visibility.
answers.C: smooth flying conditions.
answers.A: turbulence at and below the cloud level.

explanations.A:
Fair weather cumulus clouds form in
convective currents and are characterized by relatively flat bases
and dome-shaped tops. They indicate a shallow layer of
instability, some turbulence, and no significant icing.
explanations.B:
because the instability producing the
cumulus clouds provides good, not poor, visibility.
explanations.C:
because the instability producing the
cumulus clouds creates some turbulence, not smooth conditions.

questions.question: What are the requirements for the formation of a thunderstorm?

answers.B: A cumulus cloud with sufficient moisture and an inverted lapse rate.
answers.C: Sufficient moisture, an unstable lapse rate, and a lifting action.
answers.A: Acumulus cloud with sufficient moisture.

explanations.A:
because a lifting action is also required
for formation of a thunderstorm.
explanations.B:
because a lifting action and an unstable,

not inverted, lapse rate are required for the formation of a
thunderstorm.
explanations.C:
For a thunderstorm to form, the air must
have sufficient water vapor, an unstable lapse rate, and an initial
upward lifting action to start the storm process in motion. Surface
heating, converging winds, sloping terrain, a frontal surface, or
any combination of these can provide the lift.

questions.question: What is an indication that downdrafts have developed and the thunderstorm cell has entered the mature stage?

answers.A: The anvil top has completed its development.
answers.B: Precipitation begins to fall from the cloud base.
answers.C: A gust front forms.

explanations.A:
because an anvil top does not
necessarily develop over every thunderstorm.
explanations.B:
The mature stage of a thunderstorm is
signaled when rain begins falling at the surface. This means that
the downdrafts have developed sufficiently to carry water all the
way through the thunderstorm.
explanations.C: because gust front is a nonsense term.

questions.question: Which procedure is recommended if a pilot should unintentionally penetrate embedded thunderstorm activity?

answers.A: Reverse aircraft heading or proceed toward an area of known VFR conditions.
answers.B: Reduce airspeed to maneuvering speed and maintain a constant altitude.
answers.C: Set power for recommended turbulence penetration airspeed and attempt to maintain a level flight attitude.

explanations.A:
because a straight course will probably
take you out of the storm most quickly. Also, turning maneuvers
increase stresses on the aircraft.
explanations.B:
because maintaining a constant airspeed
(Va) in updrafts and downdrafts may be impossible. It is best to
set power so you will operate at or below Va. Also, attempting to

maintain constant altitude, not attitude, increases the stress on
the airplane.
explanations.C:
If a thunderstorm is penetrated, you should
always attempt to maintain a constant attitude at or below the
maneuvering or turbulence penetration speed recommended for
the airplane. Note that the airspeed cannot always be kept
constant, but the power can be set so that you will be operating
generally at or below the maneuvering speed.

questions.question: Which thunderstorms generally produce the most severe conditions, such as heavy hail and destructive winds?

answers.A: Warm front.
answers.B: Squall line.
answers.C: Air mass.

explanations.A:
because warm fronts indicate stable air,
which does not usually produce thunderstorms.
explanations.B:
A squall line is a nonfrontal narrow band of
active thunderstorms. It often contains severe, steady-state

thunderstorms and presents the single most intense weather
hazard to airplanes.
explanations.C:
because an air mass thunderstorm is the
least severe type of thunderstorm.

questions.question: Which weather phenomenon is always associated with a thunderstorm?

answers.A: Lightning.
answers.B: Heavy rain showers.
answers.C: Supercooled raindrops.

explanations.A:
A thunderstorm, by definition, has lightning,

because lightning causes the thunder. Lightning is the discharge
of electricity generated by thunderstorms.
explanations.B:
because hail may occur instead of heavy
rain showers.
explanations.C:
because supercooled raindrops may not
occur if the lifting process does not extend above the freezing
level.

questions.question: During the life cycle of a thunderstorm, which stage is characterized predominately by downdrafts?

answers.B: Dissipating.
answers.C: Mature.
answers.A: Cumulus.

explanations.A:
because the cumulus stage is the building
stage characterized by updrafts.
explanations.B:
Thunderstorms have three stages in their
life cycle: cumulus, mature, and dissipating. In the dissipating

stage, the storm is characterized by downdrafts as the storm
rains itself out.
explanations.C:
because the mature stage has both
updrafts and downdrafts, which create strong wind shears.

questions.question: If squalls are reported at your destination, what wind conditions should you anticipate?

answers.A: Sudden increases in wind speed of at least 16 knots rising to 22 knots or more, lasting for at least 1 minute.
answers.B: Peak gusts of at least 35 knots for a sustained period of 1 minute or longer.
answers.C: Rapid variation in wind direction of at least 20° and changes in speed of at least 10 knots between peaks and lulls.

explanations.A:
A squall is a sudden increase in wind
speed by at least 16 kt. rising to 22 kt. or more and lasting for at
least 1 min. In contrast, a wind gust is a brief increase in wind
with a variation between peaks and lulls of at least 10 kt. Note
that these definitions involve variations in wind speed, not wind
direction.
explanations.B:
because a squall is a sudden increase in
wind speed of at least 16 kt., rising to a peak of 22 kt. or more,
not a peak gust of at least 35 kt. lasting for at least 1 min.
explanations.C:
because squalls refer to changes in wind
speed, not direction. Additionally, the wind is reported as gusty

when there are changes in speed of at least 10 kt. between
peaks and lulls.

questions.question: What is indicated by the term “embedded thunderstorms"?

answers.A: Severe thunderstorms are embedded within a squall line.
answers.B: Thunderstorms are predicted to develop in a stable air mass.
answers.C: Thunderstorms are obscured by massive cloud layers and cannot be seen.

explanations.A:
because a squall line consists of severe
thunderstorms which can usually be seen.
explanations.B:
because thunderstorms do not usually
occur in stable air masses.
explanations.C:
The term "embedded thunderstorms"

means that the storms are embedded in clouds or thick haze
layers and cannot be seen.

questions.question: Which weather phenomenon signals the beginning of the mature stage of a thunderstorm?

answers.A: The start of rain at the surface.
answers.B: Growth rate of cloud is maximum.
answers.C: Strong turbulence in the cloud.

explanations.A:
The mature stage of a thunderstorm is
indicated when rain begins falling at the surface. This means that
downdrafts have developed sufficiently to carry water all the way
through the thunderstorm.
explanations.B:
because maximum growth rate occurs in
the first or cumulus stage.
explanations.C:
because strong turbulence can occur in
all stages.

questions.question: Which is true regarding the use of airborne weather-avoidance radar for the recognition of certain weather conditions?

answers.A: The radarscope provides no assurance of avoiding instrument weather conditions.
answers.B: The avoidance of hail is assured when flying between and just clear of the most intense echoes.
answers.C: The clear area between intense echoes indicates that visual sighting of storms can be maintained when flying between the echoes.

explanations.A:
Weather-avoidance radar provides
information on precipitation based on echo returns. Avoiding the
heaviest areas of precipitation will often (not always) keep you
out of the greatest turbulence. Radar does not show water vapor.
Thus, clouds and fog, i.e., instrument weather conditions, are not
indicated.
explanations.B:
because intense thunderstorms can often
hurl hail for miles.
explanations.C:
because visual sighting of storms is not
assured, because clouds and fog are not shown by radar.

questions.question: In which meteorological environment is aircraft structural icing most likely to have the highest rate of accumulation?

answers.A: Cumulonimbus clouds.
answers.B: High humidity and freezing temperature.
answers.C: Freezing rain.

explanations.A:
because icing does not necessarily occur

in thunderstorms due to the large variation in temperature in
thunderstorms.
explanations.B:
because visible moisture, not just high
humidity, must be present for icing.
explanations.C:
The condition most favorable for very
hazardous icing is the presence of many large, supercooled
water drops (i.e., freezing rain). The heaviest icing will usually be
found at altitudes at or slightly above the freezing level where the
temperature is never more than a few degrees below freezing.

questions.question: Test data indicate that ice, snow, or frost having a thickness and roughness similar to medium or coarse sandpaper on the leading edge and upper surface of an airfoil can

answers.A: reduce lift by as much as 50 percent and increase drag by as much as 50 percent.
answers.B: increase drag and reduce lift by as much as 25 percent.
answers.C: reduce lift by as much as 30 percent and increase drag by 40 percent.

explanations.A:
because ice, snow, or frost having a
thickness or roughness similar to medium or coarse sandpaper
on the leading edge and upper surface of an airfoil can reduce lift
by as much as 30%, not 50%, and increase drag by 40%, not
50%.
explanations.B:
because ice, snow, or frost having a
thickness or roughness similar to medium or coarse sandpaper
on the leading edge and upper surface of an airfoil can reduce lift

by as much as 30%, not 25%, and increase drag by 40%,
25%.
explanations.C:
Test data indicate that ice, snow, or frost
formations having a thickness and surface roughness similar to
medium or coarse sandpaper on the leading edge and upper
surface of an airfoil can reduce lift by as much as 30% and
increase drag by 40%. These changes in lift and drag

significantly increase stall speed, reduce controllability, and alter
aircraft flight characteristics.

questions.question: Which precipitation type normally indicates freezing rain at higher altitudes?

answers.B: Hail.
answers.C: Ice pellets.
answers.A: Snow.

explanations.A:
because snow indicates that the
temperature of the air above you is well below freezing.
explanations.B:
because hail indicates instability of the air
aloft where supercooled droplets above the freezing level begin

to freeze. Once a drop has frozen, other drops latch onto it, and
the hailstone grows.
explanations.C:
Ice pellets normally indicate that rain
droplets are freezing at a higher altitude. Warmer air above
exists from which rain is falling and freezing on the way down, as
it enters cooler air (i.¢., freezing rain exists above).

questions.question: What is an operational consideration if you fly into rain which freezes on impact?

answers.B: Temperatures are above freezing at some higher altitude.
answers.C: You have flown through a cold front.
answers.A: You have flown into an area of thunderstorms.

explanations.A:
because freezing rain does not
necessarily indicate the presence of thunderstorms.
explanations.B:
Rain which freezes on impact is called
freezing rain. If rain falls through freezing air, it will usually form

supercooled water droplets, i.e., freezing rain. It indicates that
temperatures somewhere above the airplane are above freezing.
explanations.C:
because freezing rain does not
necessarily indicate the presence of cold fronts.

questions.question: What temperature condition is indicated if wet snow is encountered at your flight altitude?

answers.A: The temperature is above freezing at your altitude.
answers.B: The temperature is below freezing at your altitude.
answers.C: You are flying from a warm air mass into a cold air mass.

explanations.A:
If snow is wet at your altitude, you are in

above-freezing temperatures because the snow has started to
melt.
explanations.B:
because the wet snow indicates the

temperature is above freezing, not below freezing, at your
altitude.
explanations.C:
because the temperature is lower above
you, but not necessarily in front of you.

questions.question: The presence of ice pellets at the surface is evidence that

answers.B: a cold front has passed.
answers.C: there is freezing rain at a higher altitude.
answers.A: there are thunderstorms in the area.

explanations.A:
because thunderstorms do not
necessarily cause ice pellets.
explanations.B:
because cold fronts do not necessarily
cause ice pellets.
explanations.C:
Ice pellets form as a result of rain freezing

at a higher altitude. Rain droplets cool as they fall from a warmer
layer through air with a temperature below freezing.

questions.question: Why is frost considered hazardous to flight operation?

answers.A: Frost changes the basic aerodynamic shape of the airfoil.
answers.B: Frost decreases control effectiveness.
answers.C: Frost causes early airflow separation resulting in a loss of lift.

explanations.A:
because frost is very thin. It does not
change the airfoil shape as structural icing does.
explanations.B:
because frost has no bearing on control
effectiveness, only airfoil lift.
explanations.C:
Frost spoils the smooth flow of air, thus
Causing a slowing of the airflow. This causes early airflow
separation over the affected airfoil, resulting in a loss of lift. A
heavy coat of hard frost will cause a 5 to 10% increase in stall
speed. Even a small amount of frost on airfoils may prevent an
aircraft from becoming airborne at normal takeoff speed.

questions.question: If the air temperature is +8 °C at an elevation of 1,350 feet and a standard (average) temperature lapse rate exists, what will be the approximate freezing level?

answers.A: 3,350 feet MSL.
answers.B: 5,350 feet MSL.
answers.C: 9,350 feet MSL.

explanations.A:
because it represents a standard lapse
rate of 4° per 1,000 ft.
explanations.B:
The decrease of temperature with altitude
is defined as the lapse rate. The standard lapse rate is 2°C per
1,000 ft. To reach the freezing level, you must have a drop of 8°C.
Thus the freezing level is 4,000 ft. (8/2 x 1,000 ft.) up, or 5,350 ft.
MSL (1,350 + 4,000).
explanations.C:
because it represents a standard lapse
rate of 1° per 1,000 ft.

questions.question: What is an important characteristic of wind shear?

answers.B: The Coriolis phenomenon in both high- and low-level air masses is the principal generating force.
answers.C: Itis an atmospheric condition that may be associated with a low-level temperature inversion, a jet stream, or a frontal zone.
answers.A: ltis an atmospheric condition that is associated exclusively with Zones of convergence.

explanations.A:
because zones of convergence are
low-pressure areas. Wind shear can occur in highs as well as
lows.
explanations.B:
because the Coriolis force is the

deflective force of the Earth's rotation which affects all wind flows,
not just wind shear.
explanations.C:
Wind shear can occur at any level where
winds are blowing in different directions or at different speeds. It
is an atmospheric condition associated with low-level
temperature inversions, the jet stream, or a frontal zone.

questions.question: A pilot reporting turbulence that momentarily causes slight, erratic changes in altitude and/or attitude should report it as

answers.A: light turbulence.
answers.B: moderate turbulence.
answers.C: light chop.

explanations.A:
Light turbulence is defined as a disturbed

air flow that momentarily causes slight erratic changes in altitude
and/or attitude.
explanations.B:
because moderate turbulence is more

intense. It is sufficient to cause changes in altitude, but the pilot
maintains control throughout.
explanations.C:
because light chop means slight or

moderate, rapid, and somewhat rhythmic bumpiness without
appreciable changes in altitude or attitude.

questions.question: What is an important characteristic of wind shear?

answers.B: It usually exists only in the vicinity of thunderstorms, but may be found near a strong temperature inversion.
answers.C: It may be associated with either a wind shift or a wind speed gradient at any level in the atmosphere.
answers.A: tis primarily associated with the lateral vortices generated by thunderstorms.

explanations.A:
because wind shear is found in
Conditions other than thunderstorm turbulence, e.g., mountain
waves, fronts, etc.
explanations.B:
because wind shear is found in

conditions other than thunderstorm turbulence, e.g., mountain
waves, fronts, etc.
explanations.C:
Wind shear can occur at any level where
winds are blowing in different directions or at different speeds.

questions.question: Where can wind shear associated with a thunderstorm be found? Choose the most complete answer.

answers.A: In front of the thunderstorm cell (anvil side) and on the right side of the cell.
answers.B: In front of the thunderstorm cell and directly under the cell.
answers.C: On all sides of the thunderstorm cell and directly under the cell.

explanations.A:
because wind shear may be found on all
sides and beneath the thunderstorm cell.
explanations.B:
because wind shear may be found on all
sides and beneath the thunderstorm cell.
explanations.C:
Wind shear associated with thunderstorms

may be found on all sides of the thunderstorm cell, including
directly beneath it and as much as 20 mii. laterally.

questions.question: Where does wind shear occur?

answers.A: Exclusively in thunderstorms.
answers.B: Wherever there is an abrupt decrease in pressure and/or temperature.
answers.C: With either a wind shift or a wind speed gradient at any level in the atmosphere.

explanations.A:
because wind shear is also caused by
barriers to wind flow, occurs behind and below airplanes
generating lift, etc.
explanations.B:
because wind shear is the result of wind
change, not a change in temperature or pressure, per se.
explanations.C:
Wind shear can occur at any level where

winds are blowing in different directions (wind shift) or at different
speeds (a wind speed gradient).

questions.question: Hazardous wind shear is commonly encountered near the ground

answers.A: during periods when the wind velocity is stronger than 35 knots.
answers.B: during periods when the wind velocity is stronger than 35 knots and near mountain valleys.
answers.C: during periods of strong temperature inversion and near thunderstorms.

explanations.A:
because any wind, not only wind shear, is
hazardous when in excess of 35 kt.
explanations.B:
because wind shear usually occurs on the
leeward side of mountains, not in valleys.
explanations.C:
Thunderstorms produce hazardous wind
shear near the ground. Wind shear during temperature inversions
is also hazardous when at low levels as it affects aircraft
approaching and departing airports.

questions.question: An aircraft that encounters a headwind of 45 knots, within a microburst, may expect a total shear across the microburst of

answers.A: 40 knots.
answers.B: 80 knots.
answers.C: 90 knots.

explanations.A:
because the total wind shear expected

across a microburst is twice the initial headwind, e.g., 45 kt. x 2 =
90 kt., not 40 kt.
explanations.B:
because the total wind shear expected
across a microburst is twice the initial headwind, e.g., 45 kt. x 2 =
90 kt., not 80 kt.
explanations.C:
If a headwind in a microburst is 45 kt., the
wind will be going in the opposite direction on the other side of
the microburst at presumably the same 45 kt., resulting in a wind
shear between the headwind and tailwind of 90 kt.

questions.question: Maximum downdrafts in a microburst encounter may be as strong as

answers.A: 8,000 feet per minute.
answers.B: 7,000 feet per minute.
answers.C: 6,000 feet per minute.

explanations.A:
because maximum downdrafts are
usually 6,000 FPM, not 8,000 FPM.
explanations.B:
because maximum downdrafts are
usually 6,000 FPM, not 7,000 FPM.
explanations.C:
Downdrafts in a microburst can be as
strong as 6,000 FPM. Horizontal winds near the surface can be

as strong as 45 Kt., resulting in a 90-kt. wind shear. The strong
horizontal winds occur within a few hundred feet of the ground.

questions.question: What is the expected duration of an individual microburst?

answers.A: Two minutes with maximum winds lasting approximately 1 minute.
answers.B: One microburst may continue for as long as 2 to 4 hours.
answers.C: Seldom longer than 15 minutes from the time the burst strikes the ground until dissipation.

explanations.A:
because microbursts last 15, not 2 min.,
and maximum winds last 2 to 4 min., not 1 min.
explanations.B:
because the maximum winds last 2 to 4

min., not 2 to 4 hr., and the microburst is usually limited to about
15 min.
explanations.C:
An individual microburst will seldom last
longer than 15 min. from the time it strikes ground until
dissipation. The horizontal winds continue to increase during the

first 5 min. with maximum-intensity winds lasting approximately 2
to 4 min.
