questions.question: AIRMETs are issued on a scheduled basis every

answers.A: 15 minutes after the hour only.
answers.B: 15 minutes until the AIRMET is canceled.
answers.C: six hours.

explanations.A:
because AIRMETs are issued on a
scheduled basis every 6 hr., not every 15 min. past the hour.
explanations.B:
because AIRMETs are issued on a

scheduled basis every 6 hr., not every 15 min. until the AIRMET is
canceled.
explanations.C:
AIRMETs are issued on a scheduled basis
every 6 hr., with unscheduled amendments issued as required.

questions.question: What is the maximum forecast period for AIRMET's?

answers.A: Two hours.
answers.B: Four hours.
answers.C: Six hours.

explanations.A:
because convective SIGMETs, not
AIRMETs, are valid for up to 2 hr.
explanations.B:
because SIGMETs, not AIRMETs, are
valid for up to 4 hr.
explanations.C:
The maximum forecast period for

AIRMETs is 6 hr. If conditions persist beyond 6 hr., the AIRMET
must be updated and reissued.

questions.question: SIGMETs are issued as a warning of weather conditions potentially hazardous

answers.A: particularly to light aircraft.
answers.B: to all aircraft.
answers.C: only to light aircraft operations.

explanations.A: because SIGMETs apply to all aircraft.
explanations.B:
SIGMETs warn of weather considered
potentially hazardous to all categories of aircraft. SIGMETs are
forecasts of tornadoes, lines of thunderstorms, embedded
thunderstorms, large hail, severe and extreme turbulence, severe
icing, and widespread sandstorms and snowstorms.
explanations.C:
because AIRMETs, not SIGMETs, apply
to light aircraft.

questions.question: Which meteorological condition is issued in the form of a SIGMET (WS)?

answers.A: Widespread sand or dust storms lowering visibility to less than 3 miles.
answers.B: Moderate icing.
answers.C: Sustained winds of 30 knots or greater at the surface.

explanations.A:
SIGMETs are issued for severe and
extreme turbulence; severe icing; and widespread dust storms,
sandstorms, or volcanic ash lowering visibility below 3 mi.
explanations.B:
because moderate icing is issued in the
form of an AIRMET, not a SIGMET.
explanations.C:
because sustained winds of 30 kt. or

greater at the surface are issued in the form of an AIRMET, not a
SIGMET.

questions.question: Pilots of IFR flights seeking ATC in-flight weather avoidance assistance should keep in mind that

answers.A: ATC radar limitations and, frequency congestion may limit the controllers capability to provide this service.
answers.B: circumnavigating severe weather can only be accommodated in the en route areas away from terminals because of congestion.
answers.C: ATC Narrow Band Radar does not provide the controller with weather intensity capability.

explanations.A:
The controllers’ primary function is to
provide safe separation between aircraft. Any additional service,
such as weather avoidance, can be provided only to the extent it
does not interfere with the primary function. Unfortunately, the

separation workload is usually greater when weather disrupts the
normal flow of traffic.
explanations.B:
because controllers can provide weather
circumnavigation in terminal areas when workload permits.
explanations.C:
because ATC narrowband radar is
replacing digitized radar weather displays in ARTCC facilities to
provide even better measurement of precipitation density.

questions.question: The Hazardous Inflight Weather Advisory Service (HIWAS) is a continuous broadcast over selected VORs of

answers.A: SIGMETs, CONVECTIVE SIGMETs, AIRMETs, Severe Weather Forecast Alerts (AWW), and Center Weather Advisories.
answers.B: SIGMETs, CONVECTIVE SIGMETs, AIRMETs, Wind Shear Advisories, and Severe Weather Forecast Alerts (AWW).
answers.C: Wind Shear Advisories, Radar Weather Reports, SIGMETs, CONVECTIVE SIGMETs, AIRMETs, and Center Weather Advisories (CWA).

explanations.A:
The Hazardous Inflight Weather Advisory
Service (HIWAS) is a continuous broadcast service over
selected VORs of in-flight weather advisories, i.e., SIGMETs,
convective SIGMETs, AIRMETs, severe weather forecast alerts
(AWW), and center weather advisories (CWA).
explanations.B:
because a runway wind shear advisory

would be given to arriving and departing aircraft by a tower
controller, not the HIWAS.
explanations.C:
because radar weather reports would be

available from the En Route Flight Advisory Service (EFAS), not
the HIWAS.

questions.question: What is meant by the entry in the remarks section of METAR surface report for KBNA? METAR KBNA 211250Z 33018KT 290V260 1/2SM R31/2700FT +SN BLSNFG VV008 00/M03 A2991 RMK RAE42SNB42

answers.A: The wind is variable from 290° to 360°.
answers.B: Heavy blowing snow and fog on runway 31.
answers.C: Rain ended 42 past the hour, snow began 42 past the hour.

explanations.A:
because the remarks section indicates
that rain ended 42 min. past the hour and snow began 42 min.
past the hour, not that the wind is variable from 290° to 360°.
explanations.B:
because the remarks section indicates
that rain ended 42 min. past the hour and snow began 42 min.

past the hour, not that there is heavy blowing snow and fog on
Rwy 31.
explanations.C:
The contraction RMK follows the altimeter
in the body and precedes remarks. RMK RAE42SNB42 means

remarks follow, rain ended 42 min. past the hour (RAE42), and
‘snow began 42 min. past the hour (SNB42).

questions.question: Aceiling is defined as the height of the

answers.A: highest layer of clouds or obscuring phenomena aloft that covers over 6/10 of the sky.
answers.B: lowest layer of clouds that contributed to the overall overcast.
answers.C: lowest layer of clouds or obscuring phenomena aloft that is reported as broken or overcast.

explanations.A:
because the ceiling is the base of the
lowest, not highest, broken or overcast layer.
explanations.B:
because the lowest layer of clouds must
be broken or overcast, not simply a contributor to the overall
overcast.
explanations.C:
For aviation purposes, the ceiling is the

lowest broken or overcast layer, or vertical visibility into an
obscuration.

questions.question: The reporting station originating this Aviation Routine Weather Report has a field elevation of 620 feet. If the reported sky cover is one continuous layer, what is its thickness (tops of OVC are reported at 6,500 feet)? METAR KMDW 121856Z AUTO 32005KT 1 1/2SM +RA BR OVC007 17/16 A2980

answers.B: 5,800 feet.
answers.C: 5,880 feet.
answers.A: 5,180 feet.

explanations.A:
The sky cover for KMDW is reported as a
ceiling of 700 ft. AGL, overcast (OVC007). The field elevation is
620 ft. MSL; thus, the base of the overcast layer is 1,320 ft. MSL
(700+620). The tops of the overcast are reported at 6,500 ft.;
thus, the thickness of the overcast layer is 5,180 ft. (6,500-1,320).
explanations.B:
because 5,800 ft. would be the thickness.
of the sky cover if the field elevation were 0 ft., not 620 ft.
explanations.C:
because 5,880 ft. is the height above

ground of the tops of the overcast layer, not the thickness of the
overcast layer.

questions.question: The station originating the following weather report has a field elevation of 1,300 feet MSL. From the bottom of the overcast cloud layer, what is its thickness (tops of OVC are reported at 3,800 feet)? SPECI KOKC 22282 28024G36KT 3/4SM BKNO08 OVC020 28/23 A3000 A_ 500 feet.

answers.B: 1,700 feet.
answers.C: 2,500 feet.

explanations.A:
The question is to determine the thickness
of the overcast layer at KOKC. The SPECI reported the base of
the overcast cloud layer at 2,000 ft. AGL (OVC020). The field
elevation is 1,300 ft. MSL; thus, the base of the overcast layer is
3,300 ft. MSL (2,000+1,300). The tops of the overcast layer are
reported at 3,800 ft. MSL; thus, the thickness of the overcast
cloud layer is 500 ft. (3,800-3,300).
explanations.B:
because 1,700 ft. is the distance from the

base of the broken (BKN), not overcast (OVC), cloud layer to the
top of the overcast.
explanations.C:
because 2,500 ft. is the height above the
ground of the tops of the overcast, not the thickness of the
overcast layer.

questions.question: What significant sky condition is reported in this METAR observation? METAR KBNA 1250Z 33018KT 290V360 1/2SM R31/2700FT +SN BLSNFG VV008 00/M03 A2991 RMK RERAE42SNB42

answers.A: Runway 31 ceiling is 2,700 feet.
answers.B: Sky is obscured with vertical visibility of 800 feet.
answers.C: Measured ceiling is 300 feet overcast.

explanations.A:
because runway 31 RVR, not ceiling, is
2,700 ft.
explanations.B:
The sky condition follows the weather
element. At KBNA, the sky cover is reported as VV008, which
means the sky is obscured (indefinite ceiling) with a vertical
visibility of 800 feet.
explanations.C:
because 00/M03 means the temperature
is 0°C and the dew point is -3°C, not that there is a measured
ceiling of 300 ft. overcast.

questions.question: Interpret this PIREP. MRB UA/OV MRB/TM 1430/FL 060/TP C182/SK BKN BL WX RAITB MDT.

answers.A: Ceiling 6,000 feet intermittently below moderate thundershowers; turbulence increasing westward.
answers.B: FL 60,000, intermittently below clouds; moderate rain, turbulence increasing with the wind.
answers.C: At 6,000 feet; between layers; moderate turbulence; moderate rain.

explanations.A:
because the flight level, not the ceiling, is

6,000 ft., and TB MDT means moderate turbulence, not
thundershowers.
explanations.B:
because the flight level is 6,000 ft., not
60,000 ft., and BL means between layers, not below clouds.
explanations.C:
The PIREP decodes as follows: pilot
report, over Martinsburg, WV at 1430 UTC, flight level is 6,000 ft.,
type of aircraft is a Cessna 182, and sky condition is broken with
the pilot reporting between layers in moderate rain and moderate
turbulence.

questions.question: Which response most closely interprets the following PIREP? UA/OV OKC 063064/TM 1522/FLO80/TP C172/TA - 04 IWV245040/TB LGT/RM IN CLR.

answers.A: 64 nautical miles on the 63 degree radial from Oklahoma City VOR at 1522 UTC, flight level 8,000 ft. Type of aircraft is a Cessna 172.
answers.B: Reported by a Cessna 172, turbulence and light rime icing in climb to 8,000 ft.
answers.C: 63 nautical miles on the 64 degree radial from Oklahoma City, thunderstorm and light rain at 1522 UTC.

explanations.A:
The PIREP decodes as follows: pilot
report, 64 NM on the 063° radial from Oklahoma City VOR at
1522 UTC, flight level is 8,000 ft., type of aircraft is a Cessna
172, outside air temperature is -4°C, wind is from 245° at 40 kt.
with light turbulence, remarks are that the pilot is in clear skies.
explanations.B:
because TB LGT RM IN CLR means light

turbulence (remark) in clear, not turbulence and rime icing in
climb.
explanations.C:
because OKC 063064 means the aircraft
was located 64 NM, not 63 NM, on the 063° radial, not the 064°
radial. Additionally, there is no report of thunderstorm and rain.

questions.question: Figure 14. (Refer to figure 4.) The Weather Depiction Chart in the area of northwestern Wyoming indicates

answers.B: 1,000-foot ceilings and visibility 3 miles or more.
answers.C: 500-foot ceilings and continuous rain, less than 3 miles visibility.
answers.A: overcast with scattered rain showers.

explanations.A:
because the chart provides data only
from observation stations. Rain showers would be reported as
intermittent, not scattered. Intermittent showers (moderate
intensity at time of observation) would be shown as two vertical,
not horizontal, dots.
explanations.B:
because the station in Wyoming is

reporting a ceiling of 500 ft., not 1,000 ft., and since visibility is

not shown, it is interpreted to mean greater than 6 SM, not 3 SM
or more.
explanations.C:
The station circle in northwestern Wyoming
indicates an overcast sky (darkened circle), 500-ft. ceiling ("5"
under the circle), and continuous rain (two dots over circle). The

station circle is in a shaded area, which indicates IFR with ceiling
less than 1,000 ft. and/or visibility less than 3 SM.

questions.question: Figure 15. (Refer to figure 4.) The Weather Depiction Chart indicates the heaviest precipitation is occurring in

answers.B: north central Minnesota.
answers.C: central South Dakota.
answers.A: north central Florida.

explanations.A:
because no precipitation is reported for
north central Florida.
explanations.B:
The heaviest precipitation is occurring in
north central Minnesota. The station near the southern edge of
the shaded area has four dots in a diamond shape above the

circle, which means continuous rain (not freezing), heavy at the
time of observation.
explanations.C:
because no precipitation is reported for
central South Dakota.

questions.question: Figure 16. (Refer to figure 4.) What is the meaning of a bracket ( ] ) plotted to the right of the station circle on a weather depiction chart?

answers.A: The station represents the en route conditions within a 50 mile radius.
answers.B: The station is an automated observation location.
answers.C: The station gives local overview of flying conditions for a six-hour period.

explanations.A:
because a bracket to the right of the
station circle means the station is an automated site. The chart
does not provide en route conditions between stations.
explanations.B:
Data for the weather depiction chart come
from the observations reported by both manual and automated
observation locations. The automated stations are denoted by a
bracket (] ) plotted to the right of the station circle.
explanations.C:
because a bracket to the right of the
station circle means that the station is an automated site, not that

the station gives a local overview of flying conditions for a 6-hr.
period.

On Fig. 8, find arrow A. Note that it points
to a dot indicating the highest top in hundreds of feet, which is

MSL, not bases of 2,800 MSL and the second level of contours

the northeast, not northwest and echo tops, not bases, are

The point of arrow C on Fig. 8 is in the

echo intensity. The 280 indicates 28,000 ft. MSL tops. The arrow

questions.question: (Refer to figure 8.) What weather conditions are depicted in the area indicated by arrow F onthe Radar Summary Chart?

answers.A: Line of echoes; thunderstorms; highest echo tops 45,000 feet MSL; no line movement indicated.
answers.B: Echo bases vary from 15,000 feet to 46,000 feet MSL; thunderstorms increasing in intensity; line of echoes moving rapidly toward the north.
answers.C: Line of severe thunderstorms moving from south to north; echo bases vary from 4,400 feet to 4,600 feet MSL; extreme echoes.

The solid line to which arrow F in Fig. 8 is
pointing is a line of echoes. They are thunderstorms as indicated

appears as 450. No movement of the line itself is indicated.
explanations.B:
because the tops, not the bases, are
approximately 46,000 ft. MSL. No movement or change in
intensity is indicated.
explanations.C:
because the tops are 44,000 to

approximately 46,000 ft. MSL, not 4,400 to 4,600. No movement
of the line is indicated.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 8.) What weather conditions are depicted in the area indicated by arrow G on the Radar Summary Chart?

answers.A: Echo bases 10,000 feet MSL; cell movement toward northeast at 15 knots; weak to moderate echoes; rain.
answers.B: Area movement toward northeast at 15 knots; rain decreasing in intensity; echo bases 1,000 feet MSL; strong echoes.
answers.C: Strong to very strong echoes; area movement toward northeast at 15 knots; echo tops 10,000 feet MSL; light rain.

explanations.A:
Arrow G in Fig. 8 points to an area of
echoes with bases of 10,000 ft. MSL moving to the northeast at
15 kt. Since the echoes are in the first level of contours, they are
weak to moderate. The R indicates rain.
explanations.B:
because the bases are 10,000 ft. MSL,
not 1,000 ft. MSL. Also, decreasing intensity would be indicated
by a minus sign after the R.
explanations.C:
because there is only one contour level,
signifying weak to moderate intensity, not strong to very strong.

questions.question: What important information is provided by the Radar Summary Chart that is not shown on other weather charts?

answers.B: Types of precipitation.
answers.C: Areas of cloud cover and icing levels within the clouds.
answers.A: Lines and cells of hazardous thunderstorms.

explanations.A:
A radar summary chart shows lines of

thunderstorms and hazardous cells that are not shown on other
weather charts.
explanations.B:
because other weather charts show types
of precipitation.
explanations.C:
because icing conditions cannot be
detected by radar.

questions.question: For the most effective use of the Radar Summary Chart during preflight planning, a pilot should

answers.B: compare it with the charts, reports, and forecasts of a three-dimensional picture of clouds and precipitation.
answers.C: utilize the chart as the only source of information regarding storms and hazardous conditions existing between reporting stations.
answers.A: consult the chart to determine more accurate measurements of freezing levels, cloud cover, and wind conditions between reporting stations.

explanations.A:
because a radar summary chart does not
show freezing levels, cloud cover, or wind conditions.
explanations.B:
A radar summary chart graphically
indicates a collection of radar reports, i.e., reports of echoes
from thunderstorms and heavy precipitation. In conjunction with
the weather depiction chart, which is a composite of METAR
reports, a radar summary chart provides a more
three-dimensional picture of clouds and precipitation.
explanations.C:
because a radar summary chart must be
used in conjunction with other reports and forecasts for an
accurate picture of weather conditions.

questions.question: From which primary source should you obtain information regarding the weather expected to exist at your destination at your estimated time of arrival?

answers.A: Weather Depiction Chart.
answers.B: Radar Summary and Weather Depiction Chart.
answers.C: Terminal Aerodrome Forecast.

explanations.A:
because a weather depiction chart is a
national weather map of observed, not forecast, weather at the
time specified on the chart. It is useful for flight planning to get a
broad overview of the observed conditions.
explanations.B:
because radar summary and weather
depiction charts are national weather maps of observed, not
forecast, weather at a specific time. They are useful for flight

planning but do not provide specific information about a
particular destination.
explanations.C:
A terminal aerodrome forecast (TAF) is a
concise statement of the expected meteorological conditions at
an airport during a specified period (usually 24 hr.). Thus, a TAF

contains information regarding the expected weather at the
destination airport at the ETA.

questions.question: Which primary source should be used to obtain forecast weather information at your destination for the planned ETA?

answers.B: Radar Summary and Weather Depiction Charts.
answers.C: Terminal Aerodrome Forecast (TAF).
answers.A: Area Forecast.

explanations.A:
because an area forecast (FA) is a
forecast of general weather conditions over an area the size of
several states, not for a specific airport. The FA is used if the
destination airport does not have a TAF.
explanations.B:
because radar summary and weather
depiction charts are national weather maps of observed weather
at a specific time. They are useful for flight planning but do not
provide specific information about a particular destination airport.
explanations.C:
A terminal aerodrome forecast (TAF) is a
concise statement of the expected meteorological conditions at
an airport during a specified period (usually 24 hr.). Thus, a TAF

contains information regarding the expected weather at the
destination airport at the ETA.

questions.question: The body of a Terminal Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) covers a geographical proximity within a

answers.A: 5 nautical mile radius of the center of an airport.
answers.B: 5 statute mile radius from the center of an airport runway complex.
answers.C: 5 to 10 statute mile radius from the center of an airport runway complex.

explanations.A:
because the TAF covers a geographic
area within a 5-SM radius of the airport's center, not a 5-NM
Tadius.
explanations.B:
The Terminal Aerodrome Forecast (TAF)
is a concise statement of the expected meteorological conditions
at an airport during a specified period (usually 24 hr.). The TAF

covers a geographic area within a 5 SM radius of the airport's
center.
explanations.C:
because the TAF covers a geographic
area within a 5 SM radius of the airport's center, not 5 to 10
statute miles. The letters VC in the TAF describe conditions that
will occur within the vicinity of the airport (5 to 10 SM), not at the

airport, and will be used only with FG (fog), SH (showers), or TS
(thunderstorms).

questions.question: Area forecasts generally include a forecast period of 18 hours and cover a

answers.B: area less than 3,000 square miles.
answers.C: area the size of several states.
answers.A: terminal area.

because a TAF, not an FA, will forecast
conditions at a terminal area.
explanations.B:
because an FA forecast covers an area

greater than, not less than, 3,000 sq. mi. and gives a general

description of clouds and weather which are significant to VFR
operations.
explanations.C:
Area forecasts (FA) generally include a

total forecast period of 18 hr. and cover a geographical area the
size of several states.

questions.question: Astation is forecasting wind and temperature aloft at FL 390 to be 300° at 200 knots; temperature -54°C. How would this data be encoded in the FD?

explanations.A:
because it indicates winds from 300° at 0

kt. However, when forecast speed is less than 5 kt., the code is
9900 for wind direction and speed.
explanations.B:
At FL 390, a 300° wind at 200 Kt. is
encoded as 809954. Note that the first two digits are the
direction. The second two digits are velocity. 200 kt. or greater
wind speeds are coded as 99 for the speed, and 50 is added to
the two-digit direction code. Here, the direction is 80 for 300°.
The temperature is the last two digits, and minus signs are
omitted above 24,000 ft. MSL.
explanations.C:
because it indicates a 99-kt. wind speed
from 300°.

questions.question: How much colder than standard temperature is the forecast temperature at 9,000 feet, as indicated in the following excerpt from the Winds and Temperature Aloft Forecast? FT 6000 9000 0737-04 1043-10 A3°C.

explanations.A:
because standard temperature at 9,000
ft. is -3°C, not -7°C.
explanations.B:
because standard temperature at 9,000
ft is -3°C, not 0°C.
explanations.C:
At 9,000 ft., the forecast temperature is
-10°C. Standard temperature is 15°C at sea level with a lapse
tate of 2°C per 1,000 ft., which would bring the standard
temperature to -3°C at 9,000 ft. (15° - 18°). Therefore, the
forecast temperature of -10°C is 7° colder than the standard
temperature of -3°C.

questions.question: What wind direction and speed is represented by the entry 9900+00 for 9,000 feet, on a Winds and Temperatures Aloft Forecast (FD)?

explanations.A:
The entry 9900 in a winds and
temperatures aloft forecast indicates light and variable winds.
+00 is the air temperature on the Celsius scale.
explanations.B:
because an example of the code for
winds over 200 kt. would be 7099, for 200° at 199 kt. or greater.
explanations.C:
because light and variable means less
than 5 kt, not 10 kt.

questions.question: When is the wind-group at one of the forecast altitudes omitted at a specific location or station in the Winds and Temperatures Aloft Forecast (FD)? When the wind

answers.A: is less than 5 knots.
answers.B: is less than 10 knots.
answers.C: at the altitude is within 1,500 feet of the station elevation.

explanations.A:
because, when forecast wind speed is
less than 5 kt., the code 9900 is used for direction and velocity.

because, when forecast wind speed is

velocity.
explanations.C:
No winds are forecast within 1,500 ft. of
the station elevation. No temperatures are forecast for the
3,000-ft. MSL or for a level within 2,500 ft. of station elevation.

questions.question: When is the temperature at one of the forecast altitudes omitted at a specific location or station in the Winds and Temperatures Aloft Forecast (FD)?

answers.A: When the temperature is standard for that altitude.
answers.B: For the 3,000-foot altitude (level) or when the level is within 2,500 feet of station elevation.
answers.C: Only when the winds are omitted for that altitude (level).

explanations.A:
because temperatures are reported
whether standard or not.
explanations.B:
No temperatures are forecast for the
3,000-ft. level or for a level within 2,500 ft. of station elevation. No
winds are forecast within 1,500 ft. of the station elevation.
explanations.C:
because the winds are omitted within

1,500 ft. of the ground and temperatures are omitted within 2,500
ft. of the ground.

Winds aloft are forecast in true direction

questions.question: Apilot planning to depart at 1100Z on an IFR flight is particularly concerned about the hazard of icing. What sources reflect the most accurate information onicing conditions (current and forecast) at the time of departure?

answers.A: Low-Level Significant Weather Prognostic Chart, and the Area Forecast.
answers.B: The Area Forecast, and the Freezing Level Chart.
answers.C: Pilot weather reports (PIREPs), AIRMETs, and SIGMETs.

explanations.A:
because low-level sig weather prog

charts do not forecast icing conditions but do forecast freezing

levels, and an area forecast does not provide any information on
icing conditions.
explanations.B:
because a freezing-level chart cannot be
used to determine current or forecast icing conditions, and an

area forecast does not provide any information on icing
conditions.
explanations.C:
Pilot reports (PIREPs) can reflect the most
current icing conditions for a specific area, including type and
intensity. AIRMET Zulu is for icing and freezing levels for a

specified time and normally an outlook. A SIGMET is issued for
areas of severe icing.

questions.question: What flight planning information can a pilot derive from constant pressure charts?

answers.A: Clear air turbulence and icing conditions.
answers.B: Levels of widespread cloud coverage.
answers.C: Winds and temperatures aloft.

explanations.A:
because clear air turbulence is shown on
the low-level prog chart.
explanations.B:
because areas and levels of widespread

Cloud coverage are shown on the weather depiction and surface
analysis charts.
explanations.C:
Constant pressure charts provide
information about the observed temperature, wind, and
temperature-dew point spread along your proposed route.

questions.question: What conclusion(s) can be drawn from a 500-milli-bar Constant Pressure Chart for a planned flight at FL 180?

answers.A: Winds aloft at FL 180 generally flow across the height contours.
answers.B: Observed temperature, wind, and temperature/dew point spread along the proposed route can be approximated.
answers.C: Upper highs, lows, troughs, and ridges will be depicted by the use of lines of equal pressure.

explanations.A:
because the winds usually flow parallel to,
not across, the height contours.
explanations.B:
From a constant pressure analysis chart,
you can approximate the observed temperature, wind, and
temperature-dew point spread along a proposed route.
explanations.C:
because heights of the specified
pressure for each station are depicted via solid lines called

contours to give a height pattern. The contours depict high height
centers and low height centers, not highs and lows.

questions.question: Which weather forecast describes prospects for an area coverage of both severe and general thunderstorms during the following 24 hours?

answers.B: Convective outlook.
answers.C: Radar Summary Chart.
answers.A: Terminal Aerodrome Forecast.

explanations.A:
because a terminal aerodrome forecast
(TAF) is a statement of expected conditions around an airport,
not a forecast of thunderstorms only.
explanations.B:
The convective outlook (AC) describes the
prospects for general thunderstorm activity during the following
24 hr. Areas with a high, moderate, or slight risk of severe
thunderstorms are included, as well as areas where
thunderstorms may approach severe limits.
explanations.C:
because a radar summary chart depicts
observed radar returns, which show precipitation intensity, at the
time shown on the chart. It provides an indication of observed, not
forecast, severe and general thunderstorms.

questions.question: The Surface Analysis Chart depicts

answers.B: frontal locations and expected movement, pressure centers, cloud coverage, and obstructions to vision at the time of chart transmission.
answers.C: actual frontal positions, pressure patterns, temperature, dew point, wind, weather, and obstructions to vision at the valid time of the chart.

because the surface analysis chart does

because expected movement of weather
systems is not depicted. This chart depicts current conditions at

The surface analysis chart provides the
locations of pressure systems, dew points, wind, and
obstructions to vision at the valid time of the chart.

questions.question: What information is provided by a Convective Outlook (AC)?

answers.A: It describes areas of probable severe icing and severe or extreme turbulence during the next 24 hours.
answers.B: It provides prospects of both general and severe thunderstorm activity during the following 24 hours.
answers.C: Itindicates areas of probable convective turbulence and the extent of instability in the upper atmosphere (above 500 MB).

explanations.A:
because areas of severe or extreme
turbulence are forecast in the significant weather prog charts, not
in anAC. Additionally, icing is not specifically forecast but is
implied in clouds and precipitation above the freezing level.
explanations.B:
The convective outlook describes the
prospects for general thunderstorm activity during the following
24 hr. Areas with a high, moderate, or slight risk of severe
thunderstorms are included, as well as areas where
thunderstorms may approach severe limits.
explanations.C:
because areas of probable convective
turbulence and with the extent of instability above 500 mb/hPa
(18,000 ft. MSL) are depicted by the contraction "CB" ina
high-level significant weather prog, not an AC.

questions.question: What does a Convective Outlook (AC) describe for a following 24-hr. period?

answers.A: General thunderstorm activity.
answers.B: A severe weather watch bulletin.
answers.C: When forecast conditions are expected to continue beyond the valid period.

explanations.A:
A convective outlook (AC) describes the

prospects for general thunderstorm activity during the following
24 hr.
explanations.B:
because a severe weather watch bulletin
is a separate product. An AC forecasts general thunderstorm
activity for the following 24 hr., while a severe weather watch
bulletin is issued as necessary to define areas of possible
severe thunderstorms or tornado activity.
explanations.C:
because an AC is a forecast of

thunderstorm activity for the following 24-hr. period, not a

statement of forecast conditions that are expected to continue
beyond the valid period.

questions.question: When are severe weather watch bulletins (WW) issued?

answers.A: Every 12 hours as required.
answers.B: Every 24 hours as required.
answers.C: Unscheduled and issued as required.

explanations.A:
because severe weather watch bulletins

are unscheduled and are issued as required, not every 12 hr. as
required.
explanations.B:
because severe weather watch bulletins

are unscheduled and are issued as required, not every 24 hr. as
required.
explanations.C:
A severe weather watch bulletin (WW)
defines areas of possible severe thunderstorms or tornado
activity. WWs are unscheduled and are issued as required by the
National Severe Storm Forecast Center.

each feather (single line) equal to 10 kt. The maximum core
speed forecast for the jet stream over Canada is 130 kt. (2
pennants + 3 feathers = 130 kt)

questions.question: Whatis the definition of MEA?

answers.A: The lowest published altitude which meets obstacle clearance requirements and assures acceptable navigational signal coverage.
answers.B: The lowest published altitude which meets obstacle requirements, assures acceptable navigational signal coverage, two-way radio communications, and provides adequate radar coverage.
answers.C: An altitude which meets obstacle clearance requirements, assures acceptable navigation signal coverage, two-way radio communications, adequate radar coverage, and accurate DME mileage.

explanations.A:
The minimum en route altitude (MEA) is
the lowest published altitude between radio fixes which assures

acceptable navigational signal coverage and meets the obstacle
clearance requirements between those fixes.
explanations.B:
because, by definition, the MEA does not

assure either two-way radio communications or adequate radar
coverage.
explanations.C:
because, by definition, the MEA is the
lowest published, not any, altitude that meets obstacle clearance
requirements and assures acceptable navigation signal
‘coverage. It does not provide for either two-way radio
communications or adequate radar coverage.

questions.question: Reception of signals from an off-airway radio facility may be inadequate to identify the fix at the designated MEA. In this case, which altitude is designated for the fix?

answers.A: MRA.
answers.B: MCA. C.MOCA.

explanations.A:
MRA (minimum reception altitude) is the
lowest altitude at which an intersection can be determined. It is
the altitude assigned for a fix when the MEA will not provide

adequate reception of an off-airway radio facility (NAVAID)
identifying the fix.
explanations.B:
because MCA (minimum crossing
altitude) is the lowest altitude at a fix at which an aircraft must
cross when proceeding in the direction of a higher MEA.
explanations.C:
because the MOCA (minimum
obstruction clearance altitude) is the lowest published altitude in
effect between radio fixes on VOR airways, off-airway routes, or
route segments which meets obstacle clearance requirements for
the entire route segment and which assures acceptable
navigation signal coverage only within 22 NM of a VOR.

questions.question: Reception of signals from a radio facility, located off the airway being flown, may be inadequate at the designated MEA to identify the fix. In this case, which altitude is designated for the fix?

answers.A: MOCA.
answers.B: MRA. C.MCA.

explanations.A:
because the MOCA (minimum
obstruction clearance altitude) is the lowest published altitude in
effect between radio fixes on VOR airways, off-airway routes, or
route segments which meets obstacle clearance requirements for
the entire route segment and which assures acceptable
navigation signal coverage only within 22 NM of a VOR.
explanations.B:
MRA (minimum reception altitude) is the
lowest altitude at which an intersection can be determined. It is
the altitude assigned for a fix when the MEA will not provide

adequate reception of an off-airway radio facility (NAVAID)
identifying the fix.
explanations.C:
because MCA (minimum crossing
altitude) is the lowest altitude at a fix at which an aircraft must
cross when proceeding in the direction of a higher MEA.

questions.question: ATC may assign the MOCA when certain special conditions exist, and when within

answers.A: 22 NM ofa VOR.
answers.B: 25 NM ofa VOR.
answers.C: 30 NM ofa VOR.

explanations.A:
MOCA (minimum obstruction clearance
altitude) is the lowest published altitude in effect between radio
fixes on VOR airways, off-airway routes, or route segments which
meets obstacle clearance requirements for the entire route
segment and which assures acceptable navigational signal
coverage only within 22 NM of a VOR. Thus, ATC may assign the
MOCA as an assigned altitude, but only within 22 NM of a VOR.
explanations.B:
because the MOCA provides acceptable
navigational signal coverage only within 25 SM, not 25 NM, of a
VOR.
explanations.C:
because ATC may assign the MOCA as
an assigned altitude only within 22 NM, not 30 NM.

questions.question: Acceptable navigational signal coverage at the MOCA is assured for a distance from the VOR of only

answers.B: 22 NM.
answers.C: 25 NM.

explanations.A:
because acceptable navigational signal
coverage at the MOCA is assured for a distance from the VOR of
22 NM, not 12 NM.
explanations.B:
MOCA (minimum obstruction clearance
altitude) is the lowest published altitude in effect between radio
fixes on VOR airways, off-airway routes, or route segments which
meets obstacle clearance requirements for the entire route
‘segment and which assures acceptable navigational signal
coverage only within 22 NM of a VOR. Thus, ATC may assign the
MOCA as an assigned altitude, but only within 22 NM of a VOR.
explanations.C:
because acceptable navigational signal

coverage at the MOCA is assured for a distance from the VOR of
22 NM, not 25 NM.

questions.question: Which aeronautical chart depicts Military Training Routes (MTR) above 1,500 feet?

answers.A: FR Planning Chart.
answers.B: IFR Low Altitude En Route Chart.
answers.C: IFR High Altitude En Route Chart.

explanations.A:
because the U.S. IFR/VFR Planning

Chart does not depict MTRs. The DOD Area Planning Chart
depicts all MTRs, not only those above 1,500 ft. AGL.
explanations.B:
IFR En Route Low-Altitude Charts depict
all IFR and VFR MTRs (IR and VR routes) that accommodate
operations above 1,500 ft. AGL.
explanations.C:
because IFR En Route High-Altitude

Charts cover altitudes at and above 18,000 ft. MSL; generally,
MTRs are established below 10,000 ft. MSL.

questions.question: The altitude that provides acceptable navigational signal coverage for the route, and meets obstacle clearance requirements is the minimum:

answers.A: obstacle clearance altitude.
answers.B: reception altitude.
answers.C: enroute altitude.

explanations.A:
because the MOCA (minimum
obstruction clearance altitude) only guarantees acceptable
navigational signal coverage and meets obstacle clearance
requirements when within 22 NM of a NAVAID, not along an

entire route that takes the aircraft more than 22 NM froma
NAVAID.
explanations.B:
because the MRA (minimum reception
altitude) is the lowest altitude at which an intersection can be
identified. It is usually higher than the MEA.
explanations.C:
The MEA (minimum en route altitude) is
the lowest published altitude between radio fixes which assures
acceptable navigational signal coverage and meets obstacle
clearance requirements between those fixes.

questions.question: Which condition is guaranteed for all of the following altitude limits: MAA, MCA, MRA, MOCA, and MEA? (Non-mountainous area.)

answers.A: Adequate navigation signals.
answers.B: Adequate communications.
answers.C: 1,000-foot obstacle clearance.

explanations.A:
because the MOCA assures acceptable
navigational signals only within 22 NM of a VOR.
explanations.B:
because the minimum IFR altitudes do
not guarantee adequate communications coverage.
explanations.C:
The MAA, MCA, MRA, MOCA, and MEA
meet the minimum obstacle clearance requirements. In
non-mountainous areas, 1,000 ft. above the highest obstacle is

guaranteed within a horizontal distance of 4 NM from the course
to be flown.

questions.question: Ifno MCA is specified, what is the lowest altitude for crossing a radio fix, beyond which a higher minimum applies?

answers.A: The MEA at which the fix is approached.
answers.B: The MRA at which the fix is approached.
answers.C: The MOCA for the route segment beyond the fix.

explanations.A:
If no MCA (minimum crossing altitude) is
specified, the lowest altitude for crossing a radio fix beyond
which a higher minimum IFR altitude exists is the MEA at which
the fix is approached. A climb must be initiated to a higher
minimum immediately after passing the point beyond which that
minimum altitude applies.
explanations.B:
because, if a higher minimum altitude
exists after the fix and a higher altitude is needed to identify a fix,
usually an MCA, not an MRA, is established at that fix.
explanations.C:
because, if there is no MCA, the higher

minimum altitude does not apply until immediately after passing
the fix.

questions.question: Inthe case of operations over an area designated as a mountainous area, no person may operate an aircraft under IFR below 2,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal distance of

answers.A: 3 SM from the course flown.
answers.B: 4 SM from the course flown.
answers.C: 4.NM from the course flown.

explanations.A:
because the horizontal distance is 4 NM,
not 3 SM, from the course flown.
explanations.B:
because the horizontal distance is 4 NM,
not SM, from the course flown.
explanations.C:
In the case of operations over an area
designated as a mountainous area where no other minimum
altitude is prescribed, no person may operate an aircraft under
IFR below 2,000 ft. above the highest obstacle within a horizontal
distance of 4 NM from the course to be flown.

questions.question: Inthe case of operations over an area designated as a mountainous area where no other minimum altitude is prescribed, no person may operate an aircraft under IFR below an altitude of

answers.A: 500 feet above the highest obstacle.
answers.B: 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle.
answers.C: 2,000 feet above the highest obstacle.

explanations.A:
because no person may operate an
aircraft under IFR below an altitude of 2,000 ft., not 500 ft., above
the highest obstacle in a mountainous area.
explanations.B:
because no person may operate an
aircraft under IFR below an altitude of 1,000 ft. above the highest
obstacle in a nonmountainous, not mountainous, area.
explanations.C:
In the case of operations over an area
designated as a mountainous area where no other minimum
altitude is prescribed, no person may operate an aircraft under
IFR below 2,000 ft. above the highest obstacle within a horizontal
distance of 4 NM from the course to be flown.

questions.question: MEA is an altitude which assures

answers.A: obstacle clearance, accurate navigational signals from more than one VORTAC, and accurate DME mileage.
answers.B: a 1,000-foot obstacle clearance within 2 miles of an airway and assures accurate DME mileage.
answers.C: acceptable navigational signal coverage and meets obstruction clearance requirements.

explanations.A: because only one VORTAC is needed at
explanations.B:
because the clearance is within 4 NM, not
2 mi., and there is no assurance of DME coverage.
explanations.C:
The minimum en route altitude (MEA) is
the lowest published altitude between radio fixes which assures

acceptable navigational signal coverage and meets the obstacle
clearance requirements between those fixes.

questions.question: Unless otherwise specified on the chart, the minimum en route altitude along a jet route is

answers.A: 18,000 feet MSL.
answers.B: 24,000 feet MSL.
answers.C: 10,000 feet MSL.

explanations.A:
Each designated jet route consists of a
direct course for navigating from 18,000 ft. MSL up to and
including FL 450 between the navigational aids and intersections
specified for that route. Thus, the MEA along a jet route is 18,000
ft MSL.
explanations.B:
because 24,000 ft. MSL (FL 240) is the

minimum altitude at which DME is required when navigating by
VOR, not the MEA for a jet route.
explanations.C:
because 10,000 ft. MSL is the minimum

altitude at which aircraft are required to operate the transponder
on Mode C, not the MEA for a jet route.

questions.question: Under which of the following circumstances will ATC issue a VFR restriction to an |FR flight?

answers.A: Whenever the pilot reports the loss of any navigational aid.
answers.B: When it is necessary to provide separation between IFR and special VFR traffic.
answers.C: When the pilot requests it.

explanations.A:
because a pilot would report only a
malfunction of navigation equipment, not a loss of any
navigational aid, to ATC.
explanations.B:
because special VFR traffic would be
found near an airport in Class B, C, or D airspace or Class E
airspace designated for an airport that is currently experiencing
IMC. Thus, ATC would not issue a VFR restriction to an IFR flight.
explanations.C:
VFR-on-top is an ATC authorization for an
IFR aircraft to operate in VFR conditions at any appropriate VFR
altitude. ATC may not authorize VFR-on-top operations unless
the pilot requests the clearance to operate in VFR conditions.

questions.question: What altitude may a pilot select upon receiving a VFR-on-Top clearance?

answers.B: Any appropriate VFR altitude at or above the MEA in VFR weather conditions.
answers.C: Any VFR altitude appropriate for the direction of flight at least 1,000 feet above the meteorological condition.
answers.A: Any altitude at least 1,000 feet above the meteorological condition.

explanations.A:
because, after receiving a VFR-on-top
clearance, the pilot may select any appropriate VFR altitude at or
above the minimum IFR altitude in VMC, not only 1,000 ft. above
the meteorological condition. This may be above, below,
between layers, or in areas where there is no meteorological
obscuration.
explanations.B:
When operating in VMC with an ATC
authorization to “maintain VFR-on-top/maintain VFR conditions,"
pilots on IFR flight plans are required to

1. Fly at the appropriate VFR altitude;

2. Comply with the VFR visibility and distance from clouds
criteria; and
3. Comply with instrument flight rules that are applicable to the

flight, i.e., minimum IFR altitudes, position reporting, course to be
flown, adherence to ATC clearances, etc.
explanations.C:
because, after receiving a VFR-on-top
clearance, the pilot may select any appropriate VFR altitude at or
above the minimum IFR altitude in VMC, not only 1,000 ft. above
the meteorological condition. This may be above, below,

between layers, or in areas where there is no meteorological
obscuration.

questions.question: Which rules apply to the pilot in command when operating on a VFR-on-Top clearance?

answers.A: VER only.
answers.B: VFR and IFR.
answers.C: VFR when “in the clear" and IFR when "in the clouds."

explanations.A:
because an ATC clearance to operate
VFR-on-top does not imply cancellation of the IFR flight plan.
explanations.B:
When operating in VMC with an ATC
authorization to “maintain VFR-on-top/maintain VFR conditions,"
pilots on IFR flight plans are required to

1. Fly at the appropriate VFR altitude;

2. Comply with the VFR visibility and distance from clouds
criteria; and

3. Comply with instrument flight rules that are applicable to the
flight, i.e., minimum IFR altitudes, position reporting, course to be
flown, adherence to ATC clearances, etc.
explanations.C:
because a VFR-on-top clearance is
issued when the pilot is in VMC and must remain in VMC unless

the VFR-on-top clearance is canceled. It does not allow a pilot to
fly in IMC.

questions.question: Which ATC clearance should instrument-rated pilots request in order to climb through a cloud layer or an area of reduced visibility and then continue the flight VFR?

answers.B: Special VFR to VFR Over-the-Top.
answers.C: VFR Over-the-Top.
answers.A: To VFR on Top.

explanations.A:
Pilots desiring to climb through a cloud,
haze, smoke, or other meteorological formation and then either
cancel their IFR flight plan or operate VFR-on-top may request an
ATC clearance to climb to VFR-on-top.
explanations.B:
because a special VFR clearance is
issued only in Class B, C, or D airspace or Class E airspace

designated for an airport, and the pilot must remain clear of
clouds, not climb through them.
explanations.C:
because it is VFR-on-top, not
VFR-over-the-top.

questions.question: When can a VFR-on-Top clearance be assigned by ATC?

answers.A: Only upon request of the pilot when conditions are indicated to be suitable.
answers.B: Any time suitable conditions exist and ATC wishes to expedite traffic flow.
answers.C: When VFR conditions exist, but there is a layer of clouds below the MEA.

explanations.A:
ATC may assign a VFR-on-top clearance
only when the pilot requests such a clearance, and the flight must
be conducted in VFR weather conditions.
explanations.B:
because ATC can issue a VFR-on-top
clearance only upon a pilot's, not ATC’s, request.
explanations.C:
because ATC can issue a VFR-on-top

clearance only upon a pilot's request; clearance is not based only
on the meteorological conditions.

questions.question: When ona VFR-on-Top clearance, the cruising altitude is based on

answers.B: magnetic course.
answers.C: magnetic heading.
answers.A: true course.

explanations.A:
because VFR cruising altitudes are
based on magnetic, not true, course.
explanations.B:
While operating under a VFR-on-top

clearance, you must fly at the appropriate VFR altitude, which is
based on magnetic course.
explanations.C:
because VFR cruising altitudes are
based on magnetic course, not heading.

questions.question: When must a pilot fly at a cardinal altitude plus 500 feet on an IFR flight plan?

answers.A: When flying above 18,000 feet in VFR conditions.
answers.B: When flying in VFR conditions above clouds.
answers.C: When assigned a VFR-on-Top clearance.

explanations.A:
because VFR-on-top is not permitted in

Class A airspace, which is from 18,000 ft. MSL to and including
FL 600.
explanations.B:
because a pilot on an IFR flight plan uses
VFR altitudes only when assigned a VFR-on-top clearance.
explanations.C:
VFR-on-top clearances are flown at VFR
altitudes, which are even or odd thousand-foot intervals plus 500
ft. This is in contrast to IFR altitudes that are at even or odd
thousand-foot intervals. Cardinal altitude means 1,000-ft.
intervals, e.g., 3,000, 4,000, etc.

questions.question: Where are VFR-on-Top operations prohibited?

answers.A: In Class A airspace.
answers.B: During off-airways direct flights.
answers.C: When flying through Class B airspace.

explanations.A:
ATC will not authorize VFR or VFR-on-top
operations in Class A airspace.
explanations.B:
because VFR-on-top operations during
off-airway direct flights are not prohibited.
explanations.C:
because VFR-on-top operations within
Class B airspace are permitted.

questions.question: You have filed an IFR flight plan with a VFR-on-Top clearance in lieu of an assigned altitude. If you receive this clearance and fly a course of 180°, at what altitude should you fly? (Assume VFR conditions.)

answers.A: Any IFR altitude which will enable you to remain in VFR conditions.
answers.B: An odd thousand-foot MSL altitude plus 500 feet.
answers.C: An even thousand-foot MSL altitude plus 500 feet.

explanations.A:
because, on VFR-on-top, one uses VFR,
not IFR, altitudes.
explanations.B:
because odd thousand-foot altitudes plus
500 ft. are for a magnetic course of 0° through 179°, not 180°.
explanations.C:
When operating in VMC with a
VFR-on-top clearance, you must fly at the appropriate VFR
cruising altitude. On a magnetic course of 180° through 359°, an
even thousand-foot MSL altitude plus 500 ft. must be flown.

questions.question: What minimums must be considered in selecting an altitude when operating with a VFR-on-Top clearance?

answers.B: At least 1,000 feet above the lowest MEA, appropriate MOCA, or existing meteorological condition.
answers.C: Minimum IFR altitude, minimum distance from clouds, and visibility appropriate to altitude selected.
answers.A: Atleast 500 feet above the lowest MEA, or appropriate MOCA, and at least 1,000 feet above the existing meteorological condition.

explanations.A:
because you must be at or above, not a
specified distance from, the minimum IFR altitude, and while ona
VFR-on-top clearance, you may operate above, below, or
between layers of, not only above, the existing meteorological
condition.
explanations.B:
because you must be at or above, not a
specified distance from, the minimum IFR altitude, and while on a
VFR-on-top clearance, you may operate above, below, or

between layers of, not only above, the existing meteorological
condition.
explanations.C:
When operating in VMC with an ATC
authorization to "maintain VFR-on-top/maintain VFR conditions,”
pilots on IFR flight plans are required to

1. Fly at the appropriate VFR altitude;

2. Comply with the VFR visibility and distance from clouds
criteria; and

3. Comply with instrument flight rules that are applicable to the
flight, ie., minimum IFR altitudes, position reporting, course to be
flown, adherence to ATC clearances, etc.

questions.question: If, while in Class E airspace, a clearance is received to "maintain VFR conditions on top," the pilot should maintain a VFR cruising altitude based on the direction of the

answers.A: true course.
answers.B: magnetic heading.
answers.C: magnetic course.

explanations.A:
because VFR cruising altitudes are
based on magnetic, not true, course.
explanations.B:
because VFR cruising altitudes are
based on magnetic course, not heading.
explanations.C:
While operating under a VFR-on-top

clearance, you must fly at the appropriate VFR cruising altitude,
which is based on magnetic course.

questions.question: In which airspace is VFR-on-Top operation prohibited?

answers.A: Class B airspace.
answers.B: Class E airspace.
answers.C: Class A airspace.

explanations.A:
because VFR-on-top operations are
permitted, not prohibited, in Class B airspace.
explanations.B:
because VFR-on-top operations are
permitted, not prohibited, in Class E airspace.
explanations.C:
ATC will not authorize VFR or VFR-on-top
operations in Class A airspace.

questions.question: What cruising altitude is appropriate for VFR on Top on a westbound flight below 18,000 feet?

answers.B: Even thousand-foot levels plus 500 feet, but not below MEA.
answers.C: Odd thousand-foot levels plus 500 feet, but not below MEA.
answers.A: Even thousand-foot levels.

explanations.A:
because an even thousand-foot level is
anlFR, not VFR, cruising altitude for a westbound flight.
\VFR-on-top clearances must maintain VFR altitudes.
explanations.B:
When operating in VMC with a VFR-on-top

clearance, you must fly at the appropriate VFR cruising altitude
but not below the minimum IFR altitude (e.g., MEA). Ona

magnetic course of 180° through 359° (i.e., westbound), an even
thousand-foot MSL altitude plus 500 ft. must be flown.
explanations.C:
because an odd thousand-foot level plus

500 ft. is for eastbound, not westbound, flight or a magnetic
course from 0° to 179°.

questions.question: What reports are required of a flight operating on an IFR clearance specifying VER on Top in a nonradar environment?

answers.A: The same reports that are required for any IFR flight.
answers.B: All normal IFR reports except vacating altitudes.
answers.C: Only the reporting of any unforecast weather.

explanations.A:
When on a VFR-on-top clearance, you
must comply with instrument flight rules that are applicable to the
flight, e.g., minimum flight altitudes, position reporting, radio
communications, course to be flown, adherence to ATC
communications, etc.
explanations.B:
because all normal IFR reports are

required when operating on a VFR-on-top clearance. You should

advise ATC prior to any altitude change to ensure the exchange
of accurate traffic information.
explanations.C:
because all IFR reports, not only

unforecast weather, must be made while operating on a
VFR-on-top clearance.

questions.question: When operating under IFR with a VFR-On-Top clearance, what altitude should be maintained?

answers.A: An FR cruising altitude appropriate to the magnetic course being flown.
answers.B: A VFR cruising altitude appropriate to the magnetic course being flown and as restricted by ATC.
answers.C: The last IFR altitude assigned by ATC.

explanations.A:
because pilots operating with a
VFR-on-top clearance should maintain a VFR, not an IFR,
cruising altitude appropriate to the magnetic course being flown.
explanations.B:
When operating in VMC with an ATC authorization to 6mé|
VFR-on-top/maintain VFR conditions,= pilots on IFR flight plans are required to

1. Fly at the appropriate UFR altitude;

2. Comply with the UFR visibility and distance from clouds criteri

3. Comply with instrument flight rules that are applicable to the
i.e., minimum IFR altitudes, position reporting, course to be
adherence to ATC clearances, etc.
explanations.C:
because pilots operating with a

VFR-on-top clearance should maintain a VFR, not anIFR,
cruising altitude.

because the COP is 50 NM west, not

the prescribed COP.

On Fig. 87, when flying east on V306 from

indicated by the symbol "hn", and the mileages are given to each
VORTAC station. The COP is 30 NM east of Daisetta and 50

questions.question: =<——= a 30. (Refer to figure 87.) At STRUT intersection headed eastbound, ATC instructs you to hold west on the 10 DME fix west of LCH on V306, standard turns. What entry procedure is recommended?

answers.A: Direct.
answers.B: Teardrop.
answers.C: Parallel.

explanations.A:
You are instructed to hold west at the 10
DME fix west of LCH VORTAC on V306. Since you are at
STRUT int, flying eastbound on V306, you should make a direct
entry to a heading of 265°. Since the direction of turn was not

specified, you should make right turns, which is a standard
holding pattern.
explanations.B:
because a teardrop entry may be used if

because a parallel entry may be used if

because ILS course symbols, not LDA,

function.

When a localizer course symbol is shown
on a low altitude en route chart, this indicates that the published
ILS localizer has a navigation function in addition to course
guidance. The localizer at Jefferson County Airport, which is

MARSA intersections. See Legend 23.
explanations.C:
because ILS course symbols, not SDF,

function.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 87.) Which VHF frequencies, other than 121.5, can be used to teceive De Ridder FSS in the Lake Charles area?

explanations.A:
because neither 122.1 nor 126.4 is an

questions.question: (Refer to figure 87.) Why is the localizer back course at Jefferson County Airport depicted?

answers.A: The back course is not aligned with a runway.
answers.B: The back course has a glide slope.
answers.C: The back course has an additional navigation function.

because the back course symbol

suggests an ILS localizer front course, which is always aligned

because a LOC back course never has a
glide slope.

Jefferson County Airport in Beaumont, TX
is located near the center of Fig. 87. The extended localizer
course symbol shown there applies to this question. This symbol
indicates that there is a published ILS localizer course with an
additional navigation function. The arrow is further identified (on

questions.question: (Refer to figure 87.) Where is the VOR changeover point on V20 between Beaumont and Hobby?

because MOCKS INT is 25 NM from

because Anahuac Beacon is not on the
airway.

questions.question: inthe event of two-way radio communications failure while operating on an IFR clearance in VFR conditions, the pilot should continue

answers.B: the flight under VFR and land as soon as practical.
answers.C: the flight by the most direct route to the fix specified in the last Clearance.

explanations.A:
because, if the failure occurs in IFR, not

questions.question: On what frequency should you obtain En Route Flight Advisory Service below FL 180?

explanations.A:
because 122.1T/112.8R is an example of
communicating with an FSS through a VOR, not the EFAS
frequency below FL 180.
explanations.B:
because you would use 122.0, not 123.6,
to contact EFAS below FL 180.
explanations.C:
En Route Flight Advisory Service (EFAS)
is a service specifically designed to provide en route aircraft with
timely and meaningful weather advisories pertinent to the type of
flight intended, route of flight, and altitude. EFAS is normally
available from 6:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m. EFAS provides
communications capabilities for aircraft flying at 5,000 ft. AGL to
17,500 ft. MSL on a common frequency of 122.0 MHz.

questions.question: law of: 45. (Refer to figure 91.) What are the two limiting cruising altitudes useable on V343 for a VFR-on-Top flight from DBS VORTAC to RANEY intersection?

explanations.A:
because the appropriate VFR-on-top
altitudes for a magnetic course of 008° are odd, not even,
thousand-foot altitudes plus 500 ft. Also, 14,500 ft. is below the

MEA.
explanations.B:
because VFR-on-top altitudes are
cardinal (1,000, 2,000, etc.) plus 500 ft.
explanations.C:
In Fig. 91, a flight from DBS VORTAC to
RANEY intersection on V343 has an MEA of 15,000 ft. A flight
with a clearance of VFR-on-top will operate at appropriate VFR
cruising altitudes, at or above the minimum IFR altitude. Ona
magnetic course of 008°, you must be at an odd thousand-foot
altitude plus 500 ft. Thus, a VFR-on-top flight is limited to only
15,500 ft. and 17,500 ft. You cannot operate VFR in Class A
airspace, i.e., 18,000 ft. MSL to FL 600.
